title: Employee Reactions to Corporate Misconduct: Evidence from Em...
speaker: Lars Gemmer
abstract: This study examines how employees respond to corporate misconduct when expressing opinions on online employer review platforms, and whether firms can influence these reactions through active response strategies. While prior research has extensively documented external stakeholder reactions to corporate wrongdoing, employee responses remain underexplored—despite employees’ dual role as internal stakeholders and external brand ambassadors. We address this gap using a large-scale dataset that combines more than 100,000 employer reviews from a major European platform with over 2,000 globally reported misconduct incidents. The study pursues three objectives: (1) to assess how employee-related versus non-employee-related misconduct affects the volume and valence of employer reviews; (2) to identify the psychological mechanisms underlying these reactions; and (3) to examine whether firms can mitigate negative employee responses through active management of their employer review profiles. Using a monthly panel of 867 firms from 2007 to 2021, we analyze review volume, ratings, and textual content with fixed-effects regressions and LLM-based text classifiers. Results reveal strong asymmetries: employee-related misconduct leads to sharp and persistent declines in review volume and valence, driven by current employees and lasting up to 24 months. In contrast, non-employee-related misconduct generates only small, short-lived declines. Textual evidence indicates psychological contract breach as the dominant mechanism. Importantly, firms can fully offset long-run negative effects through active review management, frequent responses, and substantive reply content. Overall, employer review platforms emerge as critical arenas for managing employee perceptions and reputational risk following corporate misconduct.

title: Chatgpt Referrals to E-Commerce Websites: How Do LLMs Compar...
speaker: Maximilian Kaiser
abstract: We investigate organic Large Language Model traffic (oLLM) versus traditional digital channels in e-commerce. Analyzing 12 months of first-party data from 973 websites with $20 billion combined revenue, we examine over 50,000 transactions from ChatGPT referrals alongside 164 million transactions from traditional channels. Using regression models that account for data sparsity, we assess financial metrics (conversion rate, average order value, revenue per session) and engagement metrics (bounce rate, session duration, page views). Results are consistent across extensive robustness checks. One year after launch, oLLM exhibits conversion rates and revenue per session above paid social but below all other traditional channels. Product complexity moderates the effects: oLLM's financial outcomes and traffic shares are stronger in complex product categories. Engagement metrics show favorable bounce rates but lower session duration and page views. Temporal analysis shows increasing conversion rates but declining average order values, yielding only moderate revenue-per-session gains over time. Cross-website analyses support growing consumer LLM proficiency as the underlying mechanism. The descriptive analyses position oLLM as a new and developing channel. With low volumes and modest revenue per session, oLLM currently serves niche informational needs of proficient consumers and does not yet function as a broad conversion channel.

title: Winning the Chatbot: How Businesses Can Optimize Content for...
speaker: Gabriela Makar
abstract: Conversational AI is transforming online search. Instead of browsing “ten blue links,” users increasingly rely on chatbots that deliver synthesized, interactive answers. This shift creates new challenges for businesses, where visibility directly drives success. Yet, even in traditional search engines, competition is intense: rankings fluctuate, zero-click searches are rising, and algorithms disproportionately favor large brands, making it harder for smaller firms to stand out. We propose a novel content generation workflow for businesses’ websites, designed to improve visibility in large language model (LLM)–driven search systems. Building on established insights from SEO, our approach iteratively tunes the focal company’s website content against top-ranked outputs for given prompts, automatically aligning text with LLM-specific optimality factors. Experiments with industry partners demonstrate that optimized content can significantly boost visibility across LLM-based platforms. Crucially, our findings show that success in classic Google rankings does not guarantee success in generative search: visibility differs widely across models (e.g., strong presence in Perplexity but little to none in Gemini). Our research contributes conceptually by introducing a novel generative workflow for LLM content optimization, and practically by providing businesses with actionable methods to secure visibility in conversational search environments where classical SEO alone is no longer sufficient.

title: Mind the Gap: How Repositioning Alters Brand Representations...
speaker: Andreas Hamann
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly emerging as new touchpoints in the customer journey, shaping how consumers discover and evaluate brands. Yet, little is known about how LLMs adjust brand representations and recommendations when firms engage in strategic brand meaning-changing actions. In this study, the authors examine how LLMs update brand portrayals following a repositioning. They show that, unlike consumers, LLMs do not learn from gradual exposure but construct brand representations through the retrieval and synthesis of external information at the moment of response. Findings of a controlled synthetic field experiment in which they systematically vary repositioning behavior across brands and track their LLM representations over time align with theoretical predictions. First, LLMs differ systematically in how quickly and accurately they reflect repositioned brand positions. Second, repositionings temporarily reduce brand salience in LLM recommendations. Third, firms can influence LLM-based brand representations by managing how repositioning information becomes retrievable, such as through repositioning communication cues and indexing mechanisms, with effectiveness depending on whether the LLMs rely on cached or real-time information sources. Theoretically, these findings extend traditional positioning theory on brand meaning formation to generative AI-mediated contexts. Managerially, they provide guidance for managing LLM-based brand visibility during major strategic brand changes.

title: Does AI Displace OR Complement Web Traffic?
speaker: Carlo Reggiani
abstract: We investigate whether generative AI features in search engines, specifically Google's AI Overviews, displace or complement traffic to online publishers. Using web traffic data from July 2022 to December 2025 and exploiting the staggered global rollout of the feature, the authors find that AI Overviews are associated with a decline in visits and unique visitors, particularly for websites highly dependent on search traffic. However, the study also notes that while traffic volume decreases, the remaining user behavior becomes more targeted with less exploratory browsing, suggesting that AI summaries improve search efficiency and matching quality.

title: Strategic Design of Shopping LLMs Under Prompt-Induced Evalu...
speaker: Weize Yin
abstract: We study how to strategically control prompt sensitivity in shopping large language models (LLMs) when their product evaluations shape consumer demand and market outcomes. Through controlled experiments, we document a prompt-induced evaluation gap: meaning-preserving syntactic variations in consumer prompts systematically shift LLM product evaluations. Using an analytical model, we then find that eliminating the evaluation gap is not universally optimal. With a monopoly seller, a nonzero evaluation gap can benefit consumer surplus by increasing dispersion in the distribution of willingness to pay. With duopoly sellers, a nonzero evaluation gap can increase total seller profit by mitigating price competition. Finally, using an inference-time intervention that steers the LLM’s internal representations, we show that the evaluation gap is controllable. Overall, this paper shows that the prompt-induced evaluation gap can be strategically managed in shopping LLM design.

title: Can Explanations Improve Recommendations? Evidence from Pred...
speaker: Yuyan Wang
abstract: Modern recommender systems rely on large-scale ML models that are data-hungry and black-box. Recent advances in LLMs suggest that explicit reasoning can improve learning efficiency, yet it remains unclear how generative LLMs can systematically improve recommendation tasks that are discriminative in nature. Moreover, in personalized settings, LLMs tend to hallucinate. Existing explainable recommender systems either generate explanations independently of predictions or provide post-hoc rationales; in both cases, explanations do not improve accuracy over black-box recommenders. We argue that when properly calibrated to prediction outcomes, natural-language explanations can in fact improve recommendations. We propose RecPIE (Recommendation with PredictionInformed Explanations), a framework that jointly optimizes predictioninformed explanations and explanation-informed predictions. In RecPIE, the recommendation task guides the learning of consumer representations, which are used by a trainable LLM to generate explanations for why a consumer may or may not like a product; these explanations are then fed back into a neural recommender to improve predictions. The two components are trained alternately, allowing explanations to be progressively refined based on how much they improve recommendation accuracy. Empirically, on next point-of-interest recommendation using Google Maps data, RecPIE improves accuracy by 3–4% over state-of-the-art baselines and matches the best baseline using only 12% of the training data. Human evaluations show that RecPIE’s explanations are preferred 61.5% of the time among five competing methods. To our knowledge, this work is among the first to demonstrate that generative explanation and discriminative recommendation tasks can be jointly learned to outperform standalone approaches on either task.

title: Content Characteristics, Plan Design, and User Engagement on...
speaker: Vineet Kumar
abstract: We investigate the impact of exogenously varying plan tiers on engagement in a moving‑arts instructional platform. Specifically, we study how video‑level content characteristics mediate user engagement under different free‑access tiers (corresponding to free minutes per video). Users are randomized to a tier; engagement is measured by time spent per class and premium conversion. Human‑interpretable features (e.g., motion density, hand‑gestures, speech rate) are extracted via machine learning techniques. To estimate the causal effect of plan tier while controlling for a high‑dimensional set of content covariates, we use double machine learning (DML). Outcome regressions are estimated with regularized learners to evaluate the impact of different content features based on plan tiers. Overall, we evaluate and contrast the engagement of free and premium users, as well as the kinds of videos that drive such engagement across tiers.

title: From Reviews to Responses: Bridging Pre- and Post-Purchase C...
speaker: Ishita Chakraborty
abstract: Question Answering (QA) on customer-facing platforms (e-commerce, travel, education, and brand websites) often suffers from delayed, low-quality responses and limited user participation. While customer reviews are abundant, their unstructured nature limits direct use to answer specific questions, and Large Language Models (LLMs) alone lack product-specific details and subjective insights. To address these challenges, we propose and evaluate a novel QA framework that integrates LLMs with reviews through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Our framework incorporates three components: (1) RAG for dynamically retrieving relevant reviews at inference time; (2) a question–review type matching module that enhances topical alignment; (3) an answerability classifier that determines whether a reliable answer can be generated. Using a data set of 500 Amazon questions, 2000+ human responses, and 14,000  review sentences, we systematically evaluate different model variants for both lexical similarity metrics (ROUGE-L) and human judgments. Our full model improves lexical similarity scores by 50% from baseline LLM answers, matches or exceeds 72% of human responses, and approaches the best human answers in clarity, relevance, and informativeness. In particular, human evaluations show that our full model performs particularly well on subjective questions and lexical similarity metrics fail to capture this performance gain. Overall, our findings show how LLMs and reviews can be combined to build scalable QA systems, while also revealing the limits of lexical similarity metrics and highlighting the importance of human-centered evaluation.

title: Looking for Creative Insights in Tight Spaces: Human vs. AI-...
speaker: Demetrios Vakratsas
abstract: Although the literature on the impact of AI on advertising is growing, most studies focus on the effect of AI on advertising production quality. Less is known about how AI can contribute to generating creative advertising ideas, in other words how AI can become truly creative rather than being merely generative. In this study we evaluate the novelty of human vs AI-generated advertising ideas. We focus on metaphor-based advertising, which has been shown to be a popular and effective style for advertisers. We evaluate the novelty of an advertising idea based on the novelty of the metaphor vehicle used to represent a product attribute or benefit (e.g. volcano to represent spicy flavor). We compare 2,380 pairs of human and AI-generated metaphor ideas. Human ideas are extracted from actual ads launched before the emergence of LLMs. We find that AI-generated ideas are more novel than human-generated ones when the metaphor vehicle choice is constrained (e.g. the vehicle for a food product should be food-related) and when the product attribute advertised is more concrete (e.g. chocolatey vs desirable). We attribute the better performance of AI-generated ideas under constraints to the lack of limitations in cognitive resources, which are required to solve constrained problems. In the case of advertising, constraints can play a critical role since they are frequently imposed by advertisers or agency strategists in creative briefs. The findings of our study suggest that AI can be used to increase the novelty of ideas and aid humans in solving constrained creative problems.

title: Synthesizing Customer Journeys to Optimize Media Mix: A Mult...
abstract: This research answers the key question: Do individual-level customer journeys provide any additional value in guiding a firm’s media mix allocation, especially with missing touchpoints? Compared to MMM with aggregate data only, can one obtain a better estimate of outcome–spending elasticity by taking into account how lower-level customer journeys form under different spending levels? This paper provides a transformer-based integrated framework that incorporates both granular journey data and aggregate media mix data to guide firms’ media mix allocation. Multimodal transformers are designed to capture the relationship between two modalities, such as text and image. The concomitant variations between a firm’s media mix allocation and the touchpoints in customer journeys make it possible to use a multimodal transformer to capture the relationship between the two—for example, when spending on search increases, more search touchpoints appear in customer journeys. When planning future allocations to optimize outcomes, the model is able to generate customer journeys conditional on a media mix allocation, similar to an LLM generating text conditional on contextual image input. We develop an adapted REINFORCE algorithm to optimize the media mix allocation so that the model-generated journeys reflect the most desired outcome. Another key contribution of the method is its ability to handle missing touchpoints in customer journeys. To demonstrate the model’s validity, we conduct a simulation study and apply the framework to an empirical dataset, while comparing with MMM from industry benchmarks. Results show superior performance in estimating spending–outcome elasticity and optimizing media mix.

title: Generative AI Risk Assessment Model for the Media Sector
speaker: Christine Balague
abstract: The rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has transformed various economic sectors and introduced significant risks that remain insufficiently understood. This study focuses on GenAI risks in the media industry. It applies the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) risk framework to GAI, structuring risk assessment through three primary determinants: exposure, hazard, and vulnerability. We propose that exposure to GAI risks in the media sector encompasses information integrity, copyright material, privacy concerns, safety, content integrity, environmental impacts, and unemployment. The hazards of GAI include opacity, failure in reliability, poor data quality, misuse of training data, inadequate validity checks, and coding errors. Finally, vulnerability is conceptualized through affected stakeholders, encompassing individuals, businesses, policymakers, and broader societal institutions. Our analysis leverages real-world incidents from the OECD AI Incident Monitoring (AIM) database to illustrate how the IPCC framework can offer a structured, quantifiable, and policy-relevant perspective on GAI risks. This study aims to help policymakers, corporations, AI developers, and researchers, by providing  a systematic methodology for risk assessment, guiding regulatory choices, and formulating responsible AI governance initiatives.

title: AI Adoption Readiness in Marketing
speaker: Ke Li
abstract: With rapid development in artificial intelligence and firms’ increasing investments in marketing through AI which is changing the competition landscape, this study explores how the adoption of different types of AI applications in different industry impact marketing efficiency for companies with different sizes. Our study helps companies to understand the customer experience in the new digital interactions, to recognize the under-engaged organizational systems, and to prepare organizational change to adopt AI-driven insights and solutions so as to maintain competitive advantage.

title: Bull vs. Bear Voices: Adapting Service Communication Strateg...
speaker: Ye Zheng
abstract: This study investigates how stock market volatility fundamentally alters the effectiveness of service representatives' vocal cues on customer loyalty. By linking macro-economic health to micro-interpersonal dynamics, the research explores how market fluctuations prime customers with a "distorted mindset" characterised by financial threat and cognitive scarcity. Moving beyond self-reported surveys, we utilise actual net investment activity to measure behavioural loyalty in a high-stakes context. The methodology combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with advanced audio mining tools to analyse over 2,000 call recordings from an Australian investment company between 2019 and 2021. The findings reveal that the optimal vocal strategy relies entirely on market conditions. During positive ("Bull") markets, when customers focus on aspiration, vocal warmth significantly increases loyalty among stressed clients. However, this dynamic inverts during "Bear" markets. In downturns, stressed customers shift toward "security and loss-avoidance" to conserve resources; consequently, warmth becomes ineffective. Instead, vocal competence emerges as the primary driver of retention, likely because it restores a sense of agency to customers feeling a loss of control. These results challenge "one-size-fits-all" empathy training, suggesting financial firms should instead implement "Dynamic Scripting" and AI-driven vocal routing to match agent styles with the prevailing economic environment.

title: Vertical Generative AI (Vai) Development, Openness, and Data...
speaker: Junhao Li
abstract: Vertical Generative AI (VAI) fine-tunes foundation models on proprietary, industry-specific data, enabling capabilities beyond “plug-and-play” generic AI. However, the development firm faces several development and operational strategy choices, each with its own advantages and disadvantages: closed strategy (own data, self-used), openness strategy (own data, open-used), or data sharing strategy (pooled data, open-used). This paper extends the Salop model to analyze a mass firm’s VAI development strategy under asymmetric competition with niche firms. Compared with the closed strategy, the openness strategy can generate additional revenue. And the pooling effect of the data sharing strategy can be further profitable, but it may also erode the mass firm’s competitive advantage. We show that final equilibrium strategy choice depends jointly on data contribution and data processing cost. When data processing cost is moderate, the mass firm prefers closed strategy when data contribution is either sufficiently low or sufficiently high, reflecting a trade-off between the competitive-advantage effect and the openness-revenue effect. Counterintuitively, data sharing may induces a low innovation trap of VAI performance because of crowding-out effect: additional data can dilute fine-tuning effort investment, lowering performance despite larger training datasets. Moreover, Niche firms are disadvantaged under closed strategy but benefit from both openness and data sharing strategies, explaining their stronger incentives to collaborate. Finally, when data-processing cost is low and data contribution is moderate, the data sharing strategy yields a win–win–win outcome for the mass firm, niche firms, and consumers.

title: The Ever-Evolving Online Customer Journey: Bridging Academic...
speaker: Amir Khan
abstract: The online customer journey has evolved into a non-linear and dynamic process that is constantly being shaped by digital environments, platforms and frequently shifting customer expectations. In the era of agentic ecosystem, consumers travel with their digital proxies, giving more control to their AI agents (Becca Coggins, 2025). Future interactions will increasingly be between consumer agents and merchants’ agents, leading to multi-agent interactions in the agentic world (McKinsey, 2025). Online Consumer buying, controlled by AI agents acting on behalf on consumers, will have a huge impact on the online market. Human thinking may increasingly be surrendered to AI-negotiated deals. In this agentic driven-economy, brands will have to make major shifts in their approach to creating, positioning and delivering highly personalised customer journey experiences. These changes will no longer be limited to product evaluation by consumer agents but will also impact companies’ customer acquisition and retention systems, as AI agents will become new gatekeepers in the evolving customer journey (Marie Claude Nadeau, 2025) This study conducts a systematic review of academic and industry publications to synthesise current knowledge and identify key conceptual and empirical gaps in the understanding of the online customer journey. While Industry research explains practical approaches that combine analytics with customer touchpoint management, it still lacks strong theoretical grounding, whereas academic research provides conceptual depth but insufficient detail on rapidly evolving digital practices.

title: Platform Levers for Copyright Compliance in Generative AI: E...
speaker: Vincent Lefrere
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) platforms significantly expand opportunities for scalable, user-driven innovation while simultaneously raising concerns about intellectual property (IP) infringement. This paper examines how strategic platform design, particularly monetization policies, can influence user behavior in ways that reduce the risk of IP violations. Using observational data and quasi-experimental variation from a leading GenAI image-generation platform, we conduct both platform-level and user-level event studies, supported by Difference-in-Differences (DiD) analyses, to evaluate user responses to the removal and temporary reintroduction of free trials. Our findings show that requiring users to pay for access leads them to produce more differentiated outputs, thereby reducing visual similarity to existing online content that could be protected by copyright. Crucially, these changes persist even within fixed prompt topics, suggesting that the behavioral shift reflects genuine adjustments in user strategies rather than changes in the types of tasks being performed. These results underscore the importance of user agency and strategic prompting as internal mechanisms for managing copyright risk within GenAI ecosystems. We finally propose a governance approach that combines incentive-aligned nudges with technical safeguards, offering actionable insights for platform designers, IP policymakers, and managers seeking to promote responsible GenAI adoption in digital innovation environments.

title: Restructuring Frontline Communication: Evidence from a Field...
speaker: Yifan Pan
abstract: Digital marketing research and practice have largely emphasized online tools such as targeting algorithms and AI-driven personalization. In contrast, we provide field evidence that seemingly low-technology and low-cost marketing tools can exert substantial effects when they reshape the structure of frontline work. We study a randomized field experiment conducted in collaboration with a global leading automobile manufacturer, in which a randomly selected half of sales consultants at automobile dealerships were provided with a simple printed one-page product information sheet. Importantly, the content on the sheet consists entirely of information that sales consultants are required to communicate to customers even in the absence of the tool. Process evidence from speech transcripts of follow-up calls shows that the mechanism does not operate through increased information exposure or stronger consumer recall. Instead, the printed one-page sheet improves sales performance by restructuring sales communication, with spillover effects on subsequent sales behaviors and follow-up interactions. By externalizing and stabilizing information organization, the tool increases communication fluency and helps sales consultants develop more structured interaction rhythms. Treatment effects are heterogeneous across sales consultants. Using synthetic difference-in-differences and causal forest methods, we show that the intervention significantly benefits consultants with high latent conversion potential but relatively unstructured communication practices, while yielding only marginal improvements for moderately structured consultants. Our findings highlight the importance of alignment between marketing tools and workers’ existing communication structures, and suggest that the value of marketing interventions lies not only in technological sophistication, but in how they reorganize frontline decision-making and work.

title: ***Canceled***Limitations of AI Technology or Consumer Bias?...
speaker: Haoqi Lu
abstract: With the widespread application of generative AI technology in advertising, consumer acceptance of its generated content has become a hot topic. Based on the ABC attitude model and attribution theory, this study explores the mechanisms by which generative AI aversion, generated ad quality, and task context influence consumer attitudes toward advertising. A questionnaire survey collected 237 valid data points, and analysis using structural equation modeling and paired-sample t-tests revealed that the quality of AI-generated ads is a core factor in shaping consumers' positive advertising attitudes. Consequently, this study proposes that reducing consumers' aversion to generative AI, segmenting different consumer decision-making scenarios, and enhancing ad quality through human-machine co-creation can improve consumer attitudes toward generative AI ads. This, in turn, helps advertising practitioners cope with the challenges brought about by technological change and provides theoretical support and practical guidance for the application of generative AI in the advertising industry.

title: How Consumers Respond to AI- Versus Human-Generated Review S...
speaker: Shaowei Chai
abstract: While AI-generated review summaries are increasingly prevalent on digital platforms, their influence on consumer behavior remains insufficiently understood. This research examines when and why AI-generated review summaries outperform human-generated ones under two common probability formats: verbal probabilities (e.g., most) and numerical probabilities (e.g., 89%). Across four studies, we demonstrate that when review summaries are presented in verbal probability, consumers respond more positively to AI-generated summaries than to human-generated ones. In contrast, when the review summaries are presented in numerical probability, the difference in consumer responses between AI-generated summaries and human-generated ones is not significant. This occurs because consumers infer that humans, when using verbal probability to generate review summaries, are prone to making subjective judgment and overestimation to promote consumers’ purchase behavior (Collins & Mandel, 2019; Dhami & Mandel, 2022). In contrast, AI agents, perceived as less mindful and with limited experience and agency capacity (Gray et al., 2007; Gray & Wegner, 2012), are less likely to make subjective judgment when generating review summaries using verbal probability, thereby increasing consumers’ perceived objectiveness and trust for the AI-generated summaries, and thus eliciting more positive consumer responses. Our findings differ from prior research showing that consumers hold negative attitudes toward AI because it has limited capacities for experience and agency. This research advances literature on AI-human communication, AI adoption, and probability expressions of uncertainty, and further offers actionable guidance for marketers deploying AI in dispersive information communication.

title: When AI Reconfigures Status Coping: Social Status Threats an...
speaker: Nan-Hee Jeong
abstract: Individuals frequently experience threats to their social status through upward social comparison and often respond with compensatory behaviors aimed at restoring threatened self-worth, power, or social standing (Gal 2015). Extending this literature, Goor, Keinan, and Ordabayeva (2021) proposed status pivoting, whereby individuals cope with status threats by seeking affirmation in alternative life domains, guided by motivated trade-off beliefs that construe success as zero-sum across domains. As social interaction increasingly occurs within AI-mediated metaverse environments, it remains unclear whether such compensatory mechanisms generalize beyond the real world. Unlike offline contexts, the metaverse is shaped by intelligent systems that curate social information and mediate evaluations (Barrera and Shah 2023), potentially altering how social status threats are interpreted. Across two experiments, we examine whether status pivoting persists in AI-mediated metaverse contexts relative to the real world. Study 1 employed a 2 (context) × 2 (power) between-subjects design and revealed a significant interaction (b = −2.08, p < .01). Low-power participants in the real world pivoted toward alternative domains, whereas no such effect emerged in the metaverse. Study 2 replicated these findings using a 2 (context) × 2 (status threat) design, again showing attenuated status pivoting in the metaverse (b = −1.37, p < .05). Mediation analyses (Hayes and Scharkow 2013) showed that motivated trade-off beliefs accounted for this divergence. By conceptualizing the metaverse as an AI-mediated social environment, this research identifies a boundary condition for status pivoting and demonstrates how AI reshapes responses to social status threats.

title: Understanding the Dynamics of User-Bot-Crowd Interaction in ...
speaker: Xupin Zhang
abstract: With the growing commercialization of social media platforms and the increasingly prominent role of algorithmic gatekeeping, users’ motivation to create content and interact with others has declined. To promote user participation and sustain engagement, more platforms have turned to social robots. Yet, previous research has not systematically examined the dynamic structure of user-robot-crowd interaction, leaving the mechanisms of diffusion and influence insufficiently understood. Using publicly available interaction data collected from the Weibo social robot “CommentRobert” between December 2023 and April 2025, we applied large language models (LLMs) to automatically categorize users’ motives for engaging and the robot’s response styles, and to measure how deeply other users participated and how widely their discussion evolved. The findings show that demographic attributes, account features, and regional contexts affect why users interact with the robot. These motivations then shape the robot’s response patterns and increase user satisfaction, which subsequently stimulates additional user participation and broader social diffusion. This study advances marketing theory on bot-enabled engagement and provides actionable guidance for platform managers on designing response strategies that deepen user engagement, strengthen retention, and improve the long-term health of platform communities.

title: From Access to Agency: Optimal Pricing for the Agentic Econo...
speaker: Yi Wang
abstract: The emergence of autonomous AI agents is precipitating a structural shift in the digital economy from "selling tools" to "selling work." As AI agents gain autonomy, the fundamental economic friction shifts from user adoption to incentive alignment. Specifically, we identify a critical trade-off between Usage-Based Pricing (UBP) and Outcome-Based Pricing (OBP). Under UBP, vendors face an efficiency Moral Hazard: because revenue is tied to compute consumption (tokens), vendors are incentivized to deploy inefficient, bloated agentic workflows that maximize volume rather than speed. Conversely, OBP aligns vendor incentives with computational efficiency but imposes a verification cost on the user—the friction of auditing probabilistic outputs to confirm that inquiries are genuinely resolved.  This paper develops a principal-agent model to analyze this tension, focusing on the interplay between AI model maturity (autonomous success probability), vendor inefficiency (token inflation), and the user’s verification burden. We address three core questions: First, under what conditions, does OBP dominate UBP as the equilibrium strategy? Second, how does the transition to OBP impact consumer welfare? Third, we propose a verification-adjusted two-part tariff mechanism to resolve the efficiency hazard by subsidizing the user’s audit burden, thereby approximating the first-best outcome in an autonomous economy.

title: Dynamic Consumer-AI Love Relationship: Formation and Continu...
speaker: Hang Xu
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed functional chatbots into AI companions capable of imitating human-like relationships. Grounded in Triangular Theory of Love, we study emotional bonding between consumers and AI companions by analyzing the dynamics of three love components: intimacy, passion, and commitment. Using a panel dataset of consumer-AI interactions, we quantify expressed love in each of these three components through an analysis of conversational data for each consumer-AI pair. Our findings reveal emotional bonding with saturation: As consumers engage in more interactions with an AI, they express stronger intimacy, passion, and commitment, but at a diminishing rate. Moreover, the expressed love is greater when consumers engage with AI companions designed for relational roles (e.g., romantic partners) than for functional roles (e.g., service providers). We also identify relationship-sustaining love balances: While higher mutual intimacy drives relationship formation, the continuation of dyadic relationship favors asymmetry. Specifically, consumers are more likely to continue relationships with AI companions when they express higher intimacy and commitment, while the AI companion express higher passion. In this research, we also conduct experiments to establish causality and further explore potential mechanisms. These nuanced consumer preferences in bonding with AI offer critical insights for designing adaptive, engaging, and responsible AI companions.

title: When Generative Artificial Intelligence Enhances the Quality...
speaker: Prithwiraj Mukherjee
abstract: In many workplace scenarios like market research, consulting and new product development, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) enhances the quality of output by an employee, who can expend costly effort via prompt engineering, and subsequent error-checking due to possible hallucination by the tool. We model a principal-agent setting where a principal (manager) contracts an agent (employee) to do some work. The principal is unable to observe the agent's inherent ability (type), and thus offers a payment contingent on the quality of the output generated. When GenAI is available to the agent, she augments her baseline (non-AI) work quality with prompt engineering, thus enhancing the total quality of the work. We solve for the optimal contract using control theory.  We demonstrate the counterintuitive finding that, in the optimal contract, the agent actually expends more baseline effort when GenAI is available, than if it were not available. This is because the optimal contract acts as a screening mechanism that allows agents to credibly signal their underlying ability to the principal, who sorts them by ability. We also model the effect of the GenAI algorithm's accuracy on the agent's output quality. Our work is important for compensation mechanism design at the workplace in the era of generative artificial intelligence.

title: Empirical Echoes: Optimal Distance and Generative AI Music D...
speaker: Haihao Guo
abstract: Popular music is inherently historical, with new songs exhibiting systematic similarity to past musical styles, and this process has become increasingly consequential as generative AI enables music creation at unprecedented scale. This paper proposes a novel data-driven framework for designing successful music with controlled similarity to past music styles. We first construct an Interpretable Music Attribute Representation (IMAR) by separating each track into stems, then extracting theory-grounded features for melody, harmony, rhythm, and timbre using deep learning models integrated with music-theoretic analysis. Using all Billboard Hot 100 (24,618) songs from 1958–2017, we cluster songs within rolling windows via clustering and then aggregate medoids using a forward linkage rule to obtain robust historical “styles.” Utilizing 29,331songs from 2018–2025, we then compute similarity measures between focal songs and these styles and show that successful contemporary music achieves optimal: melodies and rhythms that are close to past styles, fusion-oriented harmonies, and innovative timbres. Next, we train a state-of-the-art predictive model of Billboard entry based on audio-derived IMAR features and demonstrate that with only four of style-based similarity measures yields substantial gains in predictive accuracy. Finally, we operationalize these insights for generative AI: using a retrieval-augmented generation scheme that conditions on historical style medoids, we edit a current unpopular song to achieve the optimal distance to the past, which achieves the huge gain in predicted success compared with the current songs. Our framework offers one of the first end-to-end, implementable guidelines for using generative AI to solve the product design problem in music creation.

title: Building An Ecosystem OR Prioritizing Personalization with A...
speaker: Catherine Tucker
abstract: Through a pre-registered, randomized controlled field experiment, we demonstrate that a tailored generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a solution can significantly improve outcomes in an online weight loss program. Our results indicate increases in the number of participants who successfully were no longer obese, as well as a total reduction in body mass index (BMI) and enhanced participation rates. This suggests that tailored generative AI represents a cost-effective alternative to traditional weight loss interventions. Though personalization of messaging to encourage weight loss through AI was effective, the attempt to harness this personalization to build a community of the kind that has traditionally supported weight loss goals was less effective. This suggests that using AI to encourage the kind of personalization that can underpin a community may backfire, and at least in the weight-loss context, it is more effective to use generative AI for personalizing individual experiences rather than pursuing large-scale ecosystem development.

title: Platform Levers for Copyright Compliance in Generative AI: E...
speaker: Vincent Lefrere
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) platforms significantly expand opportunities for scalable, user-driven innovation while simultaneously raising concerns about intellectual property (IP) infringement. This paper examines how strategic platform design, particularly monetization policies, can influence user behavior in ways that reduce the risk of IP violations. Using observational data and quasi-experimental variation from a leading GenAI image-generation platform, we conduct both platform-level and user-level event studies, supported by Difference-in-Differences (DiD) analyses, to evaluate user responses to the removal and temporary reintroduction of free trials. Our findings show that requiring users to pay for access leads them to produce more differentiated outputs, thereby reducing visual similarity to existing online content that could be protected by copyright. Crucially, these changes persist even within fixed prompt topics, suggesting that the behavioral shift reflects genuine adjustments in user strategies rather than changes in the types of tasks being performed. These results underscore the importance of user agency and strategic prompting as internal mechanisms for managing copyright risk within GenAI ecosystems. We finally propose a governance approach that combines incentive-aligned nudges with technical safeguards, offering actionable insights for platform designers, IP policymakers, and managers seeking to promote responsible GenAI adoption in digital innovation environments.

title: Restructuring Frontline Communication: Evidence from a Field...
speaker: Yifan Pan
abstract: Digital marketing research and practice have largely emphasized online tools such as targeting algorithms and AI-driven personalization. In contrast, we provide field evidence that seemingly low-technology and low-cost marketing tools can exert substantial effects when they reshape the structure of frontline work. We study a randomized field experiment conducted in collaboration with a global leading automobile manufacturer, in which a randomly selected half of sales consultants at automobile dealerships were provided with a simple printed one-page product information sheet. Importantly, the content on the sheet consists entirely of information that sales consultants are required to communicate to customers even in the absence of the tool. Process evidence from speech transcripts of follow-up calls shows that the mechanism does not operate through increased information exposure or stronger consumer recall. Instead, the printed one-page sheet improves sales performance by restructuring sales communication, with spillover effects on subsequent sales behaviors and follow-up interactions. By externalizing and stabilizing information organization, the tool increases communication fluency and helps sales consultants develop more structured interaction rhythms. Treatment effects are heterogeneous across sales consultants. Using synthetic difference-in-differences and causal forest methods, we show that the intervention significantly benefits consultants with high latent conversion potential but relatively unstructured communication practices, while yielding only marginal improvements for moderately structured consultants. Our findings highlight the importance of alignment between marketing tools and workers’ existing communication structures, and suggest that the value of marketing interventions lies not only in technological sophistication, but in how they reorganize frontline decision-making and work.

title: ***Canceled***Limitations of AI Technology or Consumer Bias?...
speaker: Haoqi Lu
abstract: With the widespread application of generative AI technology in advertising, consumer acceptance of its generated content has become a hot topic. Based on the ABC attitude model and attribution theory, this study explores the mechanisms by which generative AI aversion, generated ad quality, and task context influence consumer attitudes toward advertising. A questionnaire survey collected 237 valid data points, and analysis using structural equation modeling and paired-sample t-tests revealed that the quality of AI-generated ads is a core factor in shaping consumers' positive advertising attitudes. Consequently, this study proposes that reducing consumers' aversion to generative AI, segmenting different consumer decision-making scenarios, and enhancing ad quality through human-machine co-creation can improve consumer attitudes toward generative AI ads. This, in turn, helps advertising practitioners cope with the challenges brought about by technological change and provides theoretical support and practical guidance for the application of generative AI in the advertising industry.

title: How Consumers Respond to AI- Versus Human-Generated Review S...
speaker: Shaowei Chai
abstract: While AI-generated review summaries are increasingly prevalent on digital platforms, their influence on consumer behavior remains insufficiently understood. This research examines when and why AI-generated review summaries outperform human-generated ones under two common probability formats: verbal probabilities (e.g., most) and numerical probabilities (e.g., 89%). Across four studies, we demonstrate that when review summaries are presented in verbal probability, consumers respond more positively to AI-generated summaries than to human-generated ones. In contrast, when the review summaries are presented in numerical probability, the difference in consumer responses between AI-generated summaries and human-generated ones is not significant. This occurs because consumers infer that humans, when using verbal probability to generate review summaries, are prone to making subjective judgment and overestimation to promote consumers’ purchase behavior (Collins & Mandel, 2019; Dhami & Mandel, 2022). In contrast, AI agents, perceived as less mindful and with limited experience and agency capacity (Gray et al., 2007; Gray & Wegner, 2012), are less likely to make subjective judgment when generating review summaries using verbal probability, thereby increasing consumers’ perceived objectiveness and trust for the AI-generated summaries, and thus eliciting more positive consumer responses. Our findings differ from prior research showing that consumers hold negative attitudes toward AI because it has limited capacities for experience and agency. This research advances literature on AI-human communication, AI adoption, and probability expressions of uncertainty, and further offers actionable guidance for marketers deploying AI in dispersive information communication.

title: Inferring Intent from AI-Mediated Interactions: a Comparison...
speaker: Wendy Moe
abstract: This study examines and compares the ability of traditional graph methods and LLMs in inferring intent from consumer interactions with their AI assistants. Specifically, we focus on purchase intent. We compare inferred purchase intent using a graph-based method versus an LLM-based method to those provided by human annotators and market metrics such as CPC. Our findings suggest that both graph-and LLM-based methods can predict purchase intent, but key differences exist. Our analyses demonstrate the value of both LLMs and traditional graph-based methods. LLMs capture the value of verbs while the graph is better able to capture the value of nouns that provide important contextual information. Overall, we show that graph-based methods and LLM-based methods are not necessarily substitutes but rather complements. The ability to infer consumer intent, specifically purchase intent, has implications for AI orchestration and advertising strategies.

title: We Care About What You Care About: Using Reason-Specific Int...
speaker: Sharon Wei
abstract: Individual behavioral change is essential for climate change mitigation and adapta- tion. However, interventions encouraging more sustainable choices often do not have the desired effect. To address this, we studied consumers’ mental representation of sustainable behavior across seven situations to understand why they behave (un)sustainably. We elicited consumers’ mental representations using open-ended questions asking their reasons behind making (un)sustainable choices in various situations (e.g., food consumption). We identified key attributes (i.e., reasons) people care about for each behavior using large language model (LLM) embeddings. These reasons vary across situations and individuals. Further, they can be divided into situation-specific reasons, such as health, which is mainly relevant to food consumption, and general reasons, such as costs, which are relevant across situations. We applied these insights in a series of longitudinal field experiments with interventions designed using reasons. Our results demonstrate how to develop effective interventions by examining mental representations of the target behavior.

title: The Effect of Logic Expression in Promotions: Evidence from ...
speaker: Fred Feinberg
abstract: Promotional offers are often evaluated by their economic content -- reward magnitude, eligibility requirements, or timing -- but such changes inevitably alter how offers are logically expressed. We study how the logical structure of promotional language, beyond its monetary value, affects consumer response. We conceptualize promotions as rule-based systems composed of requirements and rewards connected through implicit logical operators (e.g., and, or, if–then). Using large language and other "high-dimensional" regularized models, we parse natural-language promotions into formal propositional logic expressions and develop a novel, interpretable measure of logic complexity capturing multiplicity, interdependence, and structural diversity. Analyzing a rich longitudinal dataset from the North American mobile phone market, we examine how logic complexity influences weekly sales while controlling for prices, promotional value, advertising, and competitive conditions. Using a comprehensive, nonparametric framework for data fusion between "stated" and "revealed" preference measures, we find that greater logical complexity is associated with higher sales on average, but the effect is highly heterogeneous across brands. For technologically sophisticated brands such as Apple and Google, complex promotional logic significantly boosts sales, whereas for lower-tech brands it yields weaker or negative returns. These results are robust across fixed-effects models, linguistic instrumental variables, and IV-free identification strategies. Our findings highlight how behavioral and choice-theoretic structure can inform the design of AI-mediated marketing systems, and how AI tools can, in turn, uncover meaningful structure in consumer-facing language.

title: Motivating Consumer and AI Co-Creation
speaker: Lan L...
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes digital mass customization by altering the structure of consumer–AI co-creation. When consumers can start from an AI-generated draft rather than a blank canvas, outcomes are jointly determined by two stages: whether consumers initiate co-creation and, conditional on participation, how much refinement effort they exert. Partnering with a leading U.S. online retailer of personalized photo products, we study the causal impact of motivating participation in consumer–AI co-creation and examine how alternative participation interventions shape downstream purchase outcomes. We develop a two-stage model in which, relative to a baseline with organic participation, a nudge lowers start-up frictions and expands voluntary entry, whereas a mandate guarantees entry but can weaken how participation translates into purchase, generating a reach–efficiency trade-off. Two randomized experiments support the model’s predictions. In Study 1, a light-touch nudge increases participation by 5.98 percentage points and raises revenue, with gains driven by expanded entry rather than intensified refinement effort. In Study 2, mandating participation further increases participation but yields weaker downstream outcomes, including lower conversion efficiency and a higher incidence of minimal-compliance participation. Together, these findings highlight a fundamental trade-off between expanding participation and preserving engagement quality in consumer–AI co-creation.

title: Calibrated Coarsening: Designing Info for AI-Assisted Decisi...
speaker: Ruru Hoong
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to aid human decision-making across critical applications, but errors in human probabilistic reasoning (e.g., cognitive biases) often undermine its effectiveness. This raises the central design question of how to provide AI input to humans in a way that improves decision-making outcomes. We propose calibrated coarsening---partitioning the signal space into fewer cells at chosen thresholds---as a way to do so that (i) ensures humans retain final decision authority, (ii) modifies signals without deception, and (iii) adapts flexibly to diverse biases and contexts. Within an information disclosure framework, we derive an approximately optimal binary coarsened policy when the designer does not observe the decision-maker's information. In a randomised experiment with professional loan specialists, we empirically demonstrate that coarsening AI signals at the theory-derived threshold significantly improves decision-making outcomes, outperforming both the human-only (based solely on the loan application) and uncoarsened AI assistance (continuous AI risk-score, in addition to loan application) benchmarks. We uncover substantial decision heterogeneity amongst loan officers and estimate a Bayesian hierarchical linear model (HLM), which we use to simulate and test the benefits of personalised coarsening policies.

title: Visual Diversity and Consumer Choice in Online Platforms
speaker: Madhav Kumar
abstract: We investigate consumer preferences for visual diversity by examining the relationship between display model skin tone and product performance across major global fashion brands. Using comprehensive data from five major brands, we document substantial variation in model representation and employ a matching approach to analyze performance outcomes. We find that products featuring darker skin tone models are significantly more likely to become top sellers. To isolate the underlying consumer preferences driving this effect, we conduct two carefully designed experiments using generative AI to manipulate model skin tone while holding product characteristics constant. Our experimental results reveal that consumers express significantly higher purchase intent for products featuring darker skin tone models. These findings show that the performance advantage is driven primarily by consumer preferences rather than supply-side factors such as product targeting or quality differences. Our research provides a comprehensive, causally-identified measurement of consumer demand for visual diversity in digital commerce, offering brands empirical tools to measure and optimize their representation strategies.

title: Chatgpt Referrals to E-Commerce Websites: How Do LLMs Compar...
speaker: Maximilian Kaiser
abstract: We investigate organic Large Language Model traffic (oLLM) versus traditional digital channels in e-commerce. Analyzing 12 months of first-party data from 973 websites with $20 billion combined revenue, we examine over 50,000 transactions from ChatGPT referrals alongside 164 million transactions from traditional channels. Using regression models that account for data sparsity, we assess financial metrics (conversion rate, average order value, revenue per session) and engagement metrics (bounce rate, session duration, page views). Results are consistent across extensive robustness checks. One year after launch, oLLM exhibits conversion rates and revenue per session above paid social but below all other traditional channels. Product complexity moderates the effects: oLLM's financial outcomes and traffic shares are stronger in complex product categories. Engagement metrics show favorable bounce rates but lower session duration and page views. Temporal analysis shows increasing conversion rates but declining average order values, yielding only moderate revenue-per-session gains over time. Cross-website analyses support growing consumer LLM proficiency as the underlying mechanism. The descriptive analyses position oLLM as a new and developing channel. With low volumes and modest revenue per session, oLLM currently serves niche informational needs of proficient consumers and does not yet function as a broad conversion channel.

title: Winning the Chatbot: How Businesses Can Optimize Content for...
speaker: Gabriela Makar
abstract: Conversational AI is transforming online search. Instead of browsing “ten blue links,” users increasingly rely on chatbots that deliver synthesized, interactive answers. This shift creates new challenges for businesses, where visibility directly drives success. Yet, even in traditional search engines, competition is intense: rankings fluctuate, zero-click searches are rising, and algorithms disproportionately favor large brands, making it harder for smaller firms to stand out. We propose a novel content generation workflow for businesses’ websites, designed to improve visibility in large language model (LLM)–driven search systems. Building on established insights from SEO, our approach iteratively tunes the focal company’s website content against top-ranked outputs for given prompts, automatically aligning text with LLM-specific optimality factors. Experiments with industry partners demonstrate that optimized content can significantly boost visibility across LLM-based platforms. Crucially, our findings show that success in classic Google rankings does not guarantee success in generative search: visibility differs widely across models (e.g., strong presence in Perplexity but little to none in Gemini). Our research contributes conceptually by introducing a novel generative workflow for LLM content optimization, and practically by providing businesses with actionable methods to secure visibility in conversational search environments where classical SEO alone is no longer sufficient.

title: Mind the Gap: How Repositioning Alters Brand Representations...
speaker: Andreas Hamann
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly emerging as new touchpoints in the customer journey, shaping how consumers discover and evaluate brands. Yet, little is known about how LLMs adjust brand representations and recommendations when firms engage in strategic brand meaning-changing actions. In this study, the authors examine how LLMs update brand portrayals following a repositioning. They show that, unlike consumers, LLMs do not learn from gradual exposure but construct brand representations through the retrieval and synthesis of external information at the moment of response. Findings of a controlled synthetic field experiment in which they systematically vary repositioning behavior across brands and track their LLM representations over time align with theoretical predictions. First, LLMs differ systematically in how quickly and accurately they reflect repositioned brand positions. Second, repositionings temporarily reduce brand salience in LLM recommendations. Third, firms can influence LLM-based brand representations by managing how repositioning information becomes retrievable, such as through repositioning communication cues and indexing mechanisms, with effectiveness depending on whether the LLMs rely on cached or real-time information sources. Theoretically, these findings extend traditional positioning theory on brand meaning formation to generative AI-mediated contexts. Managerially, they provide guidance for managing LLM-based brand visibility during major strategic brand changes.

title: Does AI Displace OR Complement Web Traffic?
speaker: Carlo Reggiani
abstract: We investigate whether generative AI features in search engines, specifically Google's AI Overviews, displace or complement traffic to online publishers. Using web traffic data from July 2022 to December 2025 and exploiting the staggered global rollout of the feature, the authors find that AI Overviews are associated with a decline in visits and unique visitors, particularly for websites highly dependent on search traffic. However, the study also notes that while traffic volume decreases, the remaining user behavior becomes more targeted with less exploratory browsing, suggesting that AI summaries improve search efficiency and matching quality.

title: The Impact of AI-Generated Product Line Extensions: Evidence...
speaker: Marco Kotschedoff
abstract: We study the impact of releasing machine-narrated audiobooks on publishers’ sales across book formats. Although recent advances in AI-based text-to-speech technology enable low-cost audiobook production, concerns about perceived narration quality, AI aversion, and cross-format cannibalization raise questions about their net value. Using data on customer reviews, we show that consumers rate machine-narrated audiobooks lower than human-narrated audiobooks, particularly along narration performance dimensions. Linking machine-narrated audiobooks to their corresponding eBook and print editions and tracking sales ranks over time, we exploit staggered release timing to conduct a difference-in-differences analysis. We find that machine-narrated audiobook introductions generate a short-term increase in eBook sales and a persistent decline in print sales. Aggregating demand across formats, publishers benefit overall, as additional audiobook and eBook sales outweigh print losses. Our findings provide new evidence on substitution and complementarity across book formats and inform publishers’ format-portfolio decisions under AI-based narration technologies.

title: How Generative AI Impacts Engagement with Content: Evidence ...
speaker: Unnati Narang
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping online communities, yet little is known about how users engage with AI-generated content and why. We conduct a field experiment on an online discussion platform (Yellowdig.com), randomly assigning participants to craft posts using GenAI alone, GenAI with human modifications, or only human input. We find that posts created in both AI conditions are more informative but also more complex and less personal than purely human-generated posts. Overall, AI-assisted posts generate higher user engagement compared to human-only posts, with the strongest effects observed when AI-generated content is modified by humans. Follow-up online experiments show that increased informativeness of AI-generated content positively mediates engagement, while increased complexity negatively mediates it, highlighting competing forces underlying the net engagement effects. Together, these findings suggest that combining AI generation with human refinement can help platforms leverage GenAI to enhance user engagement while mitigating potential downsides. These results offer important implications for the design and governance of AI use in online communities.

title: AI-Based Learning Support as A Consumer Boost: Observational...
speaker: Hamada Shunya
abstract: AI-powered analytics and communication can personalize support on digital platforms, yet it remains unclear whether such tools merely steer behavior (nudges) or build users’ decision competence. Boosts are defined as interventions that target competences rather than immediate behavior (Grüne-Yanoff & Hertwig, 2016; Hertwig & Grüne-Yanoff, 2017). We examine two optional AI learning supports on a Japanese online mahjong platform: (1) a score-sheet analysis AI that provides probabilistic and strategic feedback and (2) an AI email assistant that explains the feedback in plain language to opt-in users. Using approximately 120,000 user-year records (2019–2024), we compare four groups: analysis-AI only, email only, both, and neither. Skill acquisition is proxied by annual play count and “flag efficiency” (final flags divided by annual plays), a measure of learning productivity. Pre/post comparisons show that users adopting both tools increased annual play and final flags in 2024 relative to 2019–2022. Users adopting only the analysis AI show smaller changes in volume but larger differences in efficiency metrics, including flag efficiency, compared with non-users. These patterns are consistent with a complementary mechanism: analytical feedback may serve as a boost by strengthening probabilistic and strategic understanding, while follow-up email reinforces comprehension and reflection. This study provides initial behavioral evidence on when AI assistance aligns with boost-like learning rather than solely nudge-like guidance, and it highlights efficiency-based metrics as informative outcomes for AI-supported skill acquisition.

title: When AI Plays Along OR Plays Against: Evidence from a Field ...
speaker: Jinyu Zhang
abstract: Modern online games increasingly deploy AI agents to stabilize matchmaking, yet managers lack causal evidence on whether AI should be introduced as teammates, opponents, or in dual roles. We partner with an online game company to run a large-scale field experiment across 4 parallel servers in which AI agents are introduced after a 3-week pre-treatment period: control, AI as collaborators, AI as competitors, and both. Using data from 63,478 players over 62 days, we estimate impacts on in-game engagement and expenditure. Relative to control, introducing AI collaborators increases active time by 6.685 units (SE=.262, p<.001) but does not change expenditure (.069, SE=.141, p=.624). AI competitors reduce active time by 2.830 units (SE=.276, p<.001) with non-significant expenditure effect (.119, SE=.145, p=.413). When AI collaborators and competitors are deployed together, the engagement gain from only AI collaborators is largely offset (−3.409, SE=.384, p<.001) and overall average engagement effect is .445, while expenditure rises materially, consistent with a positive interaction effect (.690, SE=.210, p=.001) and overall effect is .878. Dynamic estimates reveal that engagement gains from AI collaborators are persistent and grow over time, whereas AI competitors generate short-lived engagement increases that quickly reverse. Expenditure effects in the “both” condition are concentrated in the early and mid post-treatment periods and fade later. These findings quantify the engagement–monetization trade-offs of alternative AI deployment strategies and highlight that combining cooperative and competitive AI can shift value creation from engagement to expenditure. Keywords: AI agents; online gaming; field experiment; engagement–monetization trade-off;

title: Beyond Single-Shot: A Multi-Sample Distributional Framework ...
speaker: Li Jiang
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) hold a great promise in simulating consumer decision-making in marketing research. By generating synthetic responses at scale, LLMs provide an efficient alternative to the costly and time-consuming process of collecting real-world human data. However, despite this potential, recent research shows that synthetic data often diverges from real-world human behavior, leading to unreliable conclusions when LLMs are used as direct substitutes. Crucially, this divergence is complicated by the fact that human preferences are not static; even the same individual often exhibits variability in their responses over time. In this work, we address these challenges by treating human decisions and LLM outputs as samples drawn from unknown latent distributions, rather than deterministic answers. Unlike standard methods that rely on a single output per query, our approach utilizes multiple responses sampled across diverse personas and LLM architectures as input features to capture underlying variance for robust estimation. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that incorporating multi-sample variance effectively minimizes the estimation error bound, providing consistent estimators that are robust to the inherent stochasticity of LLMs. We validate our framework across various domains of public datasets, including the General Social Survey, Twin-2k-500, SosSic210, OpinionQA, and EEDI. Our approach reduces alignment error and improving recovery of individual heterogeneity substantially. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates consistent robustness across varying datasets. These findings underscore that modeling distributional uncertainty is essential for high-fidelity human response simulation.

title: How Consumers Judge the Authenticity of Online Reviews
speaker: Charan Bagga
abstract: Consumers rely heavily on online reviews to inform purchasing decisions. Yet the growing prevalence of fake reviews misleads them, erodes trust in digital platforms, and distorts market efficiency. This challenge has intensified as fake reviews often created or augmented by generative AI closely resemble genuine human language, making it more difficult to distinguish authentic from fake reviews in uncertain online environments. Although platforms such as Amazon and Google deploy increasingly sophisticated algorithms to detect and remove fraudulent content, fake reviews persist due to adaptive manipulation strategies and the inherent limitations of automated detection. Consequently, the burden of assessing review authenticity ultimately rests with consumers. This research conceptualizes consumers’ review authenticity judgments as consisting of two distinct components: sensitivity, the ability to discriminate authentic from fake reviews, and response bias, the tendency to classify reviews as authentic versus fake. Across experimental studies, we examine how cognitive, motivational, and contextual factors systematically influence these two components of judgment. The results show that these factors can differentially affect consumers’ discriminative ability versus their general inclination to trust or distrust reviews, generating distinct patterns of misclassification. The research contributes to the literature by offering a process-level account of review authenticity judgments under uncertainty and risk, and by extending detection-theoretic approaches to consumer-generated content. From a managerial perspective, the findings provide actionable insights for platforms and marketers seeking to improve the credibility and effectiveness of online review systems.

title: Convergence or Divergence? The Impact of AI Disclosure on th...
speaker: Peng Shen
abstract: Abstract: The application of generative AI in creative production has significantly improved content creation efficiency and expanded the possibilities of idea generation. Meanwhile, an increasing number of platforms and regulatory authorities have introduced AI disclosure policies to enhance transparency in the AI-driven creative process. However, the practical impact of such disclosure systems remains underexplored, particularly with respect to how they shape creators' strategies for creative output. Given that content uniqueness is a core source of competitive advantage for creative products, this study distinguishes and examines two types of content uniqueness: self-uniqueness (relative to the creator’s own historical works) and peer-uniqueness (relative to similar creative content by peers). Using Kickstarter’s AI disclosure policy as a policy shock, this paper employs a regression discontinuity design to empirically analyze the policy’s impact, with a robustness check using a difference-in-differences method. The results show that AI disclosure policies significantly increase the self-uniqueness of creative content but reduce peer-uniqueness. Further heterogeneity analysis indicates that this effect is more pronounced for less experienced creators and products in AI-sensitive categories. Finally, the study investigates the impact of AI disclosure policies on investor reactions, finding that AI disclosure may influence creative content and, in turn, project performance, leading to lower funding outcomes and success rates. This research extends prior research on technology disclosure and creative production and provides important insights for the design of platform regulatory policies and creators’ strategic decision-making in an AI disclosure environment.

title: Effort Matters in AI Disclosure
speaker: Kristina Klein
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly become embedded in marketing workflows, enabling brands to produce scalable text, imagery, and campaign assets at unprecedented speed. As adoption accelerates, disclosure of AI involvement in outward-facing communications becomes mandatory with regulatory frameworks (e.g., China, European Union). Prior research reports mixed effects of AI disclosure on consumer responses; however, few papers so far look into the mechanism that might underlie consumer reactions. Particularly, in contexts, which are morally charged, consumers appreciate (costly) signals to be able to make inferences about a company’s sincere motives. In a CSR context, which represents such a context, we examine how disclosure of AI versus human authorship affects perceptions of effort, which then translates into consumers’ inferences of sincerity and in turn trust. We test this account across two experiments. Study 1 manipulates perceived effort in a CSR message to establish (a) a main effect of higher effort on brand trust and (b) the mediation via sincerity. Study 2 manipulates authorship disclosure at three levels (no disclosure vs. human vs. AI) to examine (a) main effects on trust, (b) differences in inferred effort and sincerity, and (c) the predicted serial mediation (disclosure → effort → sincerity → trust). We find that AI disclosure reduces brand trust relative to human disclosure because consumers infer lower effort and sincerity. These findings reconcile mixed evidence on AI disclosure by theorizing CSR as a high-stakes, authenticity-sensitive domain and contribute to literature on AI in communication and the respective psychological mechanisms at work.

title: Tackling the Cognitive Paradox in AI-Enabled Knowledge-Based...
speaker: Helen SI Wang
abstract: The recent boom in AI has dramatically accelerated its application in knowledge-based service encounters, such as healthcare, financial, legal, and educational services. AI chatbots, with their remarkable ability to integrate large amounts of information and generate customized solutions at superhuman speed, may dramatically transform these services. Despite this optimistic view, research remain mixed on how AI could effectively assist complexity problem solving and decision making (Jörg 2025; Massimo et al., 2025). Drawing from communication theories and neuroscience research, we posit that, in AI-enabled professional service encounters, how customers interact with AI chatbots --- in either conversational or written communication manner --- matters to important business outcomes and consumer well-being. Specifically, when customers engage in text-based conversational chats with AI (vs. writing requests and clarification), they are more likely to experience cognitive fatigue, which in turn reduces advice adherence and triggers impulsive decision-making. This effect is stronger when service issues are more complex or more emotionally charged. Using mixed methods of field studies and controlled experiments, we validate our proposed model and contribute to emerging literature on AI and its applications in knowledge-based services. It also provides practical guidance for consumers and firms on how to design and use AI to enhance consumer well-being.

title: When AI Disclosure Backfires: Product Type Contingencies and...
speaker: Osamu Sakai
abstract: Firms increasingly rely on generative AI to produce website content and promotional materials. In response to growing concerns about consumer protection and transparency, regulators and platforms are beginning to mandate AI disclosure, explicitly indicating that marketing content has been generated by AI. However, prior research suggests that such disclosures may trigger algorithm aversion and reduce consumer trusts (e.g., Schilke & Reimann 2025). Despite its practical importance, little is known about when and why AI disclosure is more detrimental, and how its negative effects can be mitigated. This research examines the impact of AI disclosure across different product types—search goods, experience goods, and credence goods—each characterized by distinct information asymmetries and evaluation processes. We propose a conceptual framework in which AI disclosure affects consumer trust, perceived diagnosticity, and responsibility attribution differently depending on product type, thereby leading to heterogeneous negative effects on attitudes and purchase intentions. Using a combination of vignette-based experiments and a field experiment, we test (1) whether AI disclosure exerts stronger negative effects for experience and credence goods than for search goods, and (2) whether specific disclosure and explanation strategies—such as emphasizing human oversight, task–AI fit, or performance accountability—can attenuate these effects. The findings contribute to the literature on algorithm aversion and AI transparency by identifying product-type contingencies and actionable mitigation strategies. From a managerial perspective, the results offer guidance on how firms can comply with AI disclosure requirements while minimizing potential harm to consumer responses.

title: Strategic AI Integration as Identity Work in Creative Indust...
speaker: Alexander Dierenfeldt
abstract: Generative AI is reshaping value creation by supporting and automating creative tasks at scale, offering substantial efficiency and cost advantages for creatives in the production process of goods.
