However, creatives’ AI integration decisions can trigger tensions around identity and authenticity perceptions, as well as skepticism and aversion against the good on the consumer side. Yet, existing research has largely overlooked how creatives’ identity and consumers’ evaluation interact in the context of generative AI integration decisions. To address this gap, we develop a theory-based framework which we transform into an analytical model to capture the dynamics of identity and image in AI integration. We extend the basic model by considering demand-spillovers, remuneration dynamics, market introduction timing and competition. Using data from the music industry, we calibrate the model to simulate different scenarios and quantify implications of creatives’ decisions. The results indicate that decisions regarding the use of generative AI are influenced by established economic mechanisms, such as cost reductions and demand shifts, yet identity and image dynamics ultimately play a particularly decisive role. Creatives’ self-perceived technological orientation and authenticity signals associated with image therefore critically shape the level of AI integration. Competitive dynamics moderate these relationships, with early adoption granting advantages only when perceived as authentic, while later adoption reduces reputational risks. At the societal level, limited novelty in AI output accumulates into homogenization with social costs. These findings help creatives and managers to align AI integration without losing their creative identity and navigating through competitive dynamics without eroding brand equity.

title: Does Home Staging Work? Evidence from Redfin Listings
speaker: Nan Zhao
abstract: Home staging has become a widely used marketing tool in residential real estate, with virtual staging emerging as a lower-cost and more scalable alternative to traditional physical staging. Despite its growing prevalence, causal evidence on the effectiveness of virtual staging for sales outcomes remains limited. This study examines how virtual staging affects the sales of residential properties. We assemble a dataset by collecting listing information and images from Redfin in November 2024 for a random sample of residential listings across 28 U.S. metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs), and tracking their sales outcomes over a subsequent 14-month period. We identify unfurnished listings using a convolutional neural network (CNN) and detect virtual staging through image-pair comparisons that capture before-and-after digital furniture and décor edits. To estimate the effect of virtual staging on sales outcomes, we employ a double machine learning (DML) framework that flexibly controls for rich numeric listing characteristics and high-dimensional textual features extracted from listing descriptions using TF-IDF representations. Our preliminary results show that, relative to unfurnished listings without virtual staging, virtually staged listings are 3.8% more likely to sell during the observation window, suggesting that virtual staging may be a low-cost marketing tool for sellers and intermediaries.

title: Effectiveness of Personalization in Email Marketing
speaker: Younggon Cho
abstract: Assessing personalized email marketing effectiveness requires understanding causal effects and heterogeneity in treatment using conditional average treatment effects (CATEs). Marketing practitioners lack systematic decision rules for selecting CATE methods based on observable dataset characteristics when multiple personalization treatments (products, promotions, and content) are applied. The recent availability of large datasets with numerous covariates further complicates the computation of heterogeneous effects and the interpretation of features, necessitating efficiency and interpretability. We identify efficient, interpretable CATE estimators and investigate how personalization affects repurchase across customer segments. Explainable AI (XAI) improves accountability by providing clear, human-understandable justifications for specific  algorithmic decisions—revealing which data points (purchase history, browsing, and demographics) influenced outcomes. We leverage XAI to deliver transparent insights and address interpretability challenges. We analyze 5 million email campaign samples from randomized controlled trials (2024–2025) at a leading Benelux electronics firm, comparing personalized recommendations and offers against non-personalized campaigns. Our dataset includes customer demographics, product ownership, campaign responses, repurchase propensity scores, treatments, and outcomes. We identify heterogeneous effects, comparing Double Machine Learning, GenericML, and other modern CATE estimators. We conduct moderation analysis to explain how segment characteristics relate to treatment effects. Preliminary findings show that personalized product offers and personalized promotion type offers positively influence repurchase, with stronger effects among high-propensity segments. We empirically identify efficient CATE estimators among widely recommended methods for practitioners’ systematic decision-making, and explain segment-level variation in treatment effects in an XAI context. Final results will be presented at the conference.

title: Do Top Managers' Duchenne Smile Appeal to the Market? Eviden...
speaker: Zhenhan Hong
abstract: Top managers’ facial expressions, particularly smiles, are salient nonverbal cues that may shape how the market interprets corporate communications. While a growing marketing literature documents the persuasive power of visual and emotional signals in consumer and interpersonal contexts, evidence on whether and how managerial micro-expressions influence market reactions remains limited, largely due to the difficulty of systematically measuring such subtle visual information at scale. This study examines whether top managers’ Duchenne smiles, commonly regarded as signals of genuine positive affect, appeal to the market. Using a large sample of live streamed earnings conference calls from Chinese public firms, this paper use machine learning model to conduct frame by frame facial analysis of top managers’ micro-expressions. Based on the Facial Action Coding System, we distinguish genuine Duchenne smiles from non-Duchenne smiles that are more likely to reflect strategic impression management. The results show that managers’ Duchenne smiles are associated with more favorable market reactions, including higher abnormal returns and increased trading activity. In contrast, non-Duchenne smiles are linked to weaker or negative market responses. These findings are robust to alternative event windows, firm fixed effects, and a rich set of controls for firm performance and disclosure characteristics. Overall, the evidence suggests that the market is attentive to subtle visual cues conveyed by top managers and is able to differentiate genuine emotional expressions from strategic ones. This study contributes to the marketing and communication literature by highlighting the market impact of managerial micro-expressions.

title: A AI-Driven Interpretable Visual Features for Demand Neurofo...
speaker: Brenden Eum
abstract: Recent advances in marketing have shown that both product images and neural measures can be used for aggregate demand forecasting. However, image-based machine learning models often function as black boxes, while neuroforecasting demonstrates predictive power without explaining what neural signals reflect. This paper bridges these approaches by introducing a framework that identifies interpretable visual features underlying neural valuation signals that forecast demand. We propose that early neural valuation signals capture a common component of utility shared across consumers and that this component is partly driven by visual design elements. To test this hypothesis, we develop MotorVAE, a custom variational autoencoder designed to learn disentangled, interpretable representations from vehicle images. Unlike standard autoencoders, MotorVAE incorporates auxiliary classification objectives that encourage the latent space to align with meaningful visual structure. Our key methodological contribution is anchoring machine-learned visual features to independent neural data. We regress neural activity measured while participants view the same products onto MotorVAE latent dimensions, identifying a subset of visual features that covary with neural valuation signals known to predict aggregate demand. These neuro-anchored features are then translated into human-interpretable design elements using latent space traversal and validated through consumer judgments. Empirically, including neural data substantially improves demand prediction relative to survey-based models alone. Ongoing conjoint analyses benchmark the economic relevance of the identified features against standard industry approaches. Overall, this work moves demand modeling from prediction toward explanation, offering a transparent method for identifying which visual product attributes matter for markets.

title: Constraining Champions: How a Spending Cap Influenced Compet...
speaker: Ye Xu
abstract: In competitive markets where firms repeatedly invest to improve performance, regulators often impose financial constraints to promote balance and innovation. This study investigates the impact of a uniform spending cap on competitive dynamics, team performance, and innovation in Formula One. We construct a novel panel dataset spanning the 2018-2023 seasons, combining race outcomes, team budget data, and innovation metrics quantified and classified from media coverage using machine learning. To estimate the impact of spending caps, we employ a difference-in-differences framework that accommodates continuous treatment intensity. Results show that while the spending cap reduced the dominance of one historical leader, overall competitiveness did not improve. Mid-tier teams emerged as new winners in both innovation and performance, while resource-constrained competitors face increased barriers to catch up. These findings demonstrate that spending caps produced heterogeneous effects shaped by strategic adaptation and resource management, posing fundamental challenges for regulatory design intended to promote competitiveness and revealing unintended consequences. The study advances understanding of strategic adaptation and innovation under regulatory constraints in tournament-based markets, and provides actionable insights for policymakers evaluating financial regulation in sports and other dynamic competitive environments.

title: LLM-Driven Product Selection for Small E-Commerce
speaker: Yi Ji
abstract: Product selection is critical to the success of small businesses, yet data-driven decision-making is often prohibitively costly in resource-constrained settings. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer a promising alternative for supporting such decisions without requiring extensive data or model training. In this work, we propose Factor-Aware Comparative Evaluation for Selection (FACES), a training-free, two-stage decision framework that emphasizes comparative reasoning rather than pointwise prediction. FACES first induces a compact set of decision factors from historical campaign outcomes and then applies factor-conditioned, hierarchical comparative evaluation within carefully constructed reference groups to rank new candidates. Using real-world data from a representative small e-commerce firm engaged in international trade via Google Ads, we show that LLMs equipped with carefully constructed reference groups and comparative prompts substantially outperform pointwise LLM prompting approaches and competitive machine-learning benchmarks in predicting product-selection outcomes. We further find that larger reference groups can degrade performance, and that alternative information inclusion strategies in reference group construction lead to systematically different decision outcomes. These results provide actionable guidance for small businesses facing cold-start product selection challenges and offer new insights into how LLMs exploit relational structure in decision-making tasks.

title: User Preferences for Large Language Model Refusals: Implicat...
speaker: Maria Ana Vitorino
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) differ in their moderation and content policies, which determine which prompts these models refuse to answer. These refusals can affect user decisions of which models to use and whether to make safe or risky prompts. Using data from LMArena, where users select preferred responses to their prompts from paired LLM comparisons, we estimate a discrete choice model that captures user preferences for making risky prompts and their choice of which LLM provides the best response quality given the possibility of refusals. We leverage this model to analyze how moderation policies affect market shares across proprietary and open-source LLMs. Our findings reveal that proprietary LLMs provide higher quality responses and maintain larger market shares, but implement stricter moderation policies with higher refusal rates compared to open-source alternatives. This stricter moderation by proprietary LLMs reduces market concentration by allowing lower-quality open-source LLMs to compete effectively in the risky prompt segment. Mandating uniform moderation policies across all LLMs could increase market concentration favoring proprietary LLMs, potentially hampering competition. Our framework characterizes the efficient frontier of moderation policies that balance market concentration and safety.

title: The Impact of LLM Adoption on Online User Behavior
speaker: Nicolas Padilla
abstract: The adoption of AI tools, and especially Large Language Models (LLMs), has the potential to significantly transform how users engage with information online, potentially serving as substitutes or complements to existing digital resources. We use detailed clickstream data from 2022 and 2023 to examine users' online behavior following the adoption of large language models. We document a significant decrease in online search activity, a typical entry point to content consumption. Online searches drop slowly, suggesting a period during which users learn to use LLMs, but eventually adopters' level of online search in traditional search engines is more than 20% below the pre-adoption period, though there is heterogeneity across types of queries. We then turn to the effect of LLM adoption on website traffic. We document that while frequently visited websites are not affected, smaller websites suffer a significant drop in visits. In line with these results, we then report a significant drop in display ad exposures, especially to consumers with high levels of retail activity, though we do not find a reduction in search ad exposures. Last, we study two distinct categories of websites: education-related websites and user-generated content platforms. We document a significant drop in visits to education-related websites and heterogeneity across user-generated content platforms with a pronounced negative effect on Stack Overflow but no significant effect on Wikipedia, Reddit, and social media. We discuss implications for online content creators, for GenAI firms, and for public policy.

title: Economics of Agentic Customer Service: a Field Experiment on...
speaker: Chunhua Wu
abstract: E-commerce platforms face significant customer hassle costs and business inefficiencies in returns management, leading the industry to innovate with AI-driven returnless refund policies. We examine a policy experiment that uses an agentic system coordinating multiple AI agents to selectively provide partial refunds without requiring product returns. Through a large-scale field experiment involving nearly one million customers, we investigate the impacts on return costs, future customer value, and customer strategic behavior. We find that while the AI policy increases immediate refund costs, it generates substantially higher future customer spending that offsets additional costs associated with increased return requests and strategic behavior, demonstrating a powerful service recovery effect. Using a comprehensive economic framework analyzing key trade-offs, we establish opportunities for net economic gains, supporting the adoption of this innovative approach to returns management. This research provides the first large-scale experimental evidence on the impact of AI-automated returnless refunds on consumer and firm outcomes, providing contributions to the literature and generating practical insights for platforms.

title: ChatGPT Referrals to E-Commerce Websites: How Do LLMs Compar...
speaker: Christian Schulze
abstract: 1. We investigate organic Large Language Model traffic (oLLM) versus traditional digital channels in e-commerce. Analyzing 12 months of first-party data from 973 websites with $20 billion combined revenue, we examine over 50,000 transactions from ChatGPT referrals alongside 164 million transactions from traditional channels. Using regression models that account for data sparsity, we assess financial metrics (conversion rate, average order value, revenue per session) and engagement metrics (bounce rate, session duration, page views). Results are consistent across extensive robustness checks. One year after launch, oLLM exhibits conversion rates and revenue per session above paid social but below all other traditional channels. Product complexity moderates the effects: oLLM's financial outcomes and traffic shares are stronger in complex product categories. Engagement metrics show favorable bounce rates but lower session duration and page views. Temporal analysis shows increasing conversion rates but declining average order values, yielding only moderate revenue-per-session gains over time. Cross-website analyses support growing consumer LLM proficiency as the underlying mechanism. The descriptive analyses position oLLM as a new and developing channel. With low volumes and modest revenue per session, oLLM currently serves niche informational needs of proficient consumers and does not yet function as a broad conversion channel

title: The Ever-Evolving Online Customer Journey: Bridging Academic...
speaker: Amir Khan
abstract: The online customer journey has evolved into a non-linear and dynamic process that is constantly being shaped by digital environments, platforms and frequently shifting customer expectations. In the era of agentic ecosystem, consumers travel with their digital proxies, giving more control to their AI agents (Becca Coggins, 2025). Future interactions will increasingly be between consumer agents and merchants’ agents, leading to multi-agent interactions in the agentic world (McKinsey, 2025). Online Consumer buying, controlled by AI agents acting on behalf on consumers, will have a huge impact on the online market. Human thinking may increasingly be surrendered to AI-negotiated deals. In this agentic driven-economy, brands will have to make major shifts in their approach to creating, positioning and delivering highly personalised customer journey experiences. These changes will no longer be limited to product evaluation by consumer agents but will also impact companies’ customer acquisition and retention systems, as AI agents will become new gatekeepers in the evolving customer journey (Marie Claude Nadeau, 2025) This study conducts a systematic review of academic and industry publications to synthesise current knowledge and identify key conceptual and empirical gaps in the understanding of the online customer journey. While Industry research explains practical approaches that combine analytics with customer touchpoint management, it still lacks strong theoretical grounding, whereas academic research provides conceptual depth but insufficient detail on rapidly evolving digital practices.

title: The Invisible use of LLMs: Disclosure and Coordination
speaker: Jessie Liu
abstract: This paper focuses on an increasingly common reality in analytical modeling research: LLMs are routinely used in the pre-formal stages of theory development, often in ways that are not directly observable in published work. We document a set of “invisible” uses of LLMs in theory development, including conjecture generation, error and assumption checking, and the exploration of boundary cases. These applications influence the structure and direction of analytical arguments while leaving no verifiable artifact in the final output. We argue that this “invisible adoption” creates a tension for disclosure norms. Unlike software tools that produce auditable outputs, LLMs influence the reasoning process in a way that cannot be directly validated. As a result, voluntary disclosure may act as a noisy and potentially stigmatizing signal, rather than as a transparent indicator of research quality. We discuss how such stigma can generate adverse selection in disclosure, potentially rewarding non-disclosure even when LLMs are used to improve rigor and productivity. Taken together, this paper frames the use of LLMs as an ongoing coordination problem. The core question is how the field will coordinate on norms when the primary effects of these tools are already embedded, and largely invisible, within the research process itself.

title: When Technical Brilliance Becomes Cheap(Er): Signaling Failu...
speaker: David Godes
abstract: The adoption by analytical modelers of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, while not directly observable, seems to be increasing rapidly. This isn’t surprising given the myriad benefits these tools offer the theorist, particularly in reducing the costs associated with the executional stages of model-building such as structuring and proving complex theoretical claims. In this talk, I will argue that a potential side effect of this cost reduction is the weakening of many of the core signals of analytical skill: algebraic derivation, proof completion, and exhaustive extensions. When execution is cheap but evaluation criteria remain fixed, technically polished but conceptually thin models become easier to produce and harder to distinguish from genuinely insightful work. One potential prediction is declining returns to technical complexity, disadvantaging researchers whose comparative advantage lies in execution rather than, say, conceptual selection and/or narrative clarity. This shift has clear implications that extend beyond individual productivity to include the equilibrium quality of the literature, the training of doctoral students, refereeing norms, and tenure and promotion.

title: LLMs as Complements of, vs. Substitutes for, Researcher Judg...
speaker: Tommaso Bondi
abstract: This talk examines how large language models (LLMs) can support theoretical research in marketing by augmenting, rather than replacing, researcher judgment. I organize the discussion around a logical research workflow. First, novelty testing: while (still) not particularly effective at coming up with novel ideas, LLMs can be used as an early filter to assess whether an idea is plausibly new or risks rediscovering known results. Second, correctness: models can help check logical consistency, verify derivations, and flag gaps or unstated assumptions in propositions and proofs. Third, boundary exploration: LLMs can systematically probe when a theory breaks down, which assumptions are essential, and how results extend to nearby settings and/or have more striking interpretations. Finally, I introduce synthetic feedback, using LLMs to simulate the review process to pressure-test clarity, contribution, and positioning. I conclude by discussing limitations, including hallucinations, shallow novelty assessments, overconfidence, confirmation bias, and the risk of outsourcing judgment, and offer guidelines for responsible use.

title: The Effect of Logic Expression in Promotions: Evidence from ...
speaker: Fred Feinberg
abstract: Promotional offers are often evaluated by their economic content -- reward magnitude, eligibility requirements, or timing -- but such changes inevitably alter how offers are logically expressed. We study how the logical structure of promotional language, beyond its monetary value, affects consumer response. We conceptualize promotions as rule-based systems composed of requirements and rewards connected through implicit logical operators (e.g., and, or, if–then). Using large language and other "high-dimensional" regularized models, we parse natural-language promotions into formal propositional logic expressions and develop a novel, interpretable measure of logic complexity capturing multiplicity, interdependence, and structural diversity. Analyzing a rich longitudinal dataset from the North American mobile phone market, we examine how logic complexity influences weekly sales while controlling for prices, promotional value, advertising, and competitive conditions. Using a comprehensive, nonparametric framework for data fusion between "stated" and "revealed" preference measures, we find that greater logical complexity is associated with higher sales on average, but the effect is highly heterogeneous across brands. For technologically sophisticated brands such as Apple and Google, complex promotional logic significantly boosts sales, whereas for lower-tech brands it yields weaker or negative returns. These results are robust across fixed-effects models, linguistic instrumental variables, and IV-free identification strategies. Our findings highlight how behavioral and choice-theoretic structure can inform the design of AI-mediated marketing systems, and how AI tools can, in turn, uncover meaningful structure in consumer-facing language.

title: Motivating Consumer and AI Co-Creation
speaker: Lan L...
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes digital mass customization by altering the structure of consumer–AI co-creation. When consumers can start from an AI-generated draft rather than a blank canvas, outcomes are jointly determined by two stages: whether consumers initiate co-creation and, conditional on participation, how much refinement effort they exert. Partnering with a leading U.S. online retailer of personalized photo products, we study the causal impact of motivating participation in consumer–AI co-creation and examine how alternative participation interventions shape downstream purchase outcomes. We develop a two-stage model in which, relative to a baseline with organic participation, a nudge lowers start-up frictions and expands voluntary entry, whereas a mandate guarantees entry but can weaken how participation translates into purchase, generating a reach–efficiency trade-off. Two randomized experiments support the model’s predictions. In Study 1, a light-touch nudge increases participation by 5.98 percentage points and raises revenue, with gains driven by expanded entry rather than intensified refinement effort. In Study 2, mandating participation further increases participation but yields weaker downstream outcomes, including lower conversion efficiency and a higher incidence of minimal-compliance participation. Together, these findings highlight a fundamental trade-off between expanding participation and preserving engagement quality in consumer–AI co-creation.

title: Calibrated Coarsening: Designing Info for AI-Assisted Decisi...
speaker: Ruru Hoong
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to aid human decision-making across critical applications, but errors in human probabilistic reasoning (e.g., cognitive biases) often undermine its effectiveness. This raises the central design question of how to provide AI input to humans in a way that improves decision-making outcomes. We propose calibrated coarsening---partitioning the signal space into fewer cells at chosen thresholds---as a way to do so that (i) ensures humans retain final decision authority, (ii) modifies signals without deception, and (iii) adapts flexibly to diverse biases and contexts. Within an information disclosure framework, we derive an approximately optimal binary coarsened policy when the designer does not observe the decision-maker's information. In a randomised experiment with professional loan specialists, we empirically demonstrate that coarsening AI signals at the theory-derived threshold significantly improves decision-making outcomes, outperforming both the human-only (based solely on the loan application) and uncoarsened AI assistance (continuous AI risk-score, in addition to loan application) benchmarks. We uncover substantial decision heterogeneity amongst loan officers and estimate a Bayesian hierarchical linear model (HLM), which we use to simulate and test the benefits of personalised coarsening policies.

title: Visual Diversity and Consumer Choice in Online Platforms
speaker: Madhav Kumar
abstract: We investigate consumer preferences for visual diversity by examining the relationship between display model skin tone and product performance across major global fashion brands. Using comprehensive data from five major brands, we document substantial variation in model representation and employ a matching approach to analyze performance outcomes. We find that products featuring darker skin tone models are significantly more likely to become top sellers. To isolate the underlying consumer preferences driving this effect, we conduct two carefully designed experiments using generative AI to manipulate model skin tone while holding product characteristics constant. Our experimental results reveal that consumers express significantly higher purchase intent for products featuring darker skin tone models. These findings show that the performance advantage is driven primarily by consumer preferences rather than supply-side factors such as product targeting or quality differences. Our research provides a comprehensive, causally-identified measurement of consumer demand for visual diversity in digital commerce, offering brands empirical tools to measure and optimize their representation strategies.

title: When AI Reconfigures Status Coping: Social Status Threats an...
speaker: Nan-Hee Jeong
abstract: Individuals frequently experience threats to their social status through upward social comparison and often respond with compensatory behaviors aimed at restoring threatened self-worth, power, or social standing (Gal 2015). Extending this literature, Goor, Keinan, and Ordabayeva (2021) proposed status pivoting, whereby individuals cope with status threats by seeking affirmation in alternative life domains, guided by motivated trade-off beliefs that construe success as zero-sum across domains. As social interaction increasingly occurs within AI-mediated metaverse environments, it remains unclear whether such compensatory mechanisms generalize beyond the real world. Unlike offline contexts, the metaverse is shaped by intelligent systems that curate social information and mediate evaluations (Barrera and Shah 2023), potentially altering how social status threats are interpreted. Across two experiments, we examine whether status pivoting persists in AI-mediated metaverse contexts relative to the real world. Study 1 employed a 2 (context) × 2 (power) between-subjects design and revealed a significant interaction (b = −2.08, p < .01). Low-power participants in the real world pivoted toward alternative domains, whereas no such effect emerged in the metaverse. Study 2 replicated these findings using a 2 (context) × 2 (status threat) design, again showing attenuated status pivoting in the metaverse (b = −1.37, p < .05). Mediation analyses (Hayes and Scharkow 2013) showed that motivated trade-off beliefs accounted for this divergence. By conceptualizing the metaverse as an AI-mediated social environment, this research identifies a boundary condition for status pivoting and demonstrates how AI reshapes responses to social status threats.

title: Understanding the Dynamics of User-Bot-Crowd Interaction in ...
speaker: Xupin Zhang
abstract: With the growing commercialization of social media platforms and the increasingly prominent role of algorithmic gatekeeping, users’ motivation to create content and interact with others has declined. To promote user participation and sustain engagement, more platforms have turned to social robots. Yet, previous research has not systematically examined the dynamic structure of user-robot-crowd interaction, leaving the mechanisms of diffusion and influence insufficiently understood. Using publicly available interaction data collected from the Weibo social robot “CommentRobert” between December 2023 and April 2025, we applied large language models (LLMs) to automatically categorize users’ motives for engaging and the robot’s response styles, and to measure how deeply other users participated and how widely their discussion evolved. The findings show that demographic attributes, account features, and regional contexts affect why users interact with the robot. These motivations then shape the robot’s response patterns and increase user satisfaction, which subsequently stimulates additional user participation and broader social diffusion. This study advances marketing theory on bot-enabled engagement and provides actionable guidance for platform managers on designing response strategies that deepen user engagement, strengthen retention, and improve the long-term health of platform communities.

title: From Access to Agency: Optimal Pricing for the Agentic Econo...
speaker: Yi Wang
abstract: The emergence of autonomous AI agents is precipitating a structural shift in the digital economy from "selling tools" to "selling work." As AI agents gain autonomy, the fundamental economic friction shifts from user adoption to incentive alignment. Specifically, we identify a critical trade-off between Usage-Based Pricing (UBP) and Outcome-Based Pricing (OBP). Under UBP, vendors face an efficiency Moral Hazard: because revenue is tied to compute consumption (tokens), vendors are incentivized to deploy inefficient, bloated agentic workflows that maximize volume rather than speed. Conversely, OBP aligns vendor incentives with computational efficiency but imposes a verification cost on the user—the friction of auditing probabilistic outputs to confirm that inquiries are genuinely resolved.  This paper develops a principal-agent model to analyze this tension, focusing on the interplay between AI model maturity (autonomous success probability), vendor inefficiency (token inflation), and the user’s verification burden. We address three core questions: First, under what conditions, does OBP dominate UBP as the equilibrium strategy? Second, how does the transition to OBP impact consumer welfare? Third, we propose a verification-adjusted two-part tariff mechanism to resolve the efficiency hazard by subsidizing the user’s audit burden, thereby approximating the first-best outcome in an autonomous economy.

title: Dynamic Consumer-AI Love Relationship: Formation and Continu...
speaker: Hang Xu
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed functional chatbots into AI companions capable of imitating human-like relationships. Grounded in Triangular Theory of Love, we study emotional bonding between consumers and AI companions by analyzing the dynamics of three love components: intimacy, passion, and commitment. Using a panel dataset of consumer-AI interactions, we quantify expressed love in each of these three components through an analysis of conversational data for each consumer-AI pair. Our findings reveal emotional bonding with saturation: As consumers engage in more interactions with an AI, they express stronger intimacy, passion, and commitment, but at a diminishing rate. Moreover, the expressed love is greater when consumers engage with AI companions designed for relational roles (e.g., romantic partners) than for functional roles (e.g., service providers). We also identify relationship-sustaining love balances: While higher mutual intimacy drives relationship formation, the continuation of dyadic relationship favors asymmetry. Specifically, consumers are more likely to continue relationships with AI companions when they express higher intimacy and commitment, while the AI companion express higher passion. In this research, we also conduct experiments to establish causality and further explore potential mechanisms. These nuanced consumer preferences in bonding with AI offer critical insights for designing adaptive, engaging, and responsible AI companions.

title: Reinforcement Learning Based Computationally Efficient Condi...
speaker: Sonal Srivastava
abstract: Dynamic discrete choice (DDC) models have found widespread application in marketing. However, estimating these becomes challenging in "big data'' settings with high-dimensional state–action spaces. To address this challenge, this paper develops a Reinforcement Learning (RL)–based two-step ("computationally light'') Conditional Choice Simulation (CCS) estimation approach that combines the scalability of machine learning with the transparency, explainability, and interpretability of structural models, that is particularly valuable for counterfactual policy analysis. The method is premised on three insights: (1) the CCS ("forward simulation'') approach is a special case of RL algorithms, (2) starting from an initial state-action pair CCS updates the corresponding value function only after each simulation path has terminated, whereas RL algorithms may update for all the state-action pairs visited along a simulated path, and (3) RL focuses on inferring an agent’s optimal policy with known reward functions, whereas DDC models focus on estimating the reward functions presupposing optimal policies. The procedure’s computational efficiency over CCS estimation is demonstrated using Monte Carlos with a canonical machine replacement and a consumer food purchase model. Framing CCS estimation of DDC models as a RL problem increases their applicability and scalability to high-dimensional marketing problems while retaining both interpretability and tractability.

title: The Welfare Effects of Behavior-Based Promotion Discriminati...
speaker: Francesco Gabriele
abstract: E-commerce retailers have the power to personalize promotions based on users’ online past purchase behavior. This paper develops a structural model of consumer demand and a policy model of personalized promotions to quantify the welfare effects of behavior-based promotion discrimination (BBPD). Using data from a randomized controlled field experiment with coupons on a cosmetics e-commerce site, the structural estimation reveals an elastic and heterogeneous demand to price discount treatments. With nonparametric estimation via machine learning, the counterfactual analysis tests different targeting algorithms and shows that promotion personalization increases e-commerce profit by 24% and consumer surplus by 4% relative to the uniform pricing benchmark. Exploiting past purchase information is profitable for the e-commerce: BBPD improves personalized coupons algorithm by generating an additional 11% gain in producer surplus without harming loyal customers. This paper contributes to the current public policy debate about personalized pricing strategies in digital markets as the welfare analysis has implications for privacy and fairness concerns.

title: The Voice of Emotion: Advancing Marketing Research Through R...
speaker: Ertugrul Uysal
abstract: This paper introduces a novel methodological approach for analyzing consumer emotions through voice, leveraging recent advances in computational psychology and artificial intelligence (AI). While traditional approaches to voice analysis in marketing research have provided valuable insights on consumer emotions, we conceptually argue and empirically demonstrate that AI emotion measurements provide significant benefits to marketing research in studying consumer emotions. That is, this new method offers unprecedented granularity by measuring up to 48 distinct emotional expressions in real-time conversation. Two key methodological benefits of AI emotion measurements for marketing research are demonstrated through pilot studies. First, expanded emotional granularity more than doubles the predictive power compared to traditional emotion measurement approaches, with complex, nuanced emotions emerging as meaningful predictors of consumer outcomes. Second, the sentence-to-sentence measurement capability enables real-time emotional trajectory analysis, revealing dynamic patterns and inflection points that static measurement approaches cannot capture. The pilot demonstrations show how this methodology advances beyond basic acoustic parameters to capture the rich emotional information that voice naturally conveys. The paper concludes by discussing how this methodological framework opens new avenues for investigating the role of emotions in consumer behavior across voice-mediated contexts that are increasingly prevalent in the digital marketplace.

title: AI-Based Salesforce Performance Evaluation: Gains, Costs, an...
speaker: Qing Li
abstract: Advances in AI has motivated firms to route and record more client interactions through digital systems, enabling AI-based evaluation tools that monitor salespeople’s conversations and assess their performance. This transition fundamentally changes salesforce feedback and control by replacing infrequent, manager-curated reviews with automated, high-frequency, multidimensional performance scores. However, existing research on AI in sales and on performance feedback offers little guidance on how this shift to always-on, algorithmic evalution affects salespeople’s effort allocation, learning, and customer outcomes in the field. We study the adoption of an AI-evalution system that provides daily performance scores, that are multidimensional and capturing key aspects of salespeople’s skills and performance, derived from salespeople’s recorded sales calls, embedded within a CRM and rolled out in a quasi-experimental fashion. AI-evaluation adoption boosted new customer acquisition, with individual salespeople's new orders increased by 59.2%. At the team level, new orders and revenue rose by 42.0% and 116.2%, respectively. Concurrently, repurchase improved, as the customer retention rate increased by 2.3%. However, these gains came with significant costs, such as reduced work efficiency. Moreover, we observed substantial heterogeneity, as the impact varied significantly based on salespeople's prior performance levels. For instance, high performers saw the greatest increases in new orders, while medium performers benefited the most in revenue but also experienced the most adverse side effects after adoption. Overall, our findings offers practical insights for optimizing AI-evaluation to enhance customer acquisition and retention while mitigating heterogeneity and costs.

title: When AI Summarizes Consumer Voices: The Originality Cost of ...
speaker: Jie Li
abstract: Online reviews play a crucial role in service operations by informing firms about service quality. Traditionally, platforms helped consumers process large volumes of reviews using simple aggregates such as average ratings or frequently mentioned keywords. Recently, service firms adopted GenAI to automatically generate textual summaries of past reviews, aiming to synthesize diverse customer experiences into concise, balanced overviews. While operationally efficient, the broader effects of these AI summaries on subsequent consumer reviews remain less understood. We exploit the partial roll-out of AI-generated summaries on TripAdvisor hotel reviews to identify their causal impact on subsequent user-generated review, using consumer review data of hotels in Texas. Employing a difference-in-differences research design, we find that the introduction of AI summaries significantly reduces the perceived helpfulness of subsequent reviews. Investigating the mechanisms, we examine changes in review characteristics and find that the introduction of AI summaries reduces the diversity and originality of subsequent reviews. Specifically, after the AI summary implementation, reviews for treated hotels exhibit less dispersion in ratings, become shorter, and reflect reduced topical diversity. Moreover, subsequent reviews become increasingly similar to the AI-generated summaries in both structure and content, indicating a loss of originality in how consumers express their voices. Collectively, the findings reveal an operational trade-off in AI-enabled review summary systems: while GenAI summaries enhance information-processing efficiency, they simultaneously diminish the richness of customer feedback that firms rely on for diagnosing service issues and guiding quality improvement. The results offer new insights into the design and management of AI-enabled service operations.

title: Less is More: the Impact of AI-Generated Summary on Review R...
speaker: Min Zhang
abstract: AI-generated summary (AIGS) is an instantiation of generative AI tools that reconstructs dispersed collective wisdom into rich, balanced, and readable knowledge, increasingly piloted by leading e-commerce platforms. However, there remains a lack of empirical evidence to determine whether AIGS has causally enhanced review ratings. Drawing on expectation confirmation theory, this study employs a difference-in-differences approach on a large-scale Amazon panel to estimate the causal effect of AIGS on review ratings, measured as the average star rating of newly posted reviews in each period. Results demonstrate that AIGS improves review ratings by presenting more comprehensive information about product traits, thereby reducing mismatch risk and supporting more accurate post-purchase evaluations. This study advances theory by explicating the informational nature of AIGS and demonstrating its role as a feasible pathway to enhance review ratings. For practice, we offer actionable guidance for the strategic deployment of AIGS within online review systems.

title: How Competition in Genai Availability Shapes Consumer Review...
speaker: Weilong Gu
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly influencing the way consumers search for products and communicate their experiences. First research results document the impact of GenAI availability on consumer reviews relative to environments with where GenAI is unavailable. As markets evolve, consumers may now face variation in GenAI availability, ranging from single-tool dominance to competition among multiple tools. Yet little is known about how such variation impacts consumer behavior. This study examines the impact of competition among GenAI tools on consumer reviewing behavior. We leverage the regulatory approval for general, public use of eight LLMs in August 2023 in mainland China as an event. Following this approval, several LLMs were launched over the course of two months for consumers to use in mainland China. This setting allows us to isolate the effects of GenAI competition in mainland China and compare them to Hong Kong as a control group, where GenAI availability during the same period remained concentrated around a single tool. Using a difference-in-differences research design, we analyze hotel reviews from Ctrip.com posted by users in mainland China vs. Hong Kong. We examine the impact of GenAI competition on review similarity, volume, and sentiment. This study contributes to our understanding of the impact of Gen AI on consumer word-of-mouth behavior in online environments.

title: From Many Voices to One Summary: The Impact of Google Maps--...
speaker: Yancheng Zhang
abstract: Large language models are increasingly embedded in digital platforms to summarize user generated content, yet causal evidence on how such AI mediation affects contributor behavior remains limited. We study the introduction of Ask Maps, an AI powered feature on Google Maps that generates conversational answers based on summaries of restaurant reviews. We exploit the public release of Ask Maps on the Apple App Store in April 2025 as a natural field experiment. We compile restaurant level panel data for New York City, matching 2,999 restaurants that appear on both Google Maps and TripAdvisor. Using a difference in differences design, we compare changes in review activity on Google Maps, which adopts AI based review summarization, to TripAdvisor, which does not introduce a similar feature during the study period. We find that Ask Maps increases review volume, with effects most credibly identified at the monthly level and strengthening over time, consistent with gradual user adoption following the feature launch. The effects are heterogeneous. Increases in review activity are larger for restaurants with higher pre treatment review stocks and are driven primarily by highly active contributors, while the share of reviews written by first time contributors does not increase significantly. We also find a positive effect on restaurant ratings after excluding the initial post treatment period. Overall, AI powered review summarization raises user participation, but the gains accrue disproportionately to established restaurants and top contributors, with implications for platform design and the evolution of online content ecosystems.

title: When AI Joins the Team: Incentive Design for Human-AI Collab...
speaker: Bo Pang
abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into organizational processes necessitates a re-evaluation of traditional incentive schemes. Utilizing a principal–agent framework, this study analyzes how the integration of AI reshapes optimal contracting. Our model identifies two critical dimensions: the incentive effect, focusing on shifts in individual effort, and the selection effect, addressing changes in human capital composition. By delineating the patterns of human-AI synergy, we uncover the underlying mechanisms of these effects. The results offer a new theoretical perspective on human-AI coordination and provide actionable insights for incentive design across diverse institutional settings.

title: ***Cancelled***Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects...
speaker: Jingbo Wang
abstract: We propose a novel framework to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects in network-based quasi-experiments, addressing the challenge of interference without requiring prior assumptions on spillover mechanisms. Our approach leverages a dual neural network architecture combined with graph convolutional networks to process full non-Euclidean graph structures. We establish formal theoretical identification conditions and provide functional approximation guarantees for the neural estimator. Validated via Monte Carlo simulations and applied to a massive online multiplayer game with over 140,000 users, our method reveals that reaching level milestones increases daily transactions by 45-63%. Crucially, we uncover significant heterogeneity based on network position: socially isolated players exhibit stronger responses to content unlocks than well-connected players. These findings extend causal deep learning to networked settings and offer actionable insights for personalized player retention strategies.

title: Sense Without Sensibility? How AI-Generated Content Shapes C...
speaker: Yin Bai
abstract: AI-generated content (AIGC) is reshaping the landscape of content marketing and redefining the dynamics of online brand communication. Anchored in dual-process theory, this study examines the objective content features of AIGC and investigates how its use in advertising copy influences consumer engagement through two competing pathways: informativeness and emotionality. Leveraging large-scale field data, our empirical analysis demonstrates that a greater proportion of AIGC in advertising copy is positively associated information entropy but negatively associated with emotional arousal, which further shapes consumer engagement. Notably, the impact of AIGC varies systematically across product categories: for search products, greater reliance on AIGC attenuates consumer engagement, whereas for experience products, the effect is reversed. These divergent patterns stem from the shifting relative salience of informational versus emotional content across contexts. Collectively, this research advances the emerging literature on AI-enabled marketing and offers actionable insights for managers seeking to strategically integrate generative AI into marketing practice.

title: Generative AI and Content Homogenization: The Case of Digita...
speaker: Chaoran Liu
abstract: Traditionally, entrepreneurs and small businesses, constrained by limited resources, struggle to create high-quality marketing content, which limits consumer engagement and hampers growth. Generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) presents a powerful, yet affordable tool to overcome this challenge. However, the widespread adoption of Gen AI may have unintended consequences. Specifically, content generated by popular large language models may appear more similar to each other compared to human created content, known as content homogenization. To examine the extent of content homogenization and its potential implications, we study the restaurant industry – a highly fragmented sector where 70% of the establishments are owned by independent entrepreneurs. We leverage the country-wide ChatGPT ban in Italy during April 2023 as a natural experiment to examine how access to Gen AI affects content homogenization, consumer engagement, and volume of social media marketing content created by small business owners. Our study shows that restaurants in the treatment group—located in Milan, Italy—experienced relative decreases of 15%, 12%, 2%, and 3% in lexical, syntactic, semantic, and language style similarity in their Instagram marketing content during the ban, suggesting that access to ChatGPT leads to content homogenization. We also find the ban has a positive effect on consumer engagement – an approximate 3.5% increase in average like counts – despite negative effects on posting frequency and post length. This research aims to provide valuable insights to entrepreneurs and small businesses on how to better harness the capability of Gen AI while mitigating potential drawbacks.

title: When Everyone Gets the Same Spark: Effects of Generative AI ...
speaker: Franziska Vogel
abstract: Generative AI is expected to reshape the nature and diversity of output in the creator economy, yet its implications remain understudied and largely confined to laboratory experiments. We address this gap by conducting a quasi-experimental field study using large-scale data on creators and their outputs over time. Specifically, we study the rollout of YouTube’s Inspiration Tab, an ideation feature that provides creators with AI-generated content ideas, storylines, and visual guidance. Access was granted to creators in the United States in November 2024, while creators across Europe did not receive the feature. We construct a longitudinal panel of matched creators and combine platform data with multimodal measures derived from video transcripts, thumbnails, and viewer comments. Using difference-in-differences event studies, we examine how AI-assisted ideation affects content production, creative diversity, and user attention. We find that access to AI inspiration increases content supply along both margins: additional creators enter the platform following rollout, and incumbent creators publish more videos. Productivity effects are heterogeneous and stronger in lower-expertise domains. Turning to creative diversity, AI inspiration reshapes creators’ internal content portfolios: creators reuse more similar language and concentrate on fewer topics, while experimenting more with visual presentation. Importantly, these within-creator shifts do not translate into ecosystem-level homogenization – linguistic, topical, and visual diversity across creators remains stable. Finally, increased content supply translates into higher aggregate reach but lower per-video engagement. Views, likes, and comments per video decline, while audience sentiment remains unchanged, reflecting intensified competition for limited user attention rather than reduced content quality.

title: Will It Click? Advertising Strategy with Generative AI
speaker: Dominique Lauga
abstract: Increasingly, companies are leveraging AI technologies to interact with consumers, with many marketers adopting Generative AI tools to create personalized messages at scale. In this paper, we model the impact of GenAI on advertising strategy. Firms seek to sell a product to heterogeneous consumers and can imperfectly identify their message preferences, i.e., which creative is most likely to prompt a response (or click). The firm has a baseline advertising message template and uses GenAI to adapt it and tailor a message to each consumer. However, GenAI messages can deviate from the intended consumer’s preference. In a monopoly, the optimal advertising strategy results in a click probability that exhibits an inverted U-shape, depending on the consumer’s message preference. We also uncover an interplay between the ability to identify consumers’ preferences and GenAI technology. Specifically, when GenAI is not too accurate, improvements in the ability to identify consumers may initially lead firms to target fewer consumers. We extend the model to a competitive setting with two firms equipped with GenAI. We find that if the consumer is located closer to a firm in the message space, counterintuitively, the probability of clicking on a firm's ad decreases, while that of its rival increases, as GenAI’s accuracy improves. Consequently, improved GenAI accuracy intensifies competition and leads to reduced profits; while the reverse is true as the ability to identify consumer preferences improves. Finally, we show that firms’ investments in GenAI capability are strategic substitutes, potentially leading to asymmetric investment levels across competitors.

title: Improving the Efficacy of Online Learning Platforms Using Ar...
speaker: Chul Kim
abstract: Digital learning platforms that offer virtual education are growing rapidly, with online learning increasingly replacing or complementing traditional in-person instruction. To the extent that online learning opportunities create both societal value – by expanding access to education and economic benefits – reflected in new business models, the demand for effective online learning is accelerating. We propose an artificial intelligence (AI)-based approach for more efficacious online learning on such platforms by incorporating three theoretically and empirically supported pedagogical factors– relevancy, embeddedness, and variety. We implement the proposed approach in an online learning platform for K-12 mathematics education. Using data from a natural experiment, we obtain robust empirical evidence of the efficacy of the proposed approach in improving learners’ proficiency and key marketing outcome of learner retention. Extensive robustness analysis, including replication of the field study in a different country, provides support for these key findings. From a managerial perspective, our study offers insights into balancing service quality and operational efficiency with AI, a core challenge in the digital education landscape. In addition, from a pedagogical standpoint, our study enriches the understanding of how AI can support adaptive learning models.

title: The Price is Right: Stock Market Reactions to Pricing Inform...
speaker: Paul Seehawer
abstract: Many consider pricing to be the most powerful marketing lever for revenue, profit, and thus firm value creation. Despite this consensus, there is limited research on how pricing information affects investor behavior. This research focuses on pricing information in earnings calls, which we conceptualize as informative pricing-related signals that allow investors to form timely expectations about firm value. Using signaling theory, the authors develop a conceptual framework for pricing information in earnings calls. Empirically, this is the first marketing study to apply FinBERT, a large language model developed specifically for financial texts, to identify and classify pricing information in over 26,000 earnings call transcripts for the period 2008-2024. The study finds that managers provide pricing information in the vast majority (98.6%) of earnings calls. An event study shows that pricing information with negative sentiment has a stronger impact on firm value than positive pricing information. The authors further investigate the moderating effects of signaler- (CEO vs. CFO), signal- (cost vs. demand; past vs. future), and signaling-environment-related (part of the earnings call; actual pricing performance; inflation; industry concentration) factors. Our findings have important implications for the general power of pricing and the disclosure of pricing information in corporate communications.

title: Generative AI and the Division of Labor in Knowledge Work : ...
speaker: Lena Poinsignon
abstract: Generative AI is reshaping open source software (OSS) development by changing how developers search for information and write code. This paper examines whether the public release of ChatGPT-3.5 is associated with a reallocation of OSS activity on GitHub, and whether responses differ between institutional (firm-linked) and independent developers. We build a large-scale monthly panel from a random sample of one million developer accounts, collecting data on their public repositories, contribution activity, and visibility signals (stars and forks) via the platform’s REST API. Institutional developers are identified based on self-reported employer information and contributions to organization-owned repositories, while others are classified as independent. Exploiting the release of the ChatGPT-3.5 release, we estimate a difference-in-differences design with developer and month fixed effects. In addition, we collect GitHub Archive events to enrich the measurement of public activity. Relative to independents, institutional developers display a stronger post-shock decline in the number of public repositories. Concurrently, their remaining public projects become more visible and are more likely to rely on pre-existing work : they receive more stars and exhibit a higher share of outgoing forks. A plausible explanation for these results is that firms rationalize their open source strategy in the presence of genAI. While maintaining many public repositories could serve as brand-building and signalling technical excellence, part of these promotional work can now be achieved through AI-generated content. Firms reallocate developers’ time towards a smaller set of strategically important projects, while independent developers adjust in the same direction, but less sharply.

title: Generative AI and the Gender Gap: Evidence from a Large Digi...
speaker: Hongcan Zhou
abstract: While the rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the creative economy, its impact on gender inequality remains underexplored. We investigate gender differences in GenAI adoption, productivity, and market exit by analyzing over 500,000 creators on a leading digital content platform following a major GenAI shock. We find that following the release of a high-quality GenAI tool, a substantial gender gap in AI adoption emerges: male creators adopt AI 3.5 times more than female creators. We further document that female creators face declining productivity and are more likely to exit the platform over time, indicating a persistent disadvantage in long-term participation. Further analysis reveals that this disadvantage stems primarily from the adoption gap; conditional on adoption, female creators exhibit productivity levels comparable to their male counterparts. Our findings suggest that in the long run, this gap in AI adoption could permanently harm the platform’s diversity and creative output. Keywords: Generative AI, Gender Gap, Gender Inequality, Creative Economy

title: Content-Aligned Cover Design: A Multimodal Deep Learning App...
speaker: Yijing Xu
abstract: Cover design remains a decisive factor in how audiences evaluate media products: book covers, movie posters, and related promotional imagery shape expectations about genre, emotional tone, and narrative content, and strongly influence purchase decisions. Yet, despite the importance of these cues, firms typically rely on intuition, negotiation, and iterative trial-and-error when developing cover concepts. This process is subjective, costly, and resource-intensive, and designers must tailor every cover to the unique characteristics of the underlying content—precluding any one-size-fits-all solution. In this paper, we introduce a novel multimodal deep learning framework that supports this creative workflow by leveraging visual and text transformers. The approach first identifies semantic elements (e.g., objects, actions) and perceptual elements (e.g., colors, textures) that are predictive of cover performance given a description of the media content. It then uses generative models to propose examples of cover designs optimized along these learned drivers. By grounding the system in established theories of visual and meaning-based processing, the framework provides interpretable insights into why specific cues matter. For managers, this method offers a structured way to diagnose the components of high-performing cover designs, reduce reliance on costly manual experimentation, and enable creative teams to explore a wider range of informed concepts early in development.

title: Efficient Screening: Evidence on Question Redundancy and Tim...
speaker: Emil Palikot
abstract: AI-conducted interviews offer a scalable solution for candidate screening, yet impose substantial time costs on job seekers. In Aka et al. (2025), we demonstrate the predictive validity of AI interviews but document a stark efficiency tradeoff: for every hour of recruiter time saved, candidates collectively invest approximately 45 hours completing structured assessments. In this paper, we investigate whether AI interviews can be shortened without sacrificing information quality, thereby improving this tradeoff. Using a dataset of 10,000 interview transcripts, we first document significant redundancy in current interview protocols—many questions contribute little incremental predictive power for candidate grades or subsequent hiring manager evaluations. We identify systematic patterns in question redundancy, finding that certain question types consistently yield minimal additional signal once core competencies have been assessed. Based on these findings, we develop and experimentally test a modified interview algorithm that dynamically adjusts interview length based on accumulated information. Our results demonstrate substantial time savings for candidates with no measurable loss in predictive accuracy for either AI-generated assessments or downstream hiring outcomes. These findings offer a path toward more candidate-friendly AI recruitment processes that preserve selection quality while meaningfully reducing the burden on job seekers.

title: Bull vs. Bear Voices: Adapting Service Communication Strateg...
speaker: Ye Zheng
abstract: This study investigates how stock market volatility fundamentally alters the effectiveness of service representatives' vocal cues on customer loyalty. By linking macro-economic health to micro-interpersonal dynamics, the research explores how market fluctuations prime customers with a "distorted mindset" characterised by financial threat and cognitive scarcity. Moving beyond self-reported surveys, we utilise actual net investment activity to measure behavioural loyalty in a high-stakes context. The methodology combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with advanced audio mining tools to analyse over 2,000 call recordings from an Australian investment company between 2019 and 2021. The findings reveal that the optimal vocal strategy relies entirely on market conditions. During positive ("Bull") markets, when customers focus on aspiration, vocal warmth significantly increases loyalty among stressed clients. However, this dynamic inverts during "Bear" markets. In downturns, stressed customers shift toward "security and loss-avoidance" to conserve resources; consequently, warmth becomes ineffective. Instead, vocal competence emerges as the primary driver of retention, likely because it restores a sense of agency to customers feeling a loss of control. These results challenge "one-size-fits-all" empathy training, suggesting financial firms should instead implement "Dynamic Scripting" and AI-driven vocal routing to match agent styles with the prevailing economic environment.

title: Vertical Generative AI (Vai) Development, Openness, and Data...
speaker: Junhao Li
abstract: Vertical Generative AI (VAI) fine-tunes foundation models on proprietary, industry-specific data, enabling capabilities beyond “plug-and-play” generic AI. However, the development firm faces several development and operational strategy choices, each with its own advantages and disadvantages: closed strategy (own data, self-used), openness strategy (own data, open-used), or data sharing strategy (pooled data, open-used). This paper extends the Salop model to analyze a mass firm’s VAI development strategy under asymmetric competition with niche firms. Compared with the closed strategy, the openness strategy can generate additional revenue. And the pooling effect of the data sharing strategy can be further profitable, but it may also erode the mass firm’s competitive advantage. We show that final equilibrium strategy choice depends jointly on data contribution and data processing cost. When data processing cost is moderate, the mass firm prefers closed strategy when data contribution is either sufficiently low or sufficiently high, reflecting a trade-off between the competitive-advantage effect and the openness-revenue effect. Counterintuitively, data sharing may induces a low innovation trap of VAI performance because of crowding-out effect: additional data can dilute fine-tuning effort investment, lowering performance despite larger training datasets. Moreover, Niche firms are disadvantaged under closed strategy but benefit from both openness and data sharing strategies, explaining their stronger incentives to collaborate. Finally, when data-processing cost is low and data contribution is moderate, the data sharing strategy yields a win–win–win outcome for the mass firm, niche firms, and consumers.

title: Detecting Fake Reviewer Communities with Graph Neural Networ...
speaker: Jianwei Wang
abstract: Online reviews play a crucial role in consumer purchasing decisions on e-commerce platforms, creating strong incentives for sellers to engage in fake review manipulation. Despite extensive efforts by researchers and platforms, detecting fake reviews remains challenging due to the rise of generative AI tools and the scarcity of ground-truth labels. To address these challenges, we propose a graph neural network (GNN)–based detection method that operates on the co-review network. Our approach leverages the community structure of fake reviewers and incorporates active learning to ensure scalability in real-world e-commerce markets. We evaluate the method on multiple benchmark datasets and find that it achieves a 6% improvement in F1 score compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while requiring only 10% of the benchmark training data. Post-hoc explanatory analysis shows that our advantage arises from better capturing the community structures among fake reviewers. Applying our method to a new large-scale dataset from a leading Chinese e-commerce platform reveals that sophisticated fake reviewers uniquely identified by our method distort market information and real consumer decisions more than the naive fake reviewers detectable by traditional methods. Overall, our study contributes to understanding the organizational structures and strategic behaviors behind fake reviewers and provides managerial guidance for better platform governance over review manipulation.

title: Mapping Visitor Experience: Hotel Review Trends and Webcare
speaker: Yuho Chung
abstract: We examine how hotel reviews have evolved amid the boom in generative AI and how content and style vary across cultures. Using AI-based text analytics, including topic modeling and stylistic profiling, we extract latent dimensions of visitor experiences from a large, multilingual corpus and compare them across guests’ countries of origin and review languages. We also assess temporal shifts coinciding with widespread AI writing tools. Results show systematic cross-cultural differences in emphasis (e.g., service, amenities, value) and tone, as well as temporal changes, such as greater lexical uniformity and standardized phrasing, consistent with increased AI assistance. These insights help hotels tailor communication and services to culturally specific expectations, adapt reputation management to AI-influenced writing styles, and monitor evolving guest priorities to enhance satisfaction.

title: ***Cancelled***Benchmarking with AI Generated Prompts in Onl...
speaker: Dai Yao
abstract: Online review platforms increasingly use generative AI (GenAI) not just to summarize content but to guide users to write new content. This study examines the AI-generated review prompts (AIGP) introduced by Yelp to suggest key topics and track coverage in real time. We leverage its staggered rollout across business categories on the platform as a quasi-natural experiment to examine its dynamic benchmarking effects.  Using difference-in-differences, we document a "More Words, Fewer Stars" effect: AIGP increases review length while decreasing ratings. Consumers allocate additional text primarily to prompted attributes, especially vertical quality over horizontal taste. Mediation analysis reveals that AIGP does not directly lower ratings; instead, the decline operates through increased cognitive effort and compensatory mindset—reviewers who invest more effort become less willing to give high ratings. These findings reveal an important trade-off for platform design: while GenAI tools produce richer, more structured reviews, they tighten evaluative standards and shift rating distributions, advancing our understanding of consumer review generation and benchmarking theory.

title: Cue-Based Authenticity Judgments in AI-Generated Online Revi...
speaker: Mihai Orzan
abstract: AI-generated texts are increasingly becoming tools for online review, used by both bots and human reviewers, raising new questions about how consumers infer authenticity. Building on Information Manipulation Theory and the Heuristic–Systematic Model, our research conceptualizes source inference as cue-based judgment in which consumers combine message features (review length, specificity, wording, and sales tone) with marketplace signals (review valence) and shift between heuristic and more systematic scrutiny when cues conflict. We employ a multi-method design, which includes a repeated-measures experiment collecting trust, usefulness, and source-identification ratings, complemented by interviews, eye-tracking, and a synthetic-data extension. Participants identified AI-generated reviews more accurately than human-written reviews, and longer reviews usually increased source-identification accuracy. Review length also robustly increased perceived trust and usefulness across conditions. However, an “AI penalty” was context-dependent: it emerged most strongly in too-good-to-be-true settings and in highly positive (5-star) reviews, but was attenuated or even reversed under lower-valence conditions. Eye-tracking reveals a significant valence-by-length interaction in visual attention, consistent with context-driven shifts between heuristic and systematic processing. Qualitative evidence points to detail richness, unnatural or corporate language, and persuasive tone as key diagnostic cues. The findings advance a nuanced process for AI-review credibility evaluation, suggesting that improving review ecosystems requires increasing diagnostic richness (prompting concrete details and discouraging ultra-short extreme reviews) and targeting cue combinations that trigger trust, rather than relying on disclosure or detection tools alone.

title: The Dynamics of Retail Oligopoly
abstract: This paper empirically examines competition between supermarkets, treating it as a dynamic discrete game between heterogeneous firms. We focus on the overall impact of Walmart’s entry on incumbent supermarket firms, quantifying the effects on prices, producer surplus, consumer welfare, and overall competitive structure. Employing a thirteen-year panel dataset of store-level observations that includes every supermarket firm operating in the United States across a large sample of geographic markets, alongside the rapid proliferation of Walmart Supercenter entry, we propose and estimate a dynamic structural model of chain-level competition. In this model, incumbent firms decide each period whether to add or subtract stores or exit the market entirely, and potential entrants choose whether or not to enter. Product market competition is captured via a discrete-choice demand system, incorporating detailed information on prices and characteristics of chains, as well as unobserved heterogeneity in chain-level quality. Our estimation approach combines two-step estimation with a scalable ML-based approximate value-function iteration procedure—incorporating orthogonalization-based bias correction and automatic differentiation to accelerate computation—thereby enabling estimation of the dynamic game in this large-scale, high-dimensional setting.

title: Consumer Behavior and Algorithmic Price Competition: the Cas...
speaker: Seyedeh Neda Ahmadi Amiri
abstract: As AI and humans increasingly coexist in the marketplace, it is important to understand how human psychology interacts with algorithmic decision-making. How do consumer behavioral patterns influence algorithmic pricing and the resulting prices, profits, and consumer welfare? Do behavioral patterns make consumers more vulnerable to algorithmic collusion? Should consumer AI agents emulate human psychology or act rationally? This paper investigates how consumers' reference dependence affects price competition. We show theoretically that reference dependence creates two opposing forces on equilibrium prices: higher demand elasticity lowers prices, while easier collusion raises them. We hypothesize that the downward force dominates when algorithms set prices. We test our predictions using simulated experiments in which reinforcement-learning pricing algorithms compete repeatedly over reference-dependent demand. We find that reference dependence intensifies price competition, leading to lower prices, lower firm profits, and higher consumer welfare, even though algorithms become more collusive. These effects persist even when pricing algorithms do not account for behavioral demand features, when consumers are loss-averse, and under alternative assumptions on how consumers form reference prices. Human behavioral biases, while individually non-rational, can collectively discipline pricing and improve consumer outcomes, especially when facing algorithms. We discuss the implications of these findings for the design of consumer AI agents.

title: Fair to Whom? Algorithmic Fairness in Marketing with Multipl...
speaker: Joric Donnet
