abstract: Algorithmic decision-making is widely used in marketing applications, ranging from campaign targeting to pricing. However, a growing body of research has shown that such algorithms can automate, reproduce, and sometimes amplify discrimination embedded in the training data. In response, several approaches in the causal machine learning literature have proposed methods to design fair(er) algorithms. Most existing approaches, however, focus on a single dimension of discrimination even though, in practice, discrimination often arises through the interaction and co-occurrence of multiple protected characteristics. Motivated by this gap, we seek to incorporate a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of discrimination in the design of fair(er) algorithms. We focus on the fairness notion of statistical parity, which we argue is particularly relevant for many marketing applications. In this context, fairness entails that algorithmic decision-driven policies do not systematically over- or under-target any protected group, nor expose them to systematically different prices. The contribution of this work is twofold. First, we show that neglecting some protected attributes when designing a fairness-aware policy can generate adverse effects on other, unaccounted-for protected groups. We identify the conditions and mechanisms through which fairness interventions may paradoxically lead to less fair outcomes when evaluated from a different perspective. Second, we develop a method allowing fairness constraints to be imposed on a broader set of protected attributes. Our approach offers a flexible framework capable of accommodating a broad set of protected attributes and estimation methods, making it applicable to a wide range of causal machine learning problems.

title: Responsible AI in Customer Experience: a Multi-Method Invest...
speaker: Abas Mirzaei
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence in customer experience (CX) has transformed marketing processes, yet concerns about unintended consequences, including fairness issues and bias, have emerged as critical challenges for both practitioners and researchers. While AI-enabled CX tools promise enhanced personalization and efficiency, their implementation may inadvertently perpetuate discriminatory practices and create inequitable consumer experiences. This study addresses this gap by examining responsible AI in CX through a multi-method approach combining theoretical foundations with consumer perspectives. First, a systematic literature review synthesizes existing academic research to identify key antecedents and consequences of responsible AI implementation in customer experience contexts. This review establishes a theoretical foundation for understanding the factors that enable or hinder responsible AI implementation and the resulting impacts on consumer outcomes. Second, the study employs text mining techniques to analyze consumers' self-reported experiences with AI-enabled CX tools across multiple data sources, including Reddit threads and consumer complaint platforms. This analysis captures authentic consumer voices, revealing real-world manifestations of AI-related fairness concerns and biases that may not be apparent through traditional research methods. By integrating insights from academic literature with empirical evidence from consumer narratives, this research develops a comprehensive framework for responsible AI in customer experience. The framework offers both theoretical contributions to the emerging literature on AI ethics in marketing and forward looking practical guidance for organizations seeking to implement AI systems that prioritize fairness, transparency, and equitable treatment. The findings provide actionable insights for marketers, policymakers, and technology developers in consumer-facing applications.

title: Content Release Strategies and User Engagement on Advertisin...
speaker: Sibo Zhang
abstract: Video-on-Demand platforms increasingly differ in how they release serialized content—either all at once (“binge”) or sequentially (“episodic”)—yet little is known about how these strategies shape user engagement in advertising-based video-on-demand (AVoD) environments. Using three years of viewing records from a major AVoD platform, we examine how release strategy affects both within-show engagement (progression rate) and cross-show spillover (viewing of other series). Binge-released shows yield significantly higher progression rates and stronger positive spillover across the platform. These effects are robust across propensity-score matching and instrumental-variable specifications. Furthermore, we employ a Large Language Model (LLM) to extract content features from transcripts—such as cliffhanger strength—to investigate the heterogeneous effects of release strategies. The findings highlight release strategy as a key content-scheduling lever for sustaining engagement and maximizing advertising exposure—offering guidance for AVoD platforms and for subscription services introducing ad-supported tiers.

title: Is It Possible? Website Morphing for AI-Enhanced Websites
speaker: Yicheng Dai
abstract: Following recent breakthroughs, artificial intelligence (AI) has become a central focus for both industry and academia. Notably, the prior research in the field of marketing has often evaluated AI as a stand-alone application. However, in the e-commerce, AI is architecturally embedded in the modern retail websites. Therefore, we adopt an embedded, system‑level perspective, treating AI and the website as a unit, and expanding research scope from an AI-consumer dyad to an AI–touchpoint–consumer triad. Based on the morphing theory, we proposed a modified dynamic algorithm that can jointly optimize embedded AI applications and traditional interface elements by modeling a latent consumer state which encompasses AI-attitude, perceived interface complexity, and cognitive style. Following a hybrid partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP)–multi-armed bandit (MAB) framework, the algorithm selects the morphs that maximize the probability of conversions. To test feasibility and effectiveness of this algorithm, we considered to design a virtual website for simulation testing. The contributions of this study can be divided into two aspects. On the one hand, we extend the original theory by introducing an AI-featured consumer state. On the other hand, we provide marketing managers with a real-time AI-enhanced website optimization that balances short-term conversion rates with long-term user adaptability.

title: Debiasing OPT-in Online Surveys: Evaluating Weighting, Synth...
speaker: Afiqah Adilla
abstract: Opt‑in online surveys have become a dominant mode of data collection in marketing research due to their speed and cost efficiency. However, since respondents self‑select rather than being drawn from a probability-based sampling frame, these surveys often suffer from substantial sample bias. To understand the effectiveness of different correction strategies, we use data from a 2024 online survey containing variables that overlap with multiple Japanese national benchmarks, including the Population Census, Labour Force Survey, and Consumer Trend Survey. We evaluate four traditional weighting approaches— post-stratification, raking, propensity-based weighting, and sample matching—alongside two generative models (TVAE, CTGAN) and multiple large language model (LLM)–based synthetic data generation strategies (direct prompting and prompting with distributional information). To evaluate robustness under severe selection bias, we further conduct stress tests by artificially distorting our survey to create samples with extreme gender imbalances. Across all experiments, CTGAN produces the smallest average divergence from national benchmark distributions, and for more than 70% of held-out benchmark variables, the absolute standardized mean difference (SMD) is lower than that of the unadjusted sample, even under substantial sample distortion. LLM-based synthetic data generation exhibits higher volatility, with results varying by question type and prompting approach. Traditional weighting methods yield only incremental improvements relative to the unadjusted sample. Overall, our results identify when modern generative models can meaningfully reduce bias in opt-in online surveys, and when conventional weighting or LLM-based approaches are insufficient, offering practical guidance for marketing researchers seeking to improve the external validity of non-probability survey data.

title: Encouraging Content Creation via Public AI Chatbots: Evidenc...
speaker: Mingyang Liu
abstract: Social media platforms have deployed badges, peer recognition, social norms, and monetary rewards, yet motivating sustained user contributions remains difficult. Recent advances in natural language processing and large language models (LLMs) enable a new social nudge channel: AI chatbots that leave publicly visible comments on user posts. We assess this strategy using data from a leading social media platform, constructing a seven-month user-level panel that spans the introduction of an AI chatbot. Employing difference-in-differences methods, we find that chatbot nudges increase both the volume and the quality of user-generated content. To interpret these effects, we draw on social capital theory. The observed patterns are consistent with the pillars of relational social capital. We further test two moderators—commitment and reciprocity—and find that the nudge is more effective for more committed users and when the chatbot’s comment is provides stronger reciprocity cues (e.g., longer and posted earlier), lending additional support to the proposed interpretation. These results refine understanding of UGC incentivization and social nudges and provide actionable guidance for platforms seeking to enhance engagement through AI-driven interventions.

title: Dynamic Marketing Capabilities and Artificial Intelligence: ...
speaker: Lucas Damasio
abstract: A systematic literature review (SLR) was developed on the relationship between Dynamic Marketing Capabilities (DMCs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) applied to marketing, categorizing the findings into different perspectives. Research on CMDs focuses on antecedents, moderators, consequences, as well as the conceptualization and measurement of buildings. Studies highlight the positive influence of DMCs on innovation and competitive advantage. On the other hand, studies on AI in marketing analyze its internal (generation of efficiency and knowledge) and external (relationships and performance) impacts with a limited number of studies that connect these two themes. The study adopted the PRISMA methodology, as guided by Page at al. (2021). The realization of the SRL was motivated by the assumption that the adoption of AI and the development of a set of DMCs by companies are related phenomena. This argument is based on research that relates DMCs to the adoption of new technologies and capabilities (de Oliveira et al., 2024; Mikalef et al., 2021). However, AI presents a new set of opportunities and barriers, with possible contributions to the literature on DMCs. The findings of SLRs suggest that the relationship between DMCs and AI is strategic to promote organizational competitiveness. As an agenda for future research, this study identifies opportunities in three macro topics: AI and microfoundations of DMCs, AI as an antecedent or moderator of DMCs, and the costs and risks of AI.

title: When Emojis Backfire: Evidence from Virtual Influencer Marke...
speaker: Tingxuan Zhang
authors: ['Tingxuan Zhang', 'Shizhe Zheng', 'Cheris Wing Chi Chow', 'Matthew Tingchi Liu']
abstract: Driven by the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and computer-generated imagery, virtual influencers have emerged as a prominent force in digital marketing. Compared to human influencers, virtual influencers show greater controllability and brand consistency. Meanwhile, emojis are widely used in influencers’ online communication. While prior research on human influencer marketing evidenced that expressive cues such as emojis uniformly enhance engagement, this phenomenon may not hold in the context of virtual influencers. Using a secondary-data study of Instagram posts published by virtual influencers, we analyzed the relationship between emoji use and engagement outcomes. The results show that, for virtual influencers, posts containing emojis are associated with lower engagement compared to posts without emojis. Moreover, we classified emojis embedded in posts into facial versus non-facial categories and found that the negative association is more pronounced when facial (vs. non-facial) emojis are used. This research has several potential  contributions. Theoretically, this research contributes to the emerging literature on virtual influencers by illustrating the dark side of using emojis in virtual influencer communication and discerning its differential effect of varying types of emoji. Our findings also offer practical insights for marketers on designing effective communication strategies for virtual influencers. Future studies should incorporate laboratory experiments to examine the underlying mechanism of the relationship between the use of emojis and virtual influencer marketing.

title: Sophisticated Learners, Simple Rules: the Strategic Selectio...
speaker: Qiaochu Wang
abstract: Current debates on algorithmic collusion typically assume AI agents learn prices directly, overlooking the reality that most online sellers use repricers based on simple, pre-defined rules. We address this disconnect by modeling a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) system where agents learn to select strategies, such as Undercut, Match, or Reset, rather than specific prices. We demonstrate that sophisticated learning of these simple rules consistently yields supracompetitive prices, scalable to markets with up to ten sellers. Depending on consumer price sensitivity, we observe either stable tacit collusion or volatile Edgeworth Cycles. A key contribution of this work is our analysis of the "Reset" strategy. We identify a striking paradox: while Reset rules aid collusion in price-sensitive markets by speeding up recovery cycles, they can actually lower prices in less sensitive markets. In the latter case, the Reset mechanism acts as a "safety net" that reduces the risk of price wars, ironically emboldening agents to undercut more aggressively. Supported by empirical evidence from Amazon, our results suggest that the "menu" of rules available to AI agents is a critical determinant of market outcomes, offering vital implications for managers and policymakers.

title: Competing Multi-Product Firms Using Single-Product Pricing A...
speaker: Kohei Hayashida
abstract: Retailers are increasingly adopting AI-based automated pricing algorithms for pricing decisions. These algorithms offer scalability and ease of implementation, including the capability for automated price discovery through real-time experimentation. However, recent theoretical and empirical studies have indicated the potential for supra-competitive outcomes, sparking policy concerns. Previous studies have focused on single-product firms. This paper explores competing multi-product firms, where the complexity of joint pricing becomes intractable due to the curse of dimensionality. We assume firms either employ independent single-product algorithms for each product or a unified algorithm applying a constant markup across products. We first provide evidence that firms in practice use these algorithmic simplifications. We then show that if multi-product firms utilize single-product algorithms, supra-competitive pricing is unlikely to result. Formally, we analytically show a threshold of cross-product substitution above which single-period Nash equilibrium becomes the sole stable state. Our simulation experiments support this, showing that such algorithms often result in sub-competitive (below Nash) equilibrium. In contrast, firms using constant markups across products can reach supra-competitive steady-state prices. We show that when firms' products are demand-independent, constant markup models can support strategies akin to multi-market contact. Thus, our research refines the understanding of potential algorithmic collusion and offers policymakers insights into which algorithms might lead to supra-competitive prices.

title: Algorithmic Pricing and Consumer Price Sensitivity
speaker: Diego Aparicio
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) automates human decisions. Algorithmic pricing—an AI application for scalable price determination—is now prevalent in ride-hailing, travel, drugs, gasoline, and online retail. A common thread across all these implementations is heightened price variability due to frequent price adjustments made by the algorithms. We study the impact of this algorithmic pricing-induced price variability on consumer behavior. Using granular clickstream data from an online grocery retailer in the U.S. that implemented algorithmic pricing, we find that increased price variability exacerbates consumer price sensitivity. While extant literature shows that firms are better off using algorithmic pricing, these findings are economically consequential as AI pricing triggers side effects that undermine those gains, i.e., a more price-sensitive demand offsets some of the expected benefits of algorithmic pricing. We confirm the findings of our field study using controlled lab experiments.

title: Generative AI Risk Assessment Model for the Media Sector
speaker: Christine Balague
abstract: The rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has transformed various economic sectors and introduced significant risks that remain insufficiently understood. This study focuses on GenAI risks in the media industry. It applies the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) risk framework to GAI, structuring risk assessment through three primary determinants: exposure, hazard, and vulnerability. We propose that exposure to GAI risks in the media sector encompasses information integrity, copyright material, privacy concerns, safety, content integrity, environmental impacts, and unemployment. The hazards of GAI include opacity, failure in reliability, poor data quality, misuse of training data, inadequate validity checks, and coding errors. Finally, vulnerability is conceptualized through affected stakeholders, encompassing individuals, businesses, policymakers, and broader societal institutions. Our analysis leverages real-world incidents from the OECD AI Incident Monitoring (AIM) database to illustrate how the IPCC framework can offer a structured, quantifiable, and policy-relevant perspective on GAI risks. This study aims to help policymakers, corporations, AI developers, and researchers, by providing  a systematic methodology for risk assessment, guiding regulatory choices, and formulating responsible AI governance initiatives.

title: AI Adoption Readiness in Marketing
speaker: Ke Li
abstract: With rapid development in artificial intelligence and firms’ increasing investments in marketing through AI which is changing the competition landscape, this study explores how the adoption of different types of AI applications in different industry impact marketing efficiency for companies with different sizes. Our study helps companies to understand the customer experience in the new digital interactions, to recognize the under-engaged organizational systems, and to prepare organizational change to adopt AI-driven insights and solutions so as to maintain competitive advantage.

title: Micro-Level and Cross-Level Moderating Effects on Customer S...
speaker: Xingting Ju
abstract: Customer satisfaction in restaurants reflects multiple dimensions of perceived service quality, and local market structure may condition how strongly these dimensions translate into ratings. Building on hierarchical service-quality theory, we operationalise perceived food quality (PFQ), perceived service quality (PSQ), and perceived physical environment quality (PEQ), and draw on spatial competition theory to examine cross-level moderation by restaurant-level spatial competition. We compile 217,099 Google Maps reviews for 511 restaurants in Bilbao, San Sebastián, Vitoria-Gasteiz, and Pamplona (Spain). Rather than relying on questionnaires, we measure constructs directly from naturally occurring text, reducing respondent burden and common-method concerns while capturing evaluations close to the consumption episode. Using an auditable LLM-assisted evidence-extraction pipeline, we identify aspect–category–opinion–sentiment (ACOS) spans and aggregate evidence into review-level facet scores using a pre-specified strength-weighted rule. Early results are based on an adjudicated gold subset of 5,399 reviews nested within 286 restaurants. Random-intercept multilevel models indicate that PFQ, PSQ, and PEQ are all positively associated with star ratings, supporting nomological validity for the proposed service-quality structure, with stronger effects for food and service than for environment. Spatial competition has no direct association with ratings in this early sample, but it significantly strengthens the effects of PFQ and PSQ on satisfaction; adding cross-level interactions improves model fit. Ongoing analyses scale estimation to the full dataset and incorporate geographic proximity as an additional restaurant-level moderator. Keywords: Service quality; Spatial competition; Google Maps reviews; Text-based measurement; Multilevel modelling

title: From Text to Measure: a Framework for Psychometric Construct...
speaker: Xiaowei Cai
abstract: Latent constructs are central to marketing and decision support research, yet survey-based measurement is costly, slow to refresh, and vulnerable to response styles and common-method bias. We propose an LLM-based framework that treats unstructured text as a psychometric observation channel and converts language into auditable construct scores. The workflow (1) specifies the construct domain and facets, (2) defines item-like textual evidence units, (3) generates weak labels via theory-guided LLM coding rules, (4) builds an independent adjudicated gold reference to document reliability, (5) trains a deployable extractor for reproducible scoring beyond the LLM, (6) aggregates evidence into facet and composite scores with pre-specified rules, and (7) evaluates reliability, validity, and norms. We implement the framework in a hospitality case study using Google Maps reviews for 511 restaurants in Bilbao, San Sebastián, Vitoria-Gasteiz, and Pamplona, Spain (N=217,099). Using the ChatGPT-5.0 API, we generate 61,476 ACOS weak labels from 20,651 reviews and benchmark them against a 5,399-review adjudicated gold set. Results show usable but imperfect agreement, supporting weak labels as scalable training signals while motivating a supervised extractor for consistent deployment. Early nomological checks on the gold set indicate that text-derived perceived food, service, and environment quality facet scores are positively associated with star ratings, supporting the proposed psychometric factor structure. Ongoing analyses use Hugging Face Transformers to train an ACOS extractor on weak labels, validate on the gold set, and scale inference to the remaining 191,049 reviews. Keywords: Text-based measurement; Large language models; Psychometric factors; ACOS weak supervision; Google Maps reviews

title: The Effect of Information Disclosure: Platform-Specific Visi...
speaker: Ningjing Gao
abstract: Information disclosure on digital platforms is pervasive, yet whether official disclosure complements or substitutes for user-generated reviews remains unclear. Prior research examines how hygiene disclosure affects consumer demand and how online reviews influence restaurant performance, but largely studies each platform in isolation, leaving open the question of how disclosure reshapes review generation when consumers and firms operate across multiple platforms. We address this question by exploiting a natural experiment in which Yelp began displaying health inspection outcomes for Chicago restaurants on July 1, 2018, while Google continued to show no such information for the same establishments. This asymmetric disclosure across platforms creates a unique setting in which identical restaurants face the same quality signals under different information environments, allowing us to separate quality effects from disclosure effects. Using a panel of over 3,500 restaurants from 2013 to 2019 merged with city inspection records, we implement difference-in-differences and triple-difference designs centered on inspection improvement events. To examine mechanisms, we develop a large language model–based classification framework that systematically measures review content and management responses across multiple dimensions. Preliminary results suggest that official disclosure is associated with shifts in review behavior across platforms. Consumer discussions appear to place relatively less emphasis on objective quality dimensions and more on experiential aspects, while firms adjust their reputation management strategies across platforms facing different disclosure regimes. Overall, the project highlights how platform-level disclosure policies may reshape the informational role of user-generated content and firm responses, with implications for platform design and reputation management.

title: Dei's Double Edged Impacts: Machine-Learning-Based Causal Ev...
speaker: Masakazu Ishihara
abstract: Firms increasingly incorporate diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) themes into entertainment products, yet backlash toward DEI in gaming communities suggests that the commercial consequences may be highly heterogeneous. We study the causal impact of DEI-related game characteristics on sales and review texts in the Indie PC game market. Using a dataset of Steam games released between 2014 and 2023, we define DEI content as the presence of either a female-protagonist (FP) tag or an LGBTQ+ tag. We first estimate the causal effects of FP/LGBTQ+ content on total sales using double/debiased machine learning. To address endogeneity arising from game theme-DEI correlations, we embed game descriptions and cluster titles into six thematic groups. Treatment effects vary across clusters: FP content reduces sales in action-intensive and strategy/survival clusters but increases sales in visual-novel and narrative-heavy clusters; LGBTQ+ content shows similarly polarized effects. To uncover why DEI succeeds or fails across themes, we apply a large language model-based causal inference on text to estimate how FP content shapes the linguistic properties of reviews. Clusters exhibiting significant sales effects also show significant divergences in review discourse. In negatively affected clusters, reviewers focus on socio-political framing, para-textual moral judgments, or philosophical critiques of design, whereas unaffected reviewers focus on mechanics and technical execution. In positively affected clusters, FP content elicits deeper narrative or identity-focused engagement. Our findings provide both practical guidance for developers and theoretical insight into the mechanisms through which DEI content interacts with theme-specific player expectations and the interpretive frames that shape consumer responses.

title: Deep Learning in the Service of Customer Service: the Value ...
speaker: Elie Ofek
abstract: Customer service agents serve a critical role towards post-purchase customer satisfaction, retention, and loyalty. However, providing them performance feedback in a timely manner involves several challenges: commonly used customer survey measures suffer from delayed, scarce, and biased responses. This study addresses these challenges by presenting an AI-based deep learning algorithm, which we term Conversational Hierarchical Attention Network (C-HAN), that predicts agents’ performance for each customer service transaction in real-time. The algorithm leverages the hierarchical structure of documents, which facilitates an understanding of the context and sentiment, and incorporates various conversational features present in a customer-agent interaction—e.g., who the speaker is; when and how long each person spoke; and the total duration of the conversation—to better predict transaction quality. To understand the implications of providing timely feedback in practice and examine the effectiveness of our proposed AI-based algorithm, the study conducts a controlled field experiment in an actual business setting that presents AI-derived performance feedback to customer service agents. The results demonstrate how the ability to provide timely feedback improves overall agent performance. Yet, when relative feedback, i.e., the average team measures, is additionally presented, the performance gain diminishes. The impact of AI-derived feedback on agents of different initial abilities, call-related behavior, as well as short- and long-term performance are also studied.

title: Selective Disclosure in Pre-Launch Influencer Content
speaker: Zhe Lin
abstract: Firms increasingly rely on social media influencers to shape consumer perceptions during product launches. However, firms often exert control over the information that influencers may disclose, raising concerns about selective disclosure and potential obfuscation. This study examines whether and how selective disclosure affects information quality and market outcomes. We examine these questions in the context of the gaming industry and construct unique data that links pre-launch influencer content to downstream consumer behavior. We develop a novel measure of selective disclosure using large language models to extract and classify content at scale, distinguishing between disclosed and undisclosed information, and sentiment expressed conditional on disclosure. Our analyses show that selective disclosure is strategic rather than suspense-building: influencer content is less informative yet more positively skewed. Despite reducing transparency, higher levels of selective disclosure increase consumer interest and product demand. Furthermore, there is little evidence that consumers learn over time, even as selective disclosure becomes increasingly prevalent. We discuss the implications of these findings for marketers, consumers, platforms, and regulators.

title: Small Samples, Extended Insights? An Empirical Assessment of...
speaker: Christina Reh
abstract: Market research is increasingly incorporating artificial intelligence (AI), particularly through synthetic data generation or synthetic sample boosting, to address structural constraints such as small sample sizes and rising fieldwork costs. Despite growing adoption, the empirical validity of AI-generated data relative to traditional market research data remains insufficiently examined. This study analyses whether and under which conditions synthetic data—used both as fully synthetic panels and as a sample-boosting extension of observed survey data—can support managerial decision-making in market research applications. In collaboration with a Swiss market research institute, we first analyse a pilot application in which AI models learn statistical regularities from observed survey data and generate additional synthetic observations, effectively increasing sample sizes by a factor of two to three. We then replicate the analysis using panel data from Swiss Brand Observer across multiple industries and research contexts to assess robustness and external validity. To evaluate equivalence between observed and augmented data, we implement a difference-in-differences design that compares changes in key brand metrics—such as awareness, consideration, and purchase intention—between the original samples and their synthetically boosted counterparts over time. Pre-liminary results indicate that synthetic sample boosting can reduce estimation variance and support exploratory analyses when empirical data are constrained. At the same time, systematic deviations arise in certain subgroups and more granular analyses, highlighting limits to methodological rigor. Overall, the findings suggest that AI-based data augmentation can complement conventional market research under clearly defined conditions, but does not substitute for primary data collection in general.

title: Using LLM-Based Priors to Optimize Choice Designs in Conjoin...
speaker: Felix Eggers
abstract: Choice-based conjoint (CBC) analysis is a cornerstone of marketing research, yet its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the experimental design. Poorly constructed choice tasks, particularly those containing dominated or near-dominated alternatives, yield limited information about consumer trade-offs and reduce the value of collected data. This paper proposes the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to improve CBC designs by leveraging large language models (LLMs) as a source of prior knowledge about consumer preferences. These priors can be used to evaluate candidate choice tasks for the presence of dominated or dominating options and to optimize tasks with respect to utility balance before they are shown to respondents. In this way, LLMs enable an adaptive approach to question selection that aims to show tasks with more meaningful trade-offs. We empirically evaluate this capability in a CBC study on premium job search platforms with approximately 1,000 participants. We compare a traditional random design with designs optimized using (i) aggregate LLM-based priors and (ii) individualized priors conditioned on respondents’ demographic and usage profiles, both at different levels of utility balance. Using holdout prediction measures, we show that LLM-guided designs substantially reduce the incidence of dominated choice tasks and improve predictive accuracy. Our findings demonstrate how GenAI enables a new form of adaptive experimentation in conjoint analysis, offering a scalable and low-cost tool for improving choice designs and enhancing market forecasts in dynamic settings.

title: Predicting Behaviors with Large Language Model (LLM)-Powered...
speaker: Qiuhong (Owen) Wei
abstract: Digital twins of consumers have emerged as a promising approach to simulate consumer thinking, feeling, and decision-making. Grounded in the psychological theory, which conceptualizes behavior as a function of both personal traits and contextual factors, this research proposes and validates a dual-component framework for constructing Large Language Model (LLM)-based consumer digital twins. Fine-tuning on consumer-specific data including usergenerated content allows the model to internalize individual traits, preferences, cognitive and behavioral patterns, while retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) dynamically incorporates information specific to consumer context at inference. We demonstrate and validate the framework with Amazon e-commerce data, constructing 304 personified digital twins and evaluating their performance in predicting purchase decisions and review contents. The digital twins can predict future purchases with an average accuracy of 86% and to generate product reviews with strong semantic alignment to actual consumer-generated content (cosine similarity above 0.94). By aligning LLM adaptation techniques with the foundational psychological theory about behavior, our method enables psychologically grounded simulations of individual-level consumer behavior at a scale. This research contributes to the literature on generative AI, synthetic agents, and digital twins in consumer research, and at the same time, offers a new methodology for theory-driven modeling and privacy-compliant personalization in practice.

title: Learning from Success: Sales-Optimized Advertisement Generat...
speaker: Kunhan Wu
abstract: Short-video advertising has become a dominant form of digital marketing, but most sponsored videos fail to generate revenue. A central cause is the creative bottleneck: the difficulty of crafting an effective shootable script, a multimodal, scene-level blueprint that integrates text, visuals, and selling cues considering both creator and product context. While existing Generative AI tools lower production costs, they are optimized for linguistic fluency rather than commercial effectiveness and fail to internalize the persuasive structures that drive sales. This misalignment limits their value for advertisers and platforms that focus on conversions. To address this challenge, we propose a Sales-Optimized Video Ad Generation Framework (SOVAG). SOVAG is a prescriptive AI artifact that generates customized shootable scripts conditioned on creator and product contexts. Leveraging a large-scale dataset of sponsored TikTok videos, we first extract structured multimodal representations of human-authored advertising video content to serve as a representational foundation. We then introduce Sales-Optimized Fine-Tuning (SOFT), which utilizes Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) as an outcome-weighted supervision signal to guide the model toward creative patterns co-occurring with commercial success. This "learning-from-winners" design enables the model to transfer effective narrative structures to underperforming contexts while remaining robust to the extreme skew of sales data. We conduct comprehensive evaluations, including quantitative benchmarks and human experiments with consumers and creators, demonstrating that SOVAG-generated scripts significantly increase purchase intentions and enhance production efficiency (by 11\% and 35\% respectively compared to standard SFT). Our work illustrates how design-oriented AI can bridge content production and measurable marketing performance.

title: The Persuasive Structure of Short-Form Videos: An LLM-Based ...
speaker: Yinan Li
abstract: Short-form video platforms have given rise to revenue-sharing collaborations in which influencers directly drive product sales. Although prior research has examined various features of advertising videos, we know far less about how content should be structured to maximize performance in influencer-led sales environments. This study addresses this gap by examining how the structural composition of short-form influencer videos affects commercial outcomes. Using a dataset of more than 10,000 sponsored U.S. TikTok videos, we analyze how content components and their organization shape both social media engagement and sales performance. We define theory-driven content categories and use large language models to label each video accordingly. Our analysis reveals a distinct role of social interaction within video content as a driver of sales performance, motivating an extension of the traditional ACE framework to an ECAI ("Affect, interaction, Cognition, Experience") model that incorporates interaction as a core persuasion mechanism in social media contexts. We find that experiential and interaction-oriented content are the primary drivers of conversion. In addition, structural coherence plays a critical role: videos with clear episodic boundaries and focused messaging enhance sales outcomes, whereas high informational density impedes viewer processing and reduces effectiveness. This reliance on experiential and interactive content structures distinguishes social media persuasion from traditional advertising, where persuasive effects are largely attributed to cognitive and affective message processing. Together, these findings clarify how persuasion mechanisms shift in interactive media environments and offer evidence-based direction for designing more effective short-form video content.

title: Value of Data and Model Complexity in Retail Pricing
speaker: Aaron Kaye
authors: ['Ayush Kanodia', 'Aaron Kaye', 'Susan Athey', 'Rob Donnelly', 'Mitchell Linegar', 'Pulak Ghosh']
abstract: Across industries, firms increasingly engage in data-driven decision-making, using algorithms trained with proprietary and third-party data. Data have economic value to firms because of their potential to improve business decision-making in areas such as product offerings, inventories, and pricing. We study the economic value of consumer data in a retail setting. Using a large-scale panel of consumer shopping data from five stores and over 170 product categories, we develop a flexible demand model that combines standard consumer choice models from marketing and economics with matrix factorization techniques from machine learning, whereby users have latent preferences and products have latent attributes. We jointly estimate the demand model over all product categories and stores instead of the category-by-category approach common in the literature.   Increasing the training data size can improve the model performance by more precisely estimating the parameters of a fixed model and allowing for a more sophisticated model with more latent factors. We use the model to construct counterfactual pricing policies that maximize expected revenue by using model predictions to assign targeted discounts and evaluate counterfactual revenues using off policy evaluation methods. To evaluate the economic value of data, we re-estimate the demand model and repeat the pricing and evaluation exercise while varying the size of the training data along four dimensions: 1) length of consumer purchases histories, 2) data from other consumers, 3) data from other product categories, and 4) data recency. We find positive values of data along all dimensions, with the largest gains from user purchase histories.

title: The Voice of Emotion: Advancing Marketing Research Through R...
speaker: Ertugrul Uysal
abstract: This paper introduces a novel methodological approach for analyzing consumer emotions through voice, leveraging recent advances in computational psychology and artificial intelligence (AI). While traditional approaches to voice analysis in marketing research have provided valuable insights on consumer emotions, we conceptually argue and empirically demonstrate that AI emotion measurements provide significant benefits to marketing research in studying consumer emotions. That is, this new method offers unprecedented granularity by measuring up to 48 distinct emotional expressions in real-time conversation. Two key methodological benefits of AI emotion measurements for marketing research are demonstrated through pilot studies. First, expanded emotional granularity more than doubles the predictive power compared to traditional emotion measurement approaches, with complex, nuanced emotions emerging as meaningful predictors of consumer outcomes. Second, the sentence-to-sentence measurement capability enables real-time emotional trajectory analysis, revealing dynamic patterns and inflection points that static measurement approaches cannot capture. The pilot demonstrations show how this methodology advances beyond basic acoustic parameters to capture the rich emotional information that voice naturally conveys. The paper concludes by discussing how this methodological framework opens new avenues for investigating the role of emotions in consumer behavior across voice-mediated contexts that are increasingly prevalent in the digital marketplace.

title: AI-Based Salesforce Performance Evaluation: Gains, Costs, an...
speaker: Qing Li
abstract: Advances in AI has motivated firms to route and record more client interactions through digital systems, enabling AI-based evaluation tools that monitor salespeople’s conversations and assess their performance. This transition fundamentally changes salesforce feedback and control by replacing infrequent, manager-curated reviews with automated, high-frequency, multidimensional performance scores. However, existing research on AI in sales and on performance feedback offers little guidance on how this shift to always-on, algorithmic evalution affects salespeople’s effort allocation, learning, and customer outcomes in the field. We study the adoption of an AI-evalution system that provides daily performance scores, that are multidimensional and capturing key aspects of salespeople’s skills and performance, derived from salespeople’s recorded sales calls, embedded within a CRM and rolled out in a quasi-experimental fashion. AI-evaluation adoption boosted new customer acquisition, with individual salespeople's new orders increased by 59.2%. At the team level, new orders and revenue rose by 42.0% and 116.2%, respectively. Concurrently, repurchase improved, as the customer retention rate increased by 2.3%. However, these gains came with significant costs, such as reduced work efficiency. Moreover, we observed substantial heterogeneity, as the impact varied significantly based on salespeople's prior performance levels. For instance, high performers saw the greatest increases in new orders, while medium performers benefited the most in revenue but also experienced the most adverse side effects after adoption. Overall, our findings offers practical insights for optimizing AI-evaluation to enhance customer acquisition and retention while mitigating heterogeneity and costs.

title: The Adoption of AI Shopping Assistant in E-Commerce: Who, Wh...
speaker: Zemin (Zachary) Zhong
abstract: This paper provides early, large-scale descriptive evidence on the adoption and usage patterns of LLM-based AI assistants within e-commerce ecosystems. Using extensive data from Ctrip, the largest online travel agency (OTA) in China, we analyze ``Wendao,'' a DeepSeek-based AI assistant integrated into the platform's shopping interface. Based on a sample of 31 million users who logged in during June 2025, we establish a set of stylized facts regarding who adopts these tools, when they are used in the purchase journey, and what specific intents they serve. Demographically, we find that AI adoption is higher among older consumers, female users, and highly loyal existing users. Behaviorally, adopters are significantly more engaged with the platform. Regarding the consumer journey, the median AI chat activity occurs at the same relative position as traditional search clicks. User request are correlated with the type of products purchased. These findings provide an empirical foundation for emerging theories on AI-mediated commerce and offer critical insights for researchers and practitioners designing the next generation of digital shopping experiences.

title: Seeing is Selling? The Impact of Product Videos and AI Voice...
speaker: Sichu Chang
abstract: With the rapid growth of short-form video platforms, firms increasingly rely on video content to promote products, yet evidence on its effectiveness remains limited. In this paper, we study how short product videos influence sales on an e-commerce platform using a rich panel dataset from Taobao, the largest online marketplace in China. The data track 25,715 products across 44 categories, from household appliances to advanced smart products, between April 2024 and January 2025, yielding 174,387 product-month observations. We find that the presence of product videos significantly increases sales on average, with larger effects for hedonic, complex, and experience goods. We further examine how AI-related video elements shape these effects by studying the moderating role of voiceover type. Voiceovers are classified as human or AI based on human judgments of whether the voice sounds human. The results suggest that AI-generated voices perform no worse than human voices, provided they are not overly human-like. To better understand how humans perceive voice type, we estimate prediction models using two large-scale frame-level acoustic feature sets, eGeMAPS and ComParE16. These models accurately distinguish AI-voiced from human-voiced videos and reveal systematic differences in voice quality, voicing stability, and energy dynamics. Overall, our findings offer practical guidance for product managers on when video content is most effective and whether the use of AI voiceovers is beneficial. Our approach also provides managers with a scalable and cost-effective way to infer how consumers are likely to perceive a voice as human or AI, without relying on costly human evaluations.

title: Assessing the AI Solution Ecosystem: Adoption Status and Imp...
speaker: Inyoung Chae
abstract: Despite the growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into e-commerce platforms, rigorous empirical evidence on its real-world impact remains scarce, particularly among small and medium-sized online retailers (SMoRs) who often face unique operational constraints. This study investigates when and for whom AI adoption improves business performance by leveraging a natural field experiment conducted in partnership with Korea’s leading e-commerce platform. The platform deployed six AI-based solutions (ranging from automated keyword generation to inventory optimization) targeted at SMoRs. Using a multi-method design combining a large-scale randomized field experiment, clickstream panel analysis, and qualitative interviews with participating firms, we provide a comprehensive view of the heterogeneous effects of AI. Our findings reveal that, on average, AI adoption does not uniformly improve performance; rather, its benefits are contingent on firm characteristics and product types. In particular, smaller firms, those with fewer resources and lower baseline digital maturity, experience significantly greater improvements in traffic and sales. Moreover, the benefits are more pronounced for firms selling utilitarian products, where data-driven optimization is more actionable, compared to those selling hedonic or symbolic goods. This study contributes to the literature by moving beyond single-method approaches that dominate existing research, and by offering a rare combination of causal identification and rich contextual understanding. Our results also provide practical insights for platform providers and policymakers seeking to support AI adoption in under-resourced retail sectors. We highlight the importance of firm-AI fit and call for more nuanced, context-sensitive strategies for digital transformation in retail.

title: When AI Recommenders Mess up: Matched Recovery for AI Halluc...
speaker: Xueyan Wang
abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in e-commerce search as a conversational recommender, yet hallucinations can create different failures that undermine consumer responses. Integrating a service failure lens with a matched recovery perspective, we distinguish two hallucination types. Factuality hallucinations are outcome failures in which the AI fabricates product attributes. Faithfulness hallucinations are process failures in which the AI misaligns with the consumer intent despite producing fluent content. We propose mechanism that effective recovery depends on aligning the post-error response tactic with the failure type, and it operates through distinct cognitive mediators. Across three online experiments in an e-commerce recommendation scenario, we compare each hallucination condition against a no-error baseline and manipulate recovery quality within the matched tactic. Study 1 tests factuality hallucinations and shows that evidence-backed correction, which points consumers to platform internal verifiable sources such as the product detail page, attenuates negative effects on attitude toward the AI recommendation and purchase intention by increasing perceived provenance transparency. Study 2 tests faithfulness hallucinations and shows that clarification based preference elicitation, which asks targeted questions to refine constraints and restates the consumers’ goal, mitigates negative effects by increasing perceived intent understanding. Study 3 integrates both failure types and demonstrates that high-quality matched recovery consistently outperforms low-quality recovery while operating through failure-congruent cognitive mechanisms. This research advances consumer behavior theory on generative AI failures by formalizing outcome versus process AI hallucinations in e-commerce recommendations, establishing matched recovery quality as a boundary condition, and identifying mechanism linking recovery tactics to consumer intentions.

title: The Effect of LLM models on Creator Incentives
speaker: Dina Mayzlin
abstract: Online platforms increasingly deploy AI systems that summarize user reviews by extracting and aggregating sentiment across reviews. In particular, many aggregation systems present summary information at the product-attribute level. While prior research examines how attribute-level information influences consumer decisions, little is known about how the aggregation and presentation of such information shape consumers’ incentives to produce reviews. We study how the introduction of attribute-based AI-generated review summaries alters review production and content. We propose that AI summaries generate heterogeneous incentive effects. First, because reviews contribute to summaries even when they are not directly read, AI summaries increase participation among low-effort users who write shorter reviews and decrease participation among high-effort users who write longer, more detailed reviews. Second, AI-generated summaries create an incentive to optimize review content for AI summary inclusion rather than for human readership, shifting reviews away from narrative expression and toward enumeration of attributes. Our findings shed light on how AI-mediated aggregation systems reshape participation incentives in consumer-generated content.

title: Temporary Premium Benefits on a Multi-Channel Platform: Effe...
speaker: Matthew McGranaghan
abstract: In this paper, we study how temporary premium benefits affect user behavior on a multi-channel social livestreaming platform. We collect novel user-level panel data which captures viewership, chat engagement, and subscription purchases across popular creator channels on the platform. To estimate causal effects, we leverage quasi-exogenous variation in the allocation of premium benefits together with double-robust machine learning. The average benefit recipient increases time spent on the platform by more than three hours during the benefit period, and is 11% more likely to use the platform's chat feature. These behavioral effects are persistent for three months after the benefit period ends, and spill over to other creators on the platform. In the short run, temporary benefits cannibalize paid subscriptions to the channel where they apply, but generate more than offsetting increases in subscriptions to other channels. In the long run, benefit recipients have a greater propensity to subscribe to all observed channels. Subscription spillover effects are largest among heavy platform users who engage less with the channel where benefits apply, suggesting that targeting users outside their preferred content areas can generate cross-channel spillovers while mitigating cannibalization. We use our treatment effect estimates within a multi-objective optimization framework to investigate how platforms can target promotional access to temporary premium benefits to balance different, potentially competing, objectives.

title: Privacy Protective Market Research Using Digital Twins
speaker: Xiaoyu Ouyang
abstract: As privacy regulation and platform policies limit access to sensitive consumer data, firms increasingly rely on rich and legally safe first-party behavioral data. Given that key traditional predictors of consumer behavior—such as demographics or income—cannot be directly collected, companies face a central question: can marketers accurately predict consumer purchase intent while preserving consumer privacy? This paper proposes a privacy-protective, large language model (LLM)–based methodology for constructing digital consumer twins using only non-sensitive data. Using the Twin-2K-500 dataset, we benchmark privacy-constrained models against full-information models across econometric, machine-learning, and representation-based approaches. We find that our method achieves predictive performance comparable to full-information benchmarks and does not exacerbate sensitive-attribute leakage. We further validate these findings from a randomized, longitudinal field experiment that combines rich browsing, search, and shopping traces with survey-elicited sensitive attributes. The results characterize a practical frontier between personalization performance and privacy risk under modern regulatory constraints.

title: Generative AI in Mobile Apps: the Impact of Privacy Policy E...
speaker: Meiling Xin
abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into mobile applications is becoming increasingly widespread. While this trend drives product innovation and functional evolution, it has also significantly heightened users' concerns over the security of personal data and privacy protection. This study aims to systematically investigate the relationship between adjustments made to an application's privacy policy and user evaluations following the introduction of GenAI features. The research selects applications from the Apple App Store that have been newly launched or have undergone major updates with explicitly integrated GenAI functionality as the sample. Through programmatic crawling, a longitudinal panel dataset is constructed, which includes version update logs, functional descriptions, historical privacy policy texts, as well as user ratings, download counts, and review texts for the sampled applications. First, text analysis is employed to identify the critical time point at which an application first explicitly mentions or deploys GenAI functionality. Subsequently, the frequency of updates and version changes in its privacy policy after this point are tracked and quantified. Finally, this study conducts correlation analysis and regression modeling between the aforementioned policy-related indicators and user rating data from the app store during the same period, to empirically examine whether timely adjustments to privacy policies and the substantive strength of their protections significantly impact user evaluations. The findings provide evidence-based insights for application developers, assisting them in striking a balance between leveraging cutting-edge AI technologies and practicing responsible data governance to build sustainable user trust.

title: Sales, AI, and Competition: Evidence from Enterprise Radiolo...
speaker: Nan Clement
abstract: We study how sales activities affect competition in enterprise software markets. Using data on sales payments to individual physicians and US hospital radiology software adoption, we estimate a dynamic model of symmetric oligopoly competition. In this model, vendors’ physician payments form goodwill accumulation, and vendors strategically choose payments. Our identification strategy uses variation in conflict-of-interest policies as instruments to address endogenous effects from serially correlated unobservables. Specifically, we apply the Generalized Instrumental Variables (GIV) framework to a symmetric oligopoly of dominant software vendors and consider competition from AI-based and traditional (non-AI) fringe firms.  We measure the instrument using geographic variation in the AMSA PharmFree Scorecard rating for local academic medical centers; we classify AI and non-AI vendors by analyzing their individual product FDA approval documents; and we remove non-radiology-related physician payments by using product information in the Sunshine Act payment records. Our instrumental variables analysis confirms that sales payments are causally effective in business-to-business healthcare markets: increases in meal-based payments raise vendor adoption probability. The estimation results show that goodwill accumulated through sales payments substantially protects client retention, and AI-based fringe firms pose a qualitatively stronger competitive threat per unit of goodwill than traditional fringe firms. Growth in AI fringe firms and their competitive marketing activities may generate meaningfully larger competitive pressure to the dominant firms.

title: Rethinking Visibility in AI-Mediated Senior Care: Abstractio...
speaker: Duygu Akdevelioglu
abstract: AI systems increasingly mediate care delivery, rendering older adults vulnerable not only to physical risks but also to how algorithmic infrastructures make everyday life visible, interpretable, and actionable. Research on marketized care shows that care provision is increasingly governed by market logics that cumulatively individuate, responsibilize, and expose vulnerable subjects over time (Chatzidakis et al. 2025). In institutional eldercare settings, these dynamics generate acute tensions between safety, efficiency, and dignity, particularly when visibility is treated as a prerequisite for care (Mol 2008). This research introduces the Senior Environmental Sensing Engine for AI (Sense-AI) as a vulnerability-aware care infrastructure that advances visibility protection as an ethical design principle. Sense-AI is an ambient, AI-enabled system that combines LiDAR-based spatial sensing and environmental inputs with longitudinal analytics to detect subtle behavioral changes associated with emerging health risks. This paper examines one component of the broader Sense-AI infrastructure by focusing on how healthcare workers interpret and assess the ethical implications of visibility-constrained AI outputs. This research draws on in-depth interviews with healthcare staff at a senior care center to examine how frontline caregivers evaluate trust, autonomy, dignity, and clinical usefulness when acting on algorithmically generated information under constrained visibility. This paper contributes to consumer vulnerability research by theorizing withholding visibility as care, rather than as opacity or neglect. This research offers a practice-grounded account of how ethical AI can be designed through abstraction, constraint, and interpretive mediation in high-stakes care environments.

title: How AI Pre-Consultation Impacts Telemedicine: Evidence from ...
speaker: Jingcun Cao
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has recently been applied across various industries, including healthcare, where it demonstrates strong potential to transform telemedicine in medical consultation and diagnostic assistance. While much research has focused on response quality, safety, and improving question–answering tasks, empirical evidence of GenAI’s impact in real-world clinical settings remains limited. To address this gap, we examine the application of GenAI in the pre-consultation stage of remote medical visits and evaluate its effects on consultation efficiency, physician–patient interactions, communication patterns, and treatment decisions. We collaborate with a leading online healthcare platform in China to conduct a large-scale field experiment involving over 150,000 consultations from February to June 2025. Patients in the treatment group interact with an AI pre-consultation agent that collects symptoms, asks follow-up questions, and generates structured summaries before physicians join. This randomized design allows us to causally assess AI’s impact. We analyze outcomes across four dimensions: consultation efficiency, interaction frequency, text features, and prescribing behavior. Results show that AI pre-consultation significantly reduces consultation duration, especially from physician entry to prescription, and increases the frequency of physician-patient interactions. The average length of physician messages increases, while patient messages decrease, indicating a shift in dialogue structure. Prescribing likelihood and medication purchases also rise, suggesting improvements in clinical decision-making and consumer engagement. Our findings demonstrate that AI pre-consultation enhances efficiency, communication, and treatment decisions, providing valuable insights for online healthcare platforms, regulation, and clinical practice. Future research will explore message content in greater detail to further understand AI’s influence on telemedicine.

title: AI Incidents and Social Media: How Brand Communication Shape...
speaker: Seung Yeon Lee
abstract: As AI adoption grows, AI-related incidents—events in which the development, misuse, or malfunction of AI systems result in harm—are becoming more frequent. These events can trigger both negative evaluations and heightened monitoring of brands on social media, making it critical for firms to manage communication during such periods. Yet little is known about how consumers’ attention towards brands changes, or how firms should communicate when AI incidents occur. This study examines how AI incidents influence consumer attention, measured by changes in social media followers, and how posting volume and emotional arousal shape these reactions. We compile a dataset combining Instagram follower counts for global brands with records of recent AI incidents. We find that AI incidents are associated with increases in follower counts, suggesting that such events can trigger heightened consumer monitoring and attention toward brands. This positive effect weakens when incidents involve multiple organizations or lead to tangible outcomes, such as economic or physical harm. Moreover, the effect depends on brands’ Instagram activity: higher posting volume dampens follower growth, whereas more emotionally arousing content amplifies it. This study provides one of the first large-scale empirical examinations of how real-world AI incidents shape consumer attention on social media, addressing a critical gap in the emerging AI incident literature. By reframing AI incidents not solely as reputational threats but as events that reallocate consumer attention, the study advances theoretical understanding of consumer responses to AI-related risks and offers guidance for managers on navigating social media communication during AI incident periods.

title: The Sweet Spot of Surprise: How Post Lexical Surprisal Drive...
speaker: Angela Yi Gao
abstract: Digital platforms have made language a high‑leverage managerial decision: a single caption can shape whether audiences stop scrolling and engage. Yet despite the importance of language in the creator economy, practitioners lack systematic guidance for optimizing messaging. This is especially salient in influencer marketing, where creators compete for limited attention and are evaluated in real time through visible engagement metrics. Industry advice often encourages creators to use surprising or unconventional language, but offers little insight in the ideal level of surprise. In practice, highly novel captions sometimes increase engagement and sometimes suppress it. We ask a basic but unresolved question: how surprising should a caption be to maximize engagement? We conceptualize linguistic surprise using lexical surprisal, which captures how unexpected words are given their context. Drawing on predictive processing and processing‑fluency theories, we argue that surprise involves a trade‑off: moderate surprise can attract attention and stimulate curiosity, while excessive surprise imposes cognitive costs that discourage engagement. We test this prediction using 136,670 organic Instagram posts from 1,433 U.S.-based influencers between 2023 and 2025. Linguistic surprise is measured using surprisal scores from a pretrained large language model, and engagement is captured through commenting behavior. Panel models exploiting within‑creator variation reveal a robust inverted‑U relationship. The effect is stronger for informational creators and shifts toward lower surprise when captions are more linguistically complex. The findings clarify why advice to “be novel” yields mixed results and highlight the importance of calibrating linguistic surprise in digital content creation.

title: AI Leadership: Impact on Marketing Performance and Employee ...
speaker: Jianing Li
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organizational settings not only as a supportive tool in employees’ work processes but also as an autonomous decision agent in managerial contexts. Firms have shown an increased interest in implementing AI technology to determine and allocate employees’ daily tasks as an “AI leader”. However, existing marketing research has paid limited attention to whether AI leadership contributes to firms’ long-term marketing performance and employees’ adaptive willingness. This study aims to develop a conceptual framework to examine how AI-led task decisions and allocations affect marketing performance and employees' psychological states. Grounded in psychological capital and marketing resource allocation theory, this study conducts a field experiment in an internet company specializing in websites and mobile information systems development. The results indicate that AI leadership improves short-term task performance by optimizing resource allocation efficiency and reducing coordination ambiguity. However, it induces AI-related stressors that provoke further employees’ psychological responses. While the AI leader mitigates hindrance stress and enhances task focus, efficiency-driven task allocation may erode employees’ psychological capital, specifically hope, self-efficacy, and resilience. Consequently, AI-led decision-making prioritizes short-term marketing performance at the expense of employees’ adaptability and long-term value creation. This study contributes to the literature by illustrating the dual impact of AI leadership on marketing performance and psychological capital. To ensure both short-term performance and long-term sustainability, firms need to leverage AI for task allocation while integrating support mechanisms that promote employee well-being, such as continuous training and psychological support initiatives.

title: Attention Without Conversion? AI-Generated Versus Human-Crea...
speaker: Huimin Li
abstract: IWe study whether generative AI changes the relationship between creative attention and commercial persuasion in video advertising. Using a randomized field experiment with more than 150 unique video ads, we compare AI-generated and human-created creatives across the advertising funnel. AI-generated ads consistently outperform human-created ads on upper-funnel outcomes: they earn higher click-through rates, sustain viewer retention more effectively, and draw fewer negative reactions. Yet these gains do not extend downstream. Relative to human-created ads, AI-generated creatives are less likely to generate conversions. This pattern reveals a tension between attention efficiency and persuasive effectiveness. Generative AI appears well-suited to producing content that captures and holds attention, but attention alone is insufficient to deliver conversion when trust, credibility, or purchase intent matters. This resonates with influencer research showing that attention and engagement are not equivalent to downstream persuasion. Our findings contribute to the emerging literature on AI in marketing by showing that creative automation can improve engagement metrics without necessarily improving commercial outcomes. More broadly, the results suggest that the increasing efficiency of creative production may not translate into proportional gains in advertising effectiveness.

title: How Cross-Border Digital Platform Participation Drives Inter...
speaker: Ruiyang Hong
abstract: This study investigates the impact of cross-border digital platform participation (CDPP) on the international sales of Chinese multinational enterprises (MNEs). We propose that both the intensity and diversity of CDPP exert a positive influence on firms’ international performance, with such relationships exhibiting heterogeneous variations across different firms. We employ panel data of 554 listed MNEs spanning the period 2014 to 2024 and adopt machine learning techniques rooted in natural language processing (NLP) to analyze textual data from annual reports. Our findings reveal that larger firms derive more pronounced benefits from intensive and diversified platform participation. Born global firms demonstrate an inherent stronger compatibility with cross-border digital platforms and thus can also reap rapid gains from CDPP. However, we find these effects are only applicable to short-term performance: no significant differences in long-term performance are observed between larger firms and small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), nor between born global firms and non-born global firms. This study contributes to the literature on digital platforms by highlighting the multidimensional nature of CDPP and the contingent role of factors such as organizational size. It also provides practical guidance for MNEs to tailor their platform strategies in accordance with their inherent firm characteristics.

title: Personality-Based Nudges for Small and Medium-Sized Enterpri...
speaker: Lisa Zangger
abstract: Nudging offers low-cost yet potentially high-impact opportunities to influence customer decisions. Hence, they are ideal for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Previous studies examined nudge effectiveness in different contexts or manipulation issues. Recent studies suggest that personality-based nudges are more effective than non-tailored ones. However, little is known about how SMEs apply nudging, perceived advantages, and disadvantages. In their meta-review on nudge effectiveness Luo and colleagues (2023) examined 184 papers with over 2 million participants. They categorize nudges according to six cognitive processes: attention, perception, memory, effort, intrinsic motivation, and extrinsic motivation. Although developed outside the core marketing literature, the framework builds on choice architecture and psychological consumer decision-making theories central to marketing science. Using their framework, this study examines nudging practices in Swiss SMEs and benchmarks nudge effectiveness measurements from SMEs against their results, thereby contributing to the hitherto small body of literature around nudging practices in SMEs and personality-based nudging. Adopting a mixed-methods approach, data is collected through a quantitative survey and subsequent semi-structured qualitative interviews. The survey will inform how many SMEs know about and use nudging, nudge effectiveness estimates, subsumption of these estimates within the above framework, and knowledge of personality theories. The interviews will explore SME nudge practices, opportunities, risks, implementation barriers, nudge effectiveness measurements, and the role of AI in creating nudges. Results, which are available in May 2026 (thesis defense: June 2026), are showing current SME nudging practices, indicate unused potential, identify risks and challenges, and give practical recommendations.

title: Interpretable RL for Long-Term Revenue: Coupon Inventory and...
speaker: Leyan Xiao
abstract: Online shopping platforms increasingly use personalized coupons to influence consumer behavior over time. A central challenge is coupon management: customers hold evolving portfolios of unredeemed coupons with varying discounts and expirations, thus current issuance changes future incentives by altering coupon inventory and expiration pressure. We develop a value-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework that incorporates coupon inventory and expiration dynamics into the state, allowing the model to condition decisions on these intertemporal incentives. To address the "black-box" nature of RL, we incorporate a feature-gating mechanism that provides intrinsic interpretability by revealing which state features the policy relies on in making decisions. Using large-scale transaction data from a major online grocery platform, our model delivers significant improvement in long-term revenue, outperforming static and supervised benchmarks by over 30% and other RL baselines by approximately 9% while yielding stable off-policy evaluation estimates. Feature-gating analysis shows that inventory structure and expiration pressure are the primary drivers of policy decisions, followed by RFM-based features, whereas the contribution of demographic features is relatively limited. Policy analysis further indicates the following findings: discount intensity exhibits a U-shape as coupon inventory and expiration pressure increase; the policy adapts across age, membership tier, and tenure, while maintaining relative gender neutrality; very-high coupon users receive lower discounts, and discount intensity follows an inverted-U pattern across coupon-usage activity. Finally, we propose an LLM-simulated online environment to evaluate the policy, further demonstrating robust revenue improvements relative to baseline strategies.

title: ***Cancelled***Transforming Digital Attention into Social Ac...
speaker: Erya Ouyang
abstract: Nonprofits increasingly rely on social media platforms to mobilize public attention, raise funds, and promote social causes. Yet digital visibility such as high engagement does not reliably translate into real-world impact such as donations, volunteering, and participation. This disconnect—referred to as the attention–action gap—creates a fundamental challenge for digital philanthropy. This paper develops a multimodal, data-driven framework to understand, measure, and reduce the attention–action gap in nonprofit fundraising. First, we construct a theoretically grounded typology of multimodal communication strategies that capture how text and images, jointly create persuasive meaning. Using large-scale data from the Meta, we link these multimodal strategies to both online engagement and real-world outcomes, and then apply Double Machine Learning to causally estimate when and how online attention converts into action. Beyond quantifying the attention-action gap, the project advances a generative solution. We finetune a domain-specific vision–language model trained on nonprofit social media content to simulate, generate, and optimize multimodal fundraising messages. This model enables nonprofits to explore counterfactual content designs and identify strategies that maximize both engagement and conversion before deployment, reducing reliance on costly trial-and-error experimentation. Overall, this research produces a scalable analytic framework, actionable design guidance, and a practical AI tool that transforms digital fundraising from engagement-driven visibility into data-driven social impact.

title: Marketing to the AI: The Role of AI Mind Share in Driving Br...
speaker: Xinlan Li
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence is fundamentally restructuring the consumer decision journey. Consumers increasingly turn to conversational agents—such as ChatGPT and DouBao—to search, evaluate, and purchase products. Despite the rise of industry practices such as Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), there is still a lack of empirical evidence connecting how brands are perceived in AI systems to their market performance. Therefore, this study leverages a unique panel dataset covering over 800 brands across diverse product categories over a nine-month period to empirically examine the impact of AI Mind Share (AIMS) on brand sales performance and explore its boundary conditions across different product categories. We employ panel VAR model to examine whether AIMS predicts online sales performance above and beyond traditional marketing metrics.
