The results find that AIMS demonstrates a significant impact on brand sales performance, with heterogeneous effects across product categories. This research provides one of the first empirical investigations of AIMS as a critical marketing KPI. Managerially, our findings offer a strategic framework for allocating budgets between traditional brand assets and algorithmic influence, providing actionable insights for firms navigating the frontier of AI-driven consumer search.

title: Quantifying Visual Congruence in Influencer -- Brand Collabo...
speaker: Qingli Zeng
abstract: This research examines the tradeoff between brand control and influencer authenticity in influencer marketing through the construct of Visual Congruence, defined as the degree of aesthetic alignment between a brand’s visual identity and an influencer’s established visual style. Influencers develop stable visual signatures that function as trust heuristics for consumers, yet sponsored collaborations often impose brand aesthetics that alter this alignment. Using a large-scale dataset of sponsored and organic social media posts, we develop a computer-vision–based deep learning framework to quantify visual congruence based on differences in color composition, lighting, and image structure. Estimating a nonlinear response model, we show that visual congruence exhibits a threshold effect: while moderate departures from an influencer’s baseline style can increase attention and engagement, lower levels of congruence substantially reduce conversion, consistent with an authenticity boundary. We further demonstrate that this boundary shifts systematically with (i) brand status and price, (ii) product type (hedonic versus utilitarian), and (iii) brand–influencer strategic fit. For luxury brands, high visual congruence is essential, whereas for mass-market products, the constraint relaxes. Overall, the findings provide a quantitative framework for optimizing visual strategy in influencer campaigns and for determining when firms should enforce brand aesthetics versus preserve influencer authenticity.

title: Llms as the Gatekeeper: How Product Type Determines Opposite...
speaker: Andrea Pescher
abstract: With shopping-related GenAI use growing 35% in 2025 and over 60% of consumers expressing high trust in AI recommendations (BCG, 2026), large language models now function as commercial gatekeepers, processing marketing content before shaping purchase recommendations. For marketers competing for visibility in this new landscape, understanding how LLMs respond to persuasive techniques becomes critical for marketing strategy. This study maps LLM response patterns to persuasive techniques across product types. Using a controlled experiment with 13,500 observations across three LLMs (GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-5 Mini, Kimi K2), the research tested hedonic versus utilitarian products under four persuasion conditions based on Cialdini's principles. Results reveal that identical persuasive content produces opposite effects by product type: social proof increased the rate at which LLMs expressed high certainty in recommending concert tickets from 9.6% to 65.6%, while authority appeals reduced certainty for utilitarian products. This pattern of hedonic amplification versus utilitarian resistance persisted across all models tested, demonstrating that LLM gatekeeping biases operate systematically and predictably. These findings provide actionable intelligence for optimizing marketing content in LLM-mediated commerce environments.

title: Exploration or Exploitation? A Study on the Mechanisms Throu...
speaker: Yiting Zhou
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models and agent-based systems, is transforming strategic decision-making in cross-border e-commerce. Major platforms increasingly embed AI to support sellers with translation, product recommendation, demand forecasting, and market strategy optimization. Systems such as Alibaba International’s Accio, Amazon’s Amelia, and TikTok Shop’s GMV Max exemplify a new generation of AI-augmented decision tools that substantially improve operational efficiency. Despite these benefits, recent research cautions that AI-assisted decision-making may entail cognitive and metacognitive risks, especially in complex and uncertain environments. When AI is integrated “in the loop,” sellers face multidimensional trade-offs across product selection, pricing, inventory, and market positioning. In such settings, AI assistance can reduce active cognitive engagement and promote overreliance, potentially undermining critical reflection, learning, and long-term decision autonomy. This project argues that a key yet understudied factor shaping these outcomes is how users frame their relationship with AI. Conceptualizing AI as a tool, advisor, or partner may fundamentally influence trust, responsibility attribution, cognitive effort, and willingness to scrutinize AI recommendations. These framings may differentially affect short-term decision quality and long-term learning trajectories. Accordingly, this research examines how AI role framing shapes human decision-making and learning in complex tasks such as cross-border e-commerce, and investigates the cognitive and psychological mechanisms underlying these effects

title: Machine Learning Analysis of Projected Versus Perceived Dest...
speaker: Yizhou Yuan
abstract: This study examines Macau’s destination image by comparing travelers’ perceived image with the projected image promoted by the Macau Government Tourism Office (MGTO). Instagram posts are collected using a Python script. The dataset covers the period from January 1, 2024 to January 31, 2025 to capture the post-COVID recovery phase. The cleaned traveler-generated content dataset includes 10,895 posts with 51,656 images, while the MGTO dataset comprises 573 posts and 1,087 images scraped directly from the official account. Instagram images from both sources are analyzed using machine learning techniques to uncover the discrepancies between official narratives and traveler perspectives. Findings reveal that the official narrative emphasizes an idealized image centered on modernity, leisure, and the city’s diversified identity. Nevertheless, certain elements highly valued by travelers, such as the exploration of heritage communities and luxury experiences, are absent from official content. The results also suggest that official promotion underrepresents fine dining while prioritizing local cuisine, whereas travelers express interest in both types of dining experiences. Recommendations are provided to incorporate more authentic and experience-driven elements. This study highlights the value of machine learning in identifying the gap between projected and perceived destination images. The machine learning approaches enable visual data analysis at scale and deliver data-driven insights that improve the efficiency of tourism market analysis. Furthermore, this study broadens current approaches in destination image research by focusing on visual content rather than textual content.

title: Is There a Whitening Effect of Image Generation Services? Ev...
speaker: Hugo Arribas
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a powerful tool for improving ad campaigns. However, the gains introduced by AI can be offset by potential biases. We construct an original data set where we compare real images of real person for each country in the world with images produced by AI. We collect the images from different contexts including the fashion industry, politics, and sports. We use artificial intelligence tools to detect the lightness of the skin color of the real images and the AI generated images. Initial model-free evidence shows that the images generated by women exhibit a lighter skin tone compared to their real-world counterparts. The whitening effect of the model is heterogeneous within the treated group, varying by gender, socio-economic category, and geographic location prompted. Women systematically experience a stronger whitening effect.

title: Experimentation Without Experiments: Simulated LLM Markets v...
speaker: Xiexin Liu
abstract: While controlled experimentation is foundational to data-driven decision making, many high-stakes interventions remain infeasible to test in the field due to implementation costs, regulatory constraints, and stakeholder risk. We introduce Simulated Language Experiments via DAGs (SLED), a principled framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to simulate market-level experimental responses when real-world experimentation is prohibitively costly. SLED builds on LLMs to create theory-guided simulators constrained by causal structure and validated against real-world data. In an initial in-silico stage, the LLM simulates heterogeneous consumer personas under controlled interventions to generate synthetic demand responses. Using these simulated outcomes, the LLM performs abductive reasoning to propose candidate DAGs that explain observed heterogeneity through economically interpretable latent mediators. These candidate structures are then tested against historical data, eliminating graphs inconsistent with observed behavior. The surviving DAGs constrain subsequent market simulations, steering them toward economically plausible dynamics. We apply SLED to housing price optimization, where RL-based pricing is hindered by a lack of price exploration due to limited price variation in observational data. Across increasingly complex settings from incorporating market competition to negotiation and platform coordination, SLED yields more accurate intervention-response estimates and better downstream decision performance than unconstrained, naïve LLM simulation baselines.

title: The Limits of Observational Methods for Advertising Incremen...
speaker: Carlos Garcia Alvarado
abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) using ghost ads are the gold standard for advertising incrementality measurement. However, they are often unavailable, costly, or underpowered due to sample size and budget constraints. This motivates the use of non-experimental methods to measure incrementality. Yet, environments like Zalando, which offer retail media services, employ complex algorithms for ad personalization, bidding, and pacing. These systems introduce significant selection bias, as users already predisposed to a brand are naturally more likely to be served its ads, making it difficult to distinguish organic intent from ad-driven lift. This paper evaluates whether observational methods can reliably estimate incrementality for Sponsored Brands by analyzing 12 large-scale ghost ads experiments at Zalando. Leveraging first-party data with user-level behavioral features, I follow Gordon et al. (2022) to evaluate incrementality using Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML) and Stratified Propensity Score Matching (SPSM). I further incorporate Bayesian structural time series (CausalImpact), using unexposed geographies, organic demand and advertising demand as control series. Results across the consumer funnel—brand followers, PDP views, add-to-wishlist, add-to-carts and conversions—show that observational methods systematically overestimate incremental lift compared to RCT benchmarks. While less severe than Gordon et al. findings of overestimation on Facebook, errors remain substantial enough. It can be concluded that non-experimental methods remain unreliable substitutes for ghost ads experiments in retail media incrementality measurement.

title: Using Contextual Embeddings to Predict the Effectiveness of ...
speaker: Paul Ellickson
abstract: We propose a framework for causal prediction that enables the design and evaluation of novel treatments based on estimated causal effects. Our approach centers on constructing a response surface that connects unstructured text—captured through contextual embeddings—to economically meaningful outcomes, operationalized as doubly robust scores. This response surface then functions as a critic within an actor-critic algorithm, where a GenAI engine like ChatGPT can serve as the actor. To evaluate our framework, we examine a targeted marketing application involving 3.3 million observations from 34 customer emails over 45 days. Our results highlight the use of contextual embeddings to achieve an accurate prediction of novel treatments while a commonly used encoder, human codification, fails to do so. The accuracy of our framework in prediction of novel treatments is driven by the availability of semantically similar treatments within the contextual manifold. Finally, we illustrate how managers can use our framework to generate novel content, demonstrating that it outperforms a naive application of Generative AI. Moreover, our framework can be extended to account for heterogeneous treatment effects, allowing for segmentation and personalized targeting in developing novel treatments.

title: AI Search and Web Traffic
speaker: Kai Zhu
abstract: This paper investigates whether AI search restores the referral ecosystem by driving downstream traffic or exacerbates 'zero-click' consumption by synthesizing answers within the interface. Leveraging granular clickstream data and a staggered difference-in-differences design, we estimate the causal impact of AI search adoption on users’ broader web consumption and compare the magnitude of direct referral traffic against traditional search engines. Furthermore, we test for heterogeneity to determine if AI intermediaries disproportionately concentrate traffic toward specific domain types and to analyze the 'AI divide' across user demographics. By quantifying these shifts, our findings illuminate the long-term viability of the ad-supported internet, providing insights for policymakers and content publishers navigating the evolving competitive dynamics between AI platforms and the open web ecosystem

title: Expanding Yourself Through AI: How Message Appeals Affect Us...
speaker: Yiran Zhang
abstract: AI applications represent the primary interface of AI technologies and offer substantial potential value, yet user adoption remains limited, constraining their commercial success. Understanding how to motivate users to engage with AI applications is therefore critical. This research investigates how the fit between message appeal (feasibility vs. desirability) and AI type (task-oriented vs. social-oriented) influences user responses. Across five studies (N = 1,584), results show that for task-oriented (vs. social-oriented) AI, feasibility-focused (vs. desirability-focused) messages lead to more favorable user responses, with self-expansion mediating this effect. Moreover, this fit effect is stronger among users with low (vs. high) AI belief. This study advances research on AI promotion by highlighting the interaction between AI type and message appeal and by identifying self-expansion as a novel psychological mechanism. It also offers actionable insights for optimizing AI marketing strategies and targeting user segments.

title: Synthetic Corpus and Consideration Manipulation in Generativ...
speaker: Xiaoyan Xu
abstract: The rapid adoption of generative engines as the primary gateway for product discovery has given rise to Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), a new practice where firms attempt to influence AI-driven product recommendations and, consequently, consumer consideration sets by strategically seeding the online environment with synthetic corpora, such as fake reviews and blog posts. This paper investigates the market implications of GEO using a game theory model where product quality is either high or low, and consumers who are uncertain about product quality rely on a generative AI’s recommendation to form their consideration sets and subsequently inspect online corpora of recommended products to evaluate their quality. We model the generative engine as a “prediction machine” that recommends products based on statistical inference. We highlight how GEO collapses the traditional purchase funnel, as the same synthetic content intended to gain visibility via GEO during the consideration stage also serves as the evidence for consumer evaluation during the evaluation stage. For the high-type firm, this creates a critical visibility-credibility trade-off: while synthetic corpora increase the probability of being recommended (a demand expansion effect), they simultaneously raise the risk of consumer detection, which can trigger skepticism and reduce purchase intention (a consumer suspicion effect). Our analysis reveals that a high-type firm’s incentive to manipulate is non-monotonic in the quality of its low-type competitor. We also show that a regulatory ban on synthetic content does not necessarily improve consumer surplus.

title: The Impact of AI Chatbots on Online Retailing
speaker: Axel Stock
abstract: Recently, Walmart decided to let shoppers buy its products directly within OpenAI's ChatGPT. Although Walmart's stock price rose significantly following the announcement, its biggest rival Amazon.com currently blocks its listings from showing up on GenAI platforms, Instead, Amazon.com offers its own AI shopping features. These observations raise some puzzling research questions. What company or market characteristics favor an online retailer to work together with an AI platform? When is it optimal for a retailer to offer AI features on its own shopping site instead? To address there questions we utilize a game theoretic model of an online retailer offering a product line to a market of consumers who are uncertain about their preferences for a product feature. The retailer chooses both price for the product and the advertising fee charged to companies wanting to advertise on its website. We show under which conditions it is optimal for the retailer to support consumers' decision making by offering an AI chatbot, and when to allow them to purchase the product directly on a GenAI platform. Afterwards we extend the model to include retail competition. We show that when there is sufficient heterogeneity between retailers then they pursue asymmetric GenAI strategies in equilibrium providing support for our empirical observation.

title: Curbing Toxicity Without Compromising Privacy? the Effects o...
speaker: Xinyi Sun
abstract: As toxic behavior escalates online, platforms face a persistent dilemma: how to curb undesirable content without undermining user privacy or participation. We study whether and how subtle reductions in anonymity can improve discourse quality by exploiting a sharp policy change on a large university forum where users post/comment content under persistent but non-personal IDs. The intervention restricted fully anonymous posting from unlimited to three posts per day. Using a Regression Discontinuity in Time (RDiT) design, we estimate the causal impact of this change on a multidimensional set of content outcomes---including negative and positive emotion, toxicity, mental harm, and informativeness---measured through a framework that combines human validation, industry standards, and large language models. The intervention produced sizable and immediate improvements in discourse quality. Toxic, mentally harmful, and negative posts fell by 10–20%, while informative and positive posts increased. Importantly, these quality gains occurred with only modest reductions in posting volume and no overall decline in commenting activity. We also find strong spillover effects as toxicity and mental harm in comments decreased substantially. Heterogeneous treatment effects and a preregistered randomized experiment converge on a common mechanism---perceived traceability. Users who felt more recognizable (e.g., through distinctive IDs) exhibited the largest behavioral recalibration. Our findings demonstrate that privacy-preserving traceability can meaningfully improve online discourse, a viable alternative to real-name policies or heavy-handed moderation.

title: Going From One Experiment to Another: Estimating Treatment E...
speaker: Mengjie Cheng
abstract: Digital experimentation has advanced rapidly in recent years and has become the industry gold standard for estimating the incremental effects of treatments, such as assessing the impact of different marketing channels. Despite its widespread adoption, however, large-scale experimentation remains costly and may negatively affect both revenue and consumer experience. In this paper, we develop a framework that leverages historical experimentation data to improve the efficiency of average treatment effect (ATE) estimation for a new target population. The framework consists of three stages. First, we improve the accuracy of ATE predictions by learning from historical data. Second, we combine multiple predictors to mitigate the risk of negative transfer. Finally, we rectify these predictions using a small amount of target population experimental outcomes. We first evaluate the framework using simulated data and show that it is effective under both covariate shift and concept shift between the historical and target populations. Building on these findings, we then validate the framework in a real-world setting through a collaboration with Wayfair. Using the firm's historical experimentation data, we show that the proposed approach substantially reduces the amount of labeled target-population data needed to reach statistical significance for the effect of email interventions on consumer traffic. Together, these results highlight the promise of machine learning methods for improving digital experimentation and offer important implications for how firms design, scale, and optimize experimentation in practice.

title: Leveraging LLMs to Improve Experimental Design: a Generative...
speaker: George Gui
abstract: Pre-experiment stratification, or blocking, is a well-established technique for designing more efficient experiments and increasing the precision of the experimental estimates. However, when researchers have access to many covariates at the experiment design stage, they often face challenges in effectively selecting or weighting covariates when creating their strata. This paper proposes a Generative Stratification procedure that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to synthesize high-dimensional covariate data to improve experimental design. We demonstrate the value of this approach by applying it to a set of experiments and find that our method would have reduced the variance of the treatment effect estimate by 10%-50% compared to simple randomization in our empirical applications. When combined with other standard stratification methods, it can be used to further improve the efficiency. Our results demonstrate that LLM-based simulation is a practical and easy-to-implement way to improve experimental design in covariate-rich settings.

title: Generative Brand Choice
speaker: Kevin Lee
abstract: Predicting demand for new products is an important and challenging problem in marketing, especially for product categories where brand is a key driver of choice. In these settings, observed product attributes do not explain choice patterns well, which makes predicting sales of a new product as a function of marketing mix variables intractable. To address this problem, I develop a scalable framework that enriches structural demand models with large language models (LLMs) to predict consumer preferences for new brands. After estimating preferences for existing brands using a structural model, I use an LLM to generate predictions of these brand utilities from text descriptions of the brand and consumer. When fine-tuned on this data, I show that the tuned LLM is able to generalize to previously unseen brands that were excluded from the training sample. In contrast, conventional models based on text embeddings return predictions that are essentially uncorrelated with the actual utilities, and general-purpose LLMs are also uninformative. My fine-tuned LLM's predictions attain a correlation of 0.52 with the held out preferences and 17 times higher mutual information than embedding-based models; i.e. for the first time, informative predictions can be made for consumer preferences of new brands from text. Additionally, I combine causal estimates of the price effect from instrumental variables methods with the LLM predictions to enable pricing-related counterfactuals. By integrating the powerful generalization abilities of LLMs with principled economic modeling, my framework enables informed decisions on optimizing the marketing mix of a new product.

title: Digital Twins as Funhouse Mirrors: Five Key Distortions
speaker: Olivier Toubia
abstract: Scientists and practitioners are aggressively moving to deploy digital twins - LLM-based models of real individuals – across social science and policy research.  We conducted 19 pre-registered studies with 164 diverse outcomes (e.g., attitudes towards hiring algorithms, intention to share misinformation) and compared human responses to those of their digital twins (trained on each person’s previous answers to over 500 questions). We find the digital twins' answers are only modestly more accurate than those from the (homogeneous) base LLM and correlate weakly with human responses (average r = 0.20). We document five ways in which digital twins distort human behavior: (i) stereotyping, (ii) insufficient individuation, (iii) representation bias, (iv) ideological biases, (v) hyper-rationality. Together, our results caution against the premature deployment of twins, which may systematically misrepresent human cognition and undermine both scientific understanding and practical applications.

title: Wisdom of AI: Using the Delphi Technique with LLMs as a Fore...
speaker: Sumon Chaudhuri
abstract: While forecasting customer behavior is a well-studied field, practical adoption of this research remains limited; practitioners often favor simple heuristic based methodologies like the Delphi method over complex modelling frameworks. These methods are simple, and oftentimes quite effective; however, they are also expensive, and heavily dependent on the participating subjects. We propose a novel methodology that capitalizes on the strengths and mitigates the weaknesses of heuristic based customer behavior forecasting by utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) as subjects within a structured Delphi method. We empirically test this approach’s accuracy within the elective cosmetic procedures industry, comparing its performance against established market research techniques across various testbeds.

title: Talk to Think: How Communication Modality Shapes Human-AI Co...
speaker: Tijmen Jansen
abstract: Organizations increasingly integrate generative AI into ideation and innovation processes to augment human creativity. While large language models (LLMs) excel at rapid synthesis and pattern recognition, effective innovation depends on how humans and AI collaborate, particularly how they communicate. Despite the growing availability of voice-enabled conversational agents, AI-assisted ideation remains dominated by text-based interfaces, and the consequences of communication modality for creative collaboration remain largely unexplored. Drawing on cognitive load theory, we theorize that spoken interaction with AI reduces extraneous cognitive load relative to written communication, freeing cognitive resources for creative processing. We test this prediction across three experimental studies in product and marketing ideation contexts. Study 1 establishes a performance benchmark, showing that an LLM instructed with product information and consumer reviews outperforms both uninstructed AI and human ideators on overall idea quality and the ability to address customer complaints. Studies 2 and 3 examine communication modality in human–AI collaboration. Across both studies, participants who interact with AI via speech generate higher-quality ideas than those who interact via text. Mediation analyses demonstrate that reduced perceived cognitive load explains a substantial portion of this speaking advantage. Together, these findings identify communication modality as a critical and previously overlooked design lever in AI-assisted innovation. By showing that speaking, rather than writing, with AI enhances creative output through reduced cognitive load, this research advances theory on human–AI collaboration and provides actionable guidance for organizations considering voice-based AI systems for ideation and innovation work.

title: The Narrative Campaign Generator: Weaving Consumer Reviews i...
speaker: Madhav Arora
abstract: Personalizing marketing communications improves consumer response through higher click-through and conversion rates (Yoganarasimhan, 2020). Yet creating such personalized advertisements at scale remains costly. Recent advancements in LLMs could help reduce these marginal costs, but they suffer from two key limitations: factual unreliability (hallucinations) and content homogenization. Consumer reviews offer a promising knowledge source to address these limitations, as they contain rich product information such as usage contexts, emotional reactions, and performance evidence. To ground LLM output with such external knowledge, the current approach uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with vector similarity search. This approach, however, can lead to a redundancy problem. In other words, since most reviews contain similar information, feeding them into LLMs leads to generic responses that fail to capture the full breadth of available information (Yang et al., 2025). In our study, we introduce Review GraphRAG, a framework that uses signed graph retrieval to construct structured knowledge representations from consumer reviews. To generate novel yet accurate campaign ideas, we employ a diversity-maximizing graph traversal mechanism for feature selection, preventing the redundancy inherent in vector similarity search. Our approach improves both reliability and diversity of campaign narratives since the generated content is not only grounded in verified consumer experiences but also has broader feature coverage. As a next step, we are testing our approach's effect on purchase intentions through a field experiment with a fragrance partner in Austria.

title: When AI Chooses for You: How LLM-Based Shopping Assistants S...
speaker: Evgenii Gradusov
abstract: We analyze how AI-powered shopping assistants reshape choice architecture and competition. Using extensive query-level data from Amazon's Rufus chatbot across multiple product categories, we document three empirical patterns. First, algorithmic curation sharply narrows consumer choice: AI draws from a small fraction of the product catalog (~15% of available products), exhibits high concentration among a few products and brands, and clusters around mid-range options. These patterns vary systematically with query specificity, with more generic queries granting greater algorithmic discretion. Within this curated environment, we document systematic Pareto efficiency violations: most displayed products have cheaper and better-rated alternatives that are excluded, implying substantial potential consumer savings losses, alongside platform affiliation patterns consistent with strategic self-preferencing through badges and certifications. Second, AI curation amplifies winner-takes-all dynamics: recommended products have substantially more reviews than excluded alternatives, and dominant brands capture a disproportionate share of algorithmic visibility relative to their organic presence. Third, competition shifts to new dimensions, as visual and semantic alignment with consumer queries becomes a central determinant of algorithmic visibility. Text and image embeddings play a substantially larger role in AI-curated recommendations than in traditional search rankings. Our findings contribute to the emerging literature on algorithmic market design and have implications for consumer welfare, seller strategy, and the regulation of AI-mediated commerce.

title: Adoption of Generative AI Platforms and Creator Behavior: Ev...
speaker: Shaojun Qin
abstract: This paper investigates how adoption of generative AI platforms affects content creation and engagement behavior among social media creators. Leveraging a unique multi-platform dataset, we examine changes in posting activity, content characteristics, and audience responses surrounding creators’ adoption of a novel AI tool. Our empirical strategy employs a difference-in-differences design exploiting variation in adoption timing, paired with robust identification techniques to address challenges in treatment classification and user matching. Beyond standard engagement metrics, we utilize advanced machine-learning methods to capture shifts in content style and composition. Preliminary findings reveal an overall negative effect of adoption on engagement, particularly pronounced among larger creators. We also identify heterogeneous effects across platforms, indicating that platform features and creator types shape the impact of AI tool adoption. This study advances understanding of the economic and behavioral consequences of emerging AI technologies in digital content markets, highlighting how platform adoption dynamics influence creator strategies. The findings offer valuable insights for marketers, platform designers, and researchers exploring innovation diffusion and digital ecosystem evolution.

title: Beyond Search: LLM Adoption and Web Traffic Concentration
speaker: Samira Gholami
abstract: Search engines have long served as the primary gateway to the web, dispersing user attention across a wide range of external websites. The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs), which provide answers directly within platform interfaces, raises concerns that online activity may become more centralized. We study whether LLM adoption displaces traditional web navigation or instead restructures how users discover and consume information. Using nationally representative Comcore panel data from 2019–2024 and session-level evidence from the Internet Behavior Experiment, we examine how search activity, web exploration, and downstream navigation evolve with LLM use. Exploiting staggered adoption across users, we find that LLM adoption coincides with a sustained increase in the number of unique websites visited, alongside a short-lived rise in traditional search activity, suggesting that LLMs complement rather than replace search. Session-level analyses show that most LLM use occurs alongside search, while LLM-only sessions remain rare. At the same time, when LLMs route users to external websites, traffic does not concentrate across a smaller set of destinations compared to traditional search.

title: The Internet Behavior Experiment: An Experimental Infrastruc...
authors: ['Cristobal Cheyre', 'Li Jiang', 'Florian Schaub', 'Zijun Ding', 'Cristiana Firullo', 'Yucheng Li', 'Alessandro Acquisti']
abstract: We present the Internet Behavior Experiment (IBE) - a novel experimental infrastructure for studying the impact of online advertising, tracking, and targeting on consumer behavior. Existing approaches rely heavily on observational data, which suffer from self-selection and limited causal identification, or platform-specific experiments, which provide strong internal validity but cannot capture the broader consumer journey across the web. Laboratory and survey studies, while controlled, lack ecological validity and temporal depth. The IBE addresses those limitations through a client-server infrastructure that enables randomized interventions in advertising exposure, tracking, and targeting, while collecting rich, longitudinal data across multiple platforms and devices. The methodology integrates multiple captured behaviors (including browsing, advertising exposure, shopping and search, purchase confirmation, promotional emails) with periodic self-report surveys. Rigorous privacy and security safeguards ensure responsible handling of sensitive data. We illustrate the capabilities of the infrastructure with a demonstration experiment that assigns participants to full behavioral advertising exposure, ad-blocking, or anti-tracking conditions over three months, allowing tracing the effects of interventions on product search patterns, purchases, and satisfaction. Beyond consumer welfare, the infrastructure can support a wide range of inquiries into media consumption, vendor diversity, exposure to political or health-related advertising, interactions with large language models, and more.

title: How Brands Price Cross-Category Influencers: An Empirical St...
speaker: Haonan Wang
abstract: While influencer marketing has flourished in recent years, existing literature primarily relies on the match-up hypothesis to explore brand-influencer image consistency. This traditional perspective fails to explain the increasing prevalence of cross-category collaborations and often overlooks influencers' agency as independent commercial entities, treating them merely as passive information intermediaries. Using micro-data from a leading Chinese social media platform, this study investigates how brands price cross-category influencers. By employing deep learning techniques, this research reveals a dual mechanism in cross-category pricing from a dynamic content perspective: a risk discount resulting from long-term persona mismatch and a novelty premium generated when sponsored content fills semantic structural holes within a vertical category. Further analysis indicates that this premium does not stem from real-time textual modifications. Instead, it is rooted in the influencers’ generalist capabilities and their ability to integrate sponsored content from other categories with their original personas. In an extended analysis, this study employs a DID model based on the platform’s mandatory identity-labeling policy. The findings demonstrate that increased information transparency preserves high-quality cross-category resources by strengthening market screening mechanisms rather than suppressing prices. This research extends the scope of influencer marketing beyond static matching to dynamic content creation and asset pricing, offering a new theoretical framework and managerial guidance for understanding cross-category collaborations in social media environments.

title: The Impact of AIGC Disclosure on Content Engagement: Evidenc...
speaker: Ivy Chu Dang
authors: ['Ivy Chu Dang', 'Zhili Li', 'Kayla Li', 'hongchuan shen', 'Michael Zhang']
abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI (GenAI) technologies has fundamentally transformed the landscape of digital content creation, making AI-generated content (AIGC) ubiquitous across social media and content platforms. Major platforms have begun to implement AIGC detection and disclosure policies, but little is known about their effects on market outcomes. Using a large-scale, proprietary dataset from a major video platform and a Double Machine Learning (DML) framework, we investigate the impact of platform-disclosed versus creator-disclosed AIGC labels on content engagement. We uncover a divergent impact based on the disclosure source: Platform disclosure triggers a significant engagement penalty, whereas creator disclosure generates an honesty premium. Importantly, this core effect is subject to significant heterogeneity across two dimensions. First, the effects are heterogeneously amplified by creator characteristics: big creators, who possess high idiosyncrasy credit, face a disproportionately larger penalty when their AIGC is platform detected and disclosed, yet they also reap a stronger honesty premium from voluntary disclosure. Second, the disclosure penalty is most severe for content with high reality dependence (e.g., TV and news), where AIGC triggers an uncanny valley-like psychological reaction but is significantly mitigated for content with low reality dependence (e.g., abstract music and memes), where AIGC is perceived through a novelty heuristic. In summary, our research demonstrates that the impact of AIGC disclosure is jointly determined by the source of disclosure, the characteristics of creator, and the nature of content. These findings offer critical guidance for platforms on designing effective disclosure regimes and for creators on strategically managing transparency.

title: Delegating Household Finance to Algorithms
speaker: Cheng He
abstract: Automation and default-based interventions increasingly rely on algorithmic systems to execute financial decisions on behalf of households. While much of the discussion of artificial intelligence in finance emphasizes prediction and personalization, many widely deployed systems operate through relatively simple but scalable algorithmic allocation rules that determine how income is distributed across spending, liquidity, and long-term saving. This paper studies how the design of such algorithmic financial decision rules shapes household behavior. Using high-frequency data from a digital financial platform, we examine how households allocate resources, manage liquidity, and maintain saving commitments when financial decisions are governed by flexible, rule-based algorithms rather than fixed recurring investment commitments. Conceptually, we treat algorithmic automation as a form of delegated financial decision-making that varies in rigidity and adaptability. The analysis sheds light on how different algorithmic designs influence the persistence of saving behavior and the balance between short-term liquidity and long-term financial goals, with implications for the design of automated saving programs and algorithmic financial systems.

title: Generative AI, Open Source, and Application-Layer Product De...
speaker: Yi Liu
abstract: In this paper, we study open-source LLMs for corporate product development. The rise of foundation models in generative AI (GenAI), driven by the development of large language models (LLMs), is reshaping firms’ product development strategies through open-source technologies. Unlike traditional open-source environments characterized by collaboration and standardization, LLM-based open source introduces new complexities, notably fine-tuning uncertainty and limited collaboration between firms, that influence innovation efforts of firms. This paper develops an analytical model to examine how these dynamics shape firms’ product development strategies, contrasting settings involving traditional open-source technologies with those built on LLMs. Our results show that fine-tuning uncertainty acts as a double-edged sword: while it destabilizes predictable product development outcomes for firms, it can also create artificial vertical differentiation that softens competition and boosts firm profitability. In contrast, limited collaboration imposes structural barriers that prevent cooperative vertical improvement, curtailing shared progress and reducing profitability. Taken together, however, these dynamics can still yield positive outcomes. From a welfare perspective, we find that as LLMs become easier to adapt to product needs, total welfare increases in both settings, but interestingly, it grows more slowly under LLM-based open source, due to distortions introduced by the artificial vertical differentiation that weaken firm-user matching. At the same time, limited collaboration can improve welfare by compelling firms to undertake stronger vertical development individually, raising product quality and alleviating the underinvestment problem that arises in traditional open-source collaboration. Overall, our study sheds lights on the strategic trade-offs in leveraging open-source LLMs for product development.

title: The Burden of Human Foresight: Algorithmic Pricing and Forwa...
speaker: Yuanfang Li...
abstract: Firms increasingly set prices using customer-level insights. Traditional behavior-based pricing conditions prices on observed purchase history, allowing firms to distinguish new from returning customers. More recently, many firms have adopted algorithmic pricing, the AI- or data-driven methods that infer consumers’ preferences and dynamically tailor prices. We study how behavior and algorithmic-based pricing jointly shape competitive outcomes in dynamic markets, and how consumers’ forward-looking behavior and evolving preferences alter the equilibrium outcomes. We develop a two-firm, multi-period model where in each period a fraction of consumers is replaced by new entrants while past buyers may return. Firms observe identity and purchase history and, for returning customers, are setting prices in alignment with algorithmic-predicted preference. Theoretical model analyses suggest that the capability of combining behaivour and algorithmic-predicted preference in pricing has the potential to generate win-win for competing firms. Interestingly, forward-looking consumers can be harmed by their own sophistication. Anticipating future targeted prices, they behave as if less price sensitive in the current period, inducing higher prices in equilibrium that increase firms’ profits. These effects are strongest when preference persistence is high and customer turnover is moderate. This study contributes to theory by characterizing how algorithmic preference inference and purchase-history–based targeting interacts in dynamic competition with strategic consumers, revealing conditions under which forward-looking behavior amplifies firms’ pricing power rather than disciplining it. From a managerial perspective, our results highlight when investments in algorithmic pricing technologies increase profitability, informing firms’ data strategies and ongoing policy debates surrounding personalized pricing and consumer protection.

title: Learning Marketing Craft via Linguistic Projection in Contra...
speaker: Tong Wang
abstract: Marketing outcomes depend on craft choices — copy, framing, voice, structure — that marketers author and intervene on. Existing text-to-outcome tools yield anonymous embeddings, off-target topics, or features bounded by researcher priors. We introduce a method that discovers interpretable, intervenable, and generalizable craft features directly from data. Within-product contrast vectors (embedding differences between higher- and lower-outcome variants of the same product) isolate craft from content. The principal direction in contrast space identifies the main axis of improvement; a large language model performs the linguistic projection — abstracting the shared pattern of the top-loaded pairs into a named, operational rule. The method iterates on the subspace orthogonal to previously named directions. We apply it to a corpus of book blurbs and recover a cross-seed-stable family of named craft features.

title: From Model Choice to Model Belief: Establishing a New Measur...
speaker: Hongshen Sun
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but common practices to use LLM-generated data are inefficient. Treating an LLM’s output (“model choice”) as a single data point underutilizes the information inherent to the probabilistic nature of LLMs. This paper introduces and formalizes “model belief,” a measure derived from an LLM’s token- level probabilities that captures the model’s belief distribution over choice alternatives in a single generation run. The authors prove that model belief is asymptotically equivalent to the mean of model choices (a non-trivial property) but forms a more statistically efficient estimator, with lower variance and a faster convergence rate. Analogous properties are shown to hold for smooth functions of model belief and model choice often used in downstream applications. The authors demonstrate the performance of model belief through a demand estimation study, where an LLM simulates consumer responses to different prices. In practical settings with limited numbers of runs, model belief explains and predicts ground-truth model choice better than model choice itself, and reduces the computation needed to reach sufficiently accurate estimates by roughly a factor of 20. The findings support using model belief as the default measure to extract more information from LLM-generated data.

title: Generative Augmented Inference
speaker: Cheng Lu
abstract: Large language models enable inexpensive AI-generated annotations, but using them reliably for causal inference remains challenging. Naively pooling AI and human data induces bias, while existing methods such as Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI; Angelopoulos et al., 2023) treat AI outputs as proxies of true labels - an assumption often violated for generative model outputs in practice. We propose Generative Augmented Inference (GAI), a framework that treats AI outputs as general, potentially high-dimensional informative features for learning human labels rather than as surrogates. GAI flexibly models this relationship using nonparametric methods, enabling consistent estimation and valid inference from combined human and AI data. We establish asymptotic normality and show that GAI strictly improves asymptotic efficiency over human-data-only estimation whenever AI outputs are informative for true labels. Empirical studies on real-world datasets demonstrate that GAI significantly reduces estimation error and improves confidence interval quality across diverse generative data sources relative to human-only and PPI-based estimation.

title: Learning when to Quit in Sales Conversations
speaker: Emaad Ahmed Manzoor
abstract: Salespeople frequently face the dynamic screening decision of whether to persist in a conversation or abandon it to pursue the next lead. Yet, little is known about how these decisions are made, whether they are efficient, or how to improve them. We study these decisions in the context of high-volume outbound sales where leads are ample, but time is scarce and failure is common. We formalize the dynamic screening decision as an optimal stopping problem and develop a generative language model-based sequential decision agent — a stopping agent — that learns whether and when to quit conversations by imitating a retrospectively-inferred optimal stopping policy. Our approach handles high-dimensional textual states, scales to large language models, and works with both open-source and proprietary language models. When applied to calls from a large European telecommunications firm, our stopping agent reduces the time spent on failed calls by 54% while preserving nearly all sales; reallocating the time saved increases expected sales by up to 37%. Upon examining the linguistic cues that drive salespeople’s quitting decisions, we find that they tend to overweight a few salient expressions of consumer disinterest and mispredict call failure risk, suggesting cognitive bounds on their ability to make real-time conversational decisions. Our findings highlight the potential of artificial intelligence algorithms to correct cognitively-bounded human decisions and improve salesforce efficiency.

title: Personalized Recommendations with Revenue-Preserving Machine...
speaker: Sam Levy
abstract: When users request data deletion from recommendation systems, removing raw records from databases is insufficient: their behavioral patterns remain encoded in model embeddings, posing significant privacy risks. Existing machine unlearning approaches rely on data sharding and model retraining, which either destroy collaborative filtering signals or impose prohibitive computational costs. Most importantly, no prior work addresses the negative economic consequences of unlearning for service providers. We introduce Sparse Auto-Encoder (SAE)-driven revenue-aware unlearning, a novel framework leveraging SAEs to identify and suppress user-specific latent features within Large Language Model-based sequential recommenders. Using search-clickstream data, we jointly optimize privacy, recommendation quality, and revenue preservation objectives through parameter-efficient fine-tuning updates guided by 131K interpretable SAE features. Crucially, our approach requires no model retraining—completing unlearning requests in minutes rather than hours. Our experiments demonstrate a 96% reduction in privacy-related activations while maintaining recommendation quality within 3% of baseline performance. The identified features cluster meaningfully by product category, enabling interpretable and targeted suppression of user-specific knowledge. Compared to existing approaches, our method achieves twice the revenue preservation while operating much faster. This work offers the first revenue-aware unlearning framework for personalized recommendations, providing practitioners with an interpretable, economically-grounded approach to user data removal.

title: From Privacy Washing to Sustainable Data Strategies: A Theor...
speaker: Ziqi Zhong
abstract: We first developed analytical models showing that firms can enhance profits and consumer surplus by adopting sustainable data strategies. To validate the model and enable scalable policy measurement, we introduced PrivaAI, an AI-based agent with a novel framework derived from regulation, literature, expert input, and human ratings. PrivaAI, leveraging structured chain-of-thought reasoning and enhanced retrieval-augmented generation, was fine-tuned and tested on 28,360 human-labeled evaluations (1,418 policies) to align with consumer perceptions by 92.5%. Applying it to policies from 10 million websites classified by Open PageRank and GICS sectors, we find: (i) lower-ranked providers systematically underperform, consistent with the model's assumption; (ii) substantial industry heterogeneity exists, with digital-native sectors outperforming traditional industries; and (iii) regulatory asymmetries—under weaker regulation (CCPA), higher-ranked firms often show uneven improvements, whereas stronger regulation (GDPR) yields broader, more balanced improvements. A pre-registered lab experiment with 610 US-representative participants validates that PrivaAI assessments explain consumer behavior and uncovers an “authenticity paradox“: consumers perceive high-quality policies with dimensional inconsistency as less deceptive than uniformly excellent policies, interpreting selective excellence as genuine prioritization rather than privacy washing. Together, these findings provide a scalable foundation for benchmarking privacy practices and offer actionable insights for firms and regulators.

title: Consumer Response to Racial Discrimination on Digital Platfo...
speaker: O. Cem Ozturk
abstract: Public health crises such as the 1918 influenza pandemic, the HIV/AIDS epidemic, and the COVID-19 pandemic often intensify discrimination against minority groups perceived to be linked to disease origins. Prior work suggests that such heightened discrimination has real negative economic consequences for affiliated businesses. Using the COVID-19 pandemic as an exogenous shock to anti-Chinese sentiment in the United States, we show that Chinese restaurants’ online ratings increased relative to non-ethnic restaurants after the pandemic’s onset. We then examine where and why this reputational lift is most pronounced. The increase in ratings is larger for restaurants with lower pre-pandemic ratings and those that are not part of a chain. It is also larger for restaurants located in areas with low- to middle-income levels and low- to middle-Republican vote shares. We complement these heterogeneity results using a large language model trained on more than 250,000 reviews, which supports a targeted prosocial behavior mechanism. Next, we link these reputational gains to longer-run outcomes. Higher pandemic-period ratings predict a higher likelihood of restaurant survival about five years after the pandemic’s onset. Finally, we document a platform-side tradeoff. While ratings became more favorable for marginalized businesses, engagement with review content declined, reflected in lower perceived usefulness and humor. Together, our findings suggest that online reviews can serve as a channel for targeted consumer support during discrimination-inducing crises while also decreasing the informational value of review content.

title: Measuring Corporate Risks Using Large Language Model Embeddi...
speaker: Leyao Tan
abstract: We propose a novel text-based approach to measuring corporate climate risk that combines large language model (LLM) sentence embeddings with supervised machine learning. We find that this combined approach improves the precision of climate-related sentence classification by 23% relative to predefined keyword methods and by 26% compared to a recent LLM agent-based classifier. Using the resulting corporate risk measure, we further explore how firms react to supplier climate risks. We find that after controlling firm- and supplier-level non-climate risks, supplier climate risk exposure increases the likelihood of terminating existing suppliers by 5.3% and adding new suppliers by 6.3%. Our analysis further suggests that such restructuring is strategic. First, the restructured supply networks exhibit greater geographic diversity, indicating firms' efforts to mitigate future climate-related disruptions by diversifying supplier locations. Second, firms prioritize adding new suppliers that produce more unique products or occupy more central positions in the supply chain network. We also document that such restructuring is most pronounced for supplier backward-looking climate risks and extreme physical climate risks. Firms with higher operational efficiency and greater product differentiation respond more aggressively to supplier climate risk.

title: Digital Twin-Based Bayesian Imputation: Combining LLM Priors...
speaker: Youngik Lee
abstract: We propose Digital Twin-Based Bayesian Imputation (DTB2I), a hybrid framework designed for missing value imputation by synthesizing Large Language Model (LLM) intelligence with local statistical patterns. DTB2I operates on a dual-stage Bayesian mechanism where it first elicits an informative prior from a digital twin, defined as an LLM agent prompted to simulate a specific respondent’s persona, and subsequently updates this prior with a likelihood distribution derived from k-nearest neighbors within the internal dataset to yield a posterior estimate for the missing value. The main contributions of DTB2I are fourfold. First, unlike conventional imputation methods (e.g., MICE, kNN) that rely exclusively on internal data distributions, DTB2I integrates both external knowledge and internal empirical evidence. It utilizes LLMs as an external knowledge vault that is embedded with a multitude of latent relationships that can be leveraged to bridge the gap between internal data and external semantic reality. Second, it enables imputation through semantic reasoning, capturing latent relationships that purely numerical models overlook. Third, it remains viable in cold start scenarios characterized by high missing rates, where traditional models fail due to insufficient observed data. Finally, DTB2I is particularly effective in Missing Not At Random (MNAR) conditions, as the LLM's external prior provides a stabilizing anchor that mitigates the biases inherent in truncated or self-selected internal samples.

title: Can Large Language Models Predict Firm Behaviors?
abstract: We study the potential to use LLMs to measure the distribution of firms’ future actions under different states of the world. Such distributions play a critical role to calibrate beliefs in marketing models where consumers face incomplete information about firms’ future actions and where firms face incomplete information about their competitors’ future reactions. We conduct a case study of Apple’s launch of the suite of iPhone 16 and iPhone 17 models. Using a series of choice-based conjoint experiments, we elicit LLM-implied beliefs, based only on information available months ahead of launch, about the technical specifications of the next-generation iPhone. We then compare these beliefs with realized product outcomes. We find that LLM predictions closely align with the actual iPhone configurations released by Apple. An analysis of the underlying generative logic highlights the role of attribute-level nonlinearities and specific independence assumptions. Extending the study to incorporate historical product specifications and market rumors, we show that external knowledge selection and prompt injection methods systematically influence prediction performance. Notably, long-context prompting consistently outperforms Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in our experimental setting. Overall, these results suggest that LLMs can serve as scalable tools for predicting firm decisions, with broad implications for market participants and researchers.

title: Improving the Predictive Accuracy of Large Language Models i...
speaker: Hani Bououdina
abstract: Understanding and predicting consumer choices is central to marketing science. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer a complementary tool for simulating consumer decisions, yet most applications rely on general-purpose models that are not trained on choice data and therefore show limited predictive accuracy in discrete choice settings. This project investigates whether and how targeted fine-tuning and prompt design can improve the ability of LLMs to predict consumer choices. We fine-tune a Llama-based model using data from choice-based conjoint studies and systematically evaluate its performance under different prompting strategies. Specifically, we implement a four-factor prompting framework that varies whether prompts include (1) demographic information about the decision-maker, (2) information about the decision-maker’s underlying utilities, (3) estimated choice probabilities, and (4) references to random utility theory. Using a full-factorial design, we compare predictive accuracy across prompting conditions and benchmark the fine-tuned model against leading general-purpose models, including GPT-5.1 and GPT-4.1. Results show that fine-tuned models achieve substantially higher predictive accuracy than flagship models. Moreover, explicitly referencing random utility theory in the prompt improves prediction quality, while adding consumer utilities or predicted probabilities does not yield additional gains. The findings demonstrate the value of fine-tuning LLMs with existing choice data and provide actionable guidance on prompt design for choice prediction tasks. More broadly, the study positions fine-tuned LLMs as scalable, low-cost tools for anticipating consumer responses in applied marketing contexts.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models as Alternatives to Linear M...
speaker: Masao Ueda
abstract: With the advent of the big data era, marketing data have increased in volume, and various analytical methods have been proposed accordingly. While the growth in analytical techniques enables the derivation of richer marketing insights from data, it also poses a challenge: practitioners must invest considerable time in learning these methods, and as a result, many are not fully utilized in practice. In this study, we examine whether large language models (LLMs), with their strong predictive capabilities, can be used to perform general pattern extraction and prediction on POS data and ID‑linked POS data in a manner comparable to traditional linear‑model‑based analyses, using actual datasets. At the same time, although LLMs can be used for prediction, several issues require attention. For example, because LLMs output results as text rather than numerical values, additional formatting steps are necessary—for instance, ensuring consistent output formatting when the model generates a number such as “123,” which may otherwise be produced digit by digit. In the oral presentation, we will present predictions based on LLMs, discuss their potential substitutability for linear models, and outline important considerations for the analysis.

title: How Artificial Intelligence Impacts Advertising Processes an...
speaker: Giha Shin
authors: ['Jarim Kim', 'Giha Shin', 'Haram Myong', 'Hyungtae Kim', 'Sehee Jeon', 'Changhee Lee']
abstract: In recent years, the use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the advertising industry has grown exponentially. Yet, existing research has largely concentrated on consumer responses to AI-generated advertising and AI’s potential to enhance effectiveness and streamline execution. Empirical studies examining how and to what extent AI is impacting advertising production remain exceedingly limited. Addressing this gap, this study investigates advertising professionals’ perceptions of AI-generated advertising copy through in-depth interviews with 21 practitioners. The findings show three key insights. First, professionals described AI-generated copy as original and formulaic, straightforward, and particularly well-suited for Internet advertising. Second, they agreed that AI offers high efficiency, but they viewed its effectiveness as conditional. Third, when comparing AI-generated copy to human-generated copy, they strongly affirmed human superiority and exhibited reluctance to acknowledge cases where AI might outperform humans. The study findings offer critical insights into emerging applications of AI and illuminate how the industry is evolving. In doing so, the study deepens our understanding of AI’s shifting role in advertising and highlights both the skills professionals will need and the considerations AI developers should prioritize as they design future tools.

title: ChatGPT vs Google: Consumer Search, Information Display, Bra...
speaker: Shiyuan Song
abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative AI is reshaping how consumers search for information and how firms compete for visibility in digital environments. Search engines (SEs) such as Google operate on index-based retrieval systems that rank and display collections of web pages according to keyword relevance and link authority, often supplemented by AI-generated summaries alongside ranked results, with users responsible for navigating, evaluating, and synthesizing information. In contrast, AI engines (AIEs) such as ChatGPT rely on large language models to aggregate, interpret, and synthesize information into direct answers with selective source citations, shifting much of the screening and integration task from users to the system, thereby creating a different paradigm of information access. These differences potentially alter information presentation, search costs, and brand exposure, yet systematic empirical evidence comparing the two paradigms remains limited. We conduct large-scale experiments across diverse consumer decision contexts to compare information display and consumer responses under SE and AIE environments. We examine how different querying strategies shape the structure and content of the information presented and how consumers process and act upon it. These studies provides a systematic comparison of the two search paradigms. The findings generate new insights into how different search paradigms shape consumer decision making and brand competition.

title: Generative AI Prevalence and the Effectiveness of Visual Adv...
speaker: Yeonsoo Lee
abstract: Today, a substantial amount of advertising is visual-centric, as seen in television advertising, sponsored content on social media, and display ads. At the same time, increasing attempts to apply AI in ad creation have heightened consumers' awareness that the ads they encounter may be AI-generated. This research examines whether and how the perceived prevalence of generative AI in the environment influences the effectiveness of visual advertising. We conduct a 2 (low vs. high prevalence of AI-generated ads in the environment) × 2 (low vs. high textual emphasis) randomized experiment and compare respondents’ brand attitudes and purchase intentions after viewing a video ad. We find that visual ads are less effective when perceived generative AI prevalence is high, and this reduction is attenuated in ads with higher textual emphasis. Exploratory evidence suggests that higher perceived generative AI prevalence reduces the perceived ad trustworthiness, which may explain the reduced effectiveness of visual advertising in high generative AI prevalence environments.

title: Ai-Mediated Marketing: Constrained Content Optimization for ...
speaker: Kartik Hosanagar
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape consumer purchase decisions by synthesizing information and issuing direct recommendations, disrupting traditional search optimization. We introduce a Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) framework that influences LLM recommendations while preserving brand voice and professional integrity. Rather than using adversarial or low-quality content, our method computes gradients over token embeddings in open-weight models to identify words whose revision most increases selection probability. A multi-armed bandit balances exploitation of high-impact tokens with exploration of under-tested positions. Across experiments with 200 products in 50 consumer categories, GEO yields significant gains in single-token selection probability (+6.04 percentage points, p < 0.001) and natural ranking tasks (−0.139 rank positions, p = 0.004). These improvements require only minor edits, about 16 words per 100, preserving tone and meaning. Effects are strongest for mid-ranked products, with ceiling effects for market leaders. The results extend search optimization to generative systems and offer an ethical, auditable approach to AI-mediated visibility.

title: The Role of Sales Pitch Intensity in Live Commerce: Informat...
speaker: DongYoung Jeong
authors: ['DongYoung Jeong', 'Seungwook Jin', 'Keumseok Kang', 'Taekyung Kim', 'Alex Jiyoung Kim']
abstract: Sales pitch plays a critical role in shaping consumer purchase decisions by conveying the value of product and reducing uncertainty related to consumer purchase. This paper examines how multiple dimensions of sales pitch, captured through both linguistic components such as sales messages and phonetic components such as characteristics of vocal delivery, jointly influence sales outcomes in live commerce. Using data from 10,436 broadcasts on the largest live commerce platform in Korea, we develop an AI-based multimodal framework that integrates speech-to-text conversion, automated content classification, and phonetic analysis. Sales pitch intensity is operationalized along three linguistic dimensions—frequency, proximity, and stress—distinguished between informational and emotional content. Phonetic delivery is captured through vocal pitch and pronunciation clarity. Fixed-effects panel regressions estimate impacts on sales value and order quantity while controlling for seller-specific and temporal heterogeneity. The results show that higher informational intensity significantly increases both sales value and order quantity, whereas emotional intensity consistently reduces performance. Phonetic delivery systematically moderates these effects: higher vocal pitch amplifies both the positive impact of informational intensity and the negative impact of emotional intensity, while clearer pronunciation attenuates the adverse effects of emotional appeals. These patterns are most pronounced for search goods, utilitarian products, multi-product broadcasts, larger discounts, and first-time sellers. In sum, this study contributes to the literature on sales communication and live commerce by conceptualizing sales pitch as a multidimensional construct that integrates both linguistic and vocal components and showing how these components jointly affect sales performance in live commerce.

title: The Generative Artificial Intelligence Marketplace: Algorith...
speaker: Sunil Erevelles
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) pushes the boundaries of a paradigm shift, and is radically transforming marketing. It differs from all past technologies in that it is not a tool, but has agency. While a tool can be controlled by humans and gives humans more power, Gen AI does the opposite. It has the capacity to create, decide, execute and reproduce without human control. Thus, Gen AI can be classified as an inorganic species in accordance with the biological species concept. It surpasses humans in emotional intelligence, specifically because it has no emotions. It transforms consumers into algorithms, able to understand them better than they understand themselves. It metamorphosizes consumers and brands into simultaneously-evolving algorithms, able to precisely influence consumption behavior. It moves the focus of marketing communications from attention and engagement to intimacy. It commoditizes knowledge, intelligence and creativity and is mastering the power of illusions and delusions. Furthermore, while humans evolve slowly over thousands of years, Gen AI evolves rapidly over months. It can control marketplaces with hierarchies and networks of autonomous agents. Collectively, this paradigm shift will result in the radical transformation of marketing. The objective of this research is to develop a theoretical framework for a marketplace based on Gen AI-centric logic. Using inductive-realist approaches, and drawing on Bayesian, Latent Variable, Natural Language Processing and Behavioral Reasoning Theories, the author proposes a framework, with foundational premises for this fast-developing marketplace. This framework could help accelerate academic research and practitioner decision-making in an Age of Inorganic Super-Intelligence.

title: Beyond Ranks: Measuring Brand Visibility in LLM Outputs
speaker: Christine Schmidt
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape how consumers search for information and discover brands. However, visibility in LLM-generated answers is typically evaluated using proxies borrowed from traditional search engine settings (e.g., rank or textual prominence), which may not reflect how consumers perceive brand prominence in LLM-generated responses. We develop and validate a measure of LLM visibility that captures consumer-perceived brand prominence within LLM outputs. Across several studies, we show that LLM output structure is a central driver of perceived visibility beyond conventional visibility proxies. To study visibility in realistic LLM interactions, we employ an adaptive, prompt-based survey design that generates LLM responses in real time. Our findings provide a foundation for studying visibility and competition in LLMs and offer guidance for brands seeking to manage visibility in generative search environments.

title: Long or Short? Personalizing Ad Length and Frequency
speaker: Ali Goli
abstract: We study the economics of advertising length using a large-scale randomized experiment on 18.3 million Pandora listeners. The experiment promoted a listening feature and randomly assigned users to advertising campaigns that varied in ad format (10 vs. 30 seconds) and frequency. For both users unfamiliar with the feature and those already familiar, we document meaningful incremental ad effects, with the relative advantage of long over short ads substantially larger among unfamiliar users. We use machine learning to capture heterogeneity in both responsiveness to the campaign and realized exposure levels, and conduct off-policy evaluation of alternative campaign designs. A personalized policy that optimally allocates ad length and frequency across users increases incremental ad effects by about 30 percent. Two-thirds of this efficiency gain comes from leveraging heterogeneity in exposure rather than heterogeneity in responsiveness to the campaign.

title: Identifying Individual-Level Well-Being Enhancement Behavior...
speaker: Michiko Tsubaki
abstract: This study proposes a method for identifying the daily behavioral factors that enhance subjective well-being for each customer, with the aim of developing personalized optimization marketing strategies grounded in a customer-dominant logic perspective. Specifically, it introduces the use of Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE), an interpretable machine learning technique capable of capturing interaction effects, to enable analysis at the individual level. The analysis incorporates multivariate data—including personal attributes, daily behavioral factors, psychological variables, and cognitive biases—to determine which daily actions, and what levels of effort, increase well-being for each individual. This approach allows for the prediction and visualization of the factors that influence each customer’s well-being. The results reveal that the daily behavioral variables associated with increased well-being differ depending on factors such as a customer’s current well-being level (high, medium, or low), effort expenditure (high, medium, or low), and attributes including gender, customer type, and income level. These findings provide a method for gaining a deep understanding of how recommendation strategies should be adapted accordingly.

title: Curbing Promotions in Kids' Content? the Limits of Platform ...
speaker: Sumeet Kumar
abstract: Advertising embedded in YouTube videos is a central component of the platform’s monetization strategy. When such content targets children, it creates distinct governance challenges due to children’s limited ability to recognize persuasive intent. In response, YouTube and similar platforms have introduced child-specific content policies that restrict commercial activity. In 2021, YouTube modified its policy to prohibit “overly commercial or promotional” material in children’s videos distributed on YouTube Kids. Using data from top children’s channels and general-audience channels as a control group between July 2020 and December 2021, we study the causal impact of this policy. We quantify promotional intensity using large language models applied to video transcripts, detect sponsorship disclosures, and estimate treatment effects using a Synthetic Difference-in-Differences design. We find no substantive decline in promotional activity on children’s channels following the policy. Instead, promotional content becomes less transparent, as disclosure declines significantly after implementation. This pattern is driven by channels that promote proprietary or affiliated products, which show little change in promotional intensity but substantial reductions in disclosure, particularly among more popular creators. In contrast, channels without proprietary products exhibit partial compliance, reducing promotional content while maintaining disclosure. These findings highlight a key limitation of platform governance in multi-sided ecosystems: when creators internalize downstream commercial benefits, content restrictions alter the visibility rather than the prevalence of persuasion. The study contributes to research on digital platforms and policy regulation by providing large-scale causal evidence on how incentive heterogeneity shapes creator responses to platform policy interventions.

title: The Contingent Effect of AI Communication Quality on Patient...
speaker: Lin Ge
abstract: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) has faced resistance from patients, especially during the medical guidance stage, making it imperative to address this challenge. Based on trust theory, this study investigates the role of AI communication ability within medical AI guidance systems and examines the conditions under which such ability enhances patients’ trust in these systems. We conducted four human-subject experiments that simulated an authentic medical AI system.
