We find that higher levels of medical AI communication ability promote trust compared to lower levels (Study 1). Furthermore, patients with higher privacy concerns (Study 2) and a greater propensity to change (Study 3) show stronger trust in medical AI guidance when communication ability is high rather than low. However, perceived threat of AI does not show a significant moderating effect (Study 4). Our research contributes to mitigating patient resistance toward medical AI guidance and provides practical suggestions for designing and implementing effective AI among medical AI guidance systems.

title: Strength of Tie with Virtual Friends: The Role of Emotional ...
speaker: Elham Yazdani
abstract: This project explores how perceived emotional and cognitive intelligence in virtual conversational agents shapes users’ sense of relationship strength—the extent to which a user experiences a virtual friend as emotionally close, trustworthy, or socially supportive. While prior work on chatbots and social robots has shown that empathy and reasoning each enhance user satisfaction, little is known about how different blends of emotional versus cognitive intelligence jointly influence tie strength, particularly among young adults accustomed to AI-mediated communication. Understanding this distinction matters for both human–AI interaction theory and for commercial applications such as sales chatbots, brand companions, and AI customer service agents, where building relational trust is critical to conversion and retention. We will run a within‑subjects study on a secure web platform. Each participant is deterministically assigned to three conversational agents that vary in pre‑set levels of EI and CI. After each brief chat, the participant completes a post‑chat survey capturing perceived EI/CI, trust, tie strength, and willingness to follow recommendations; chat transcripts and metadata (message counts, duration) are stored under coded IDs. We expect perceived EI and CI to predict relational outcomes depending on lay beliefs and task context. Participants who believe virtual agents can have emotional intelligence should exhibit higher tie strength, trust, and recommendation adoption after high‑EI interactions, whereas those who endorse agent cognitive competence should be more influenced by high‑CI agents (especially in informational/problem‑solving contexts). We further anticipate mediation via trust (perceived EI/CI → trust → tie strength/recommendation adoption) and moderation by beliefs and context.

title: Deconstructing the Roles of Brand, Design, and Consistency i...
speaker: Jungeun Lim
abstract: At the point of purchase, consumers rely heavily on brand and packaging to evaluate products. However, because strong brands typically invest in superior design, managers face uncertainty in attributing sales outcomes to brand equity versus visual designs. This study develops a unified framework to disentangle three critical components of consumer evaluation: the design effect, the brand equity effect, and the brand–design inconsistency penalty. We examine these across aesthetic, functional, and symbolic perceptions, recognizing that different consumer segments prioritize different perceptual attributes. To operationalize this framework, we used generative AI to create a corpus of 5,582 shampoo product images, including existing market designs, systematically modified features, and entirely new AI-generated concepts. Each design was evaluated in two versions: paired with an established brand (branded) and a fictitious brand (unbranded). Design effects were estimated using a brand-agnostic AI model, while brand effects were identified by comparing matched versions of identical designs and modeled as a function of visual consistency. Our framework contributes by separately identifying brand, design, and inconsistency effects while estimating segment-level preferences for multiple attributes. This allows us to score existing and new designs and predict sales responses to targeted perception changes. Results show that brands act as credibility shortcuts for functional attributes, while design effectively communicates aesthetic and symbolic meaning. Visual consistency reinforces functional credibility, whereas deviation can assist symbolic repositioning. Together, these findings provide a diagnostic tool for forecasting the impact of packaging changes and advance research on the intersection of branding and visual marketing.

title: Spoken the Unspoken: Need-Aware LLM for Customer Service Aut...
speaker: Keyan Li
abstract: Customer service is a large and costly function that is difficult to scale, making large language models (LLMs) a promising alternative. Using customer-service data from one of the world's largest open-source software providers, we document that LLM service agents underperform human agents, and this gap is substantially wider when customer needs are unspoken or ambiguous than when they are explicit. This asymmetric gap arises partly from differences in training processes: human agents are incentivized to look beyond the current response, and inferring unspoken needs helps move the conversation forward, whereas LLMs receive no explicit training reward for doing so. Motivated by this, we propose Need-Aware LLM, an LLM agent that leverages established marketing research on needs. The algorithm comprises two stages: one that distills customer-need-related insights from the marketing literature, and another that optimally searches and incorporates these insights into an LLM-based need-prediction task, which in turn regularizes the agent's response generation. Our approach does not predefine a reasoning model; instead, it harnesses the process only with literature-derived data and the accompanying need-prediction component. Across multiple validation exercises - including human evaluations and prediction-powered inference (PPI)-calibrated LLM-as-a-judge assessments based on human labels - Need-Aware LLM significantly narrows the performance gap between LLM and human agents, especially in cases involving unspoken customer needs. The method is readily adaptable to a wide range of online customer-service and personal-selling applications.

title: Generative Embeddings for Marketing Text Refinement and Vali...
speaker: Finn Honer
abstract: The creation of short marketing texts, such as product claims or text message nudges, follows steps similar to new product innovation: ideation, refinement, and validation. With the rise of generative AI, marketing text ideation has become cheaper and less labor intensive. However, systematic refinement and rigorous validation remain challenging, especially when incorporating prior market research insights in a controlled and interpretable manner. The authors introduce the Generative Embedder, a method that enables AI-supported refinement and validation of marketing texts. The Generative Embedder allows marketers to refine texts based on prior market research insights in a deterministic and reproducible way. For idea validation, the method enables more efficient design and analysis of market research studies, similar to conjoint analysis, by representing texts as linear combinations of learned semantic attributes. The Generative Embedder estimates low-dimensional generative embeddings that capture key dimensions of variation. By manipulating these dimensions, marketers can systematically extrapolate beyond observed texts to generate refined variants with improved predicted marketing outcomes. Unlike prompting, the Generative Embedder provides parametric control over semantic attributes in generation. The authors validate the approach using product claims from a market research agency and vaccination nudges from Milkman et al. (2022), refining existing nudges to generate new variants predicted to be highly effective, making them promising candidates for future field testing. The authors outline a general framework for ideating, refining, and validating marketing texts in the age of generative AI, with the Generative Embedder as a bridge between generative models and established market research methods.

title: Unlocking Customer Diversity: a Novel Approach to More Accur...
speaker: Alexander Junod
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show immense promise for "silicon sampling" in market research. However, while recent studies confirm LLMs potential to accurately replicate average consumer responses, they consistently fail to capture customer heterogeneity, a phenomenon known as "mode collapse." This limitation renders synthetic data inadequate for strategic marketing tasks reliant on the dispersion of data, such as segmentation, targeting, and positioning. This work introduces Distributional Sampling, a novel prompting method designed to recover customer diversity without sacrificing mean accuracy. By combining Verbalized Sampling (prompting the model to externalize latent uncertainty via probability distributions) with Batch Prompting (providing contextual anchoring via simultaneous persona generation), our method effectively helps in simulating the "tails" of consumer preference distributions. We validate this approach using large-scale corporate identity surveys for two major European companies across two industries (Transportation and Telecommunications), benchmarking synthetic outputs against a representative human sample (N =1,000 each). Results demonstrate that Distributional Sampling occupies a Pareto-optimal zone: it improves distributional fidelity (measured via Wasserstein Distance) by up to >40% compared to standard sequential or batch prompting, while maintaining high accuracy regarding sample means. Our findings refute the assumption that LLMs are inherently limited to central tendency. Instead, we show that mode collapse can an artifact of deterministic prompting. By shifting synthetic data generation from simple estimation to probabilistic simulation, Distributional Sampling provides a robust foundation for next-generation market research, taking a step in the direction of enabling managers to accurately model the complex heterogeneity of real-world markets.

title: Conversing with the Future: How LLMs Fuel Marketing&Rsquo;S ...
speaker: Sanghak Lee
authors: ['Martin Mende', 'Juneha Baek', 'Donghyuk Shin', 'Sanghak Lee', 'Maura Scott', 'Amy Ostrom']
abstract: Extending prior work on co-occurrence networks-based knowledge discovery, this research introduces an LLM-augmented framework to identify and predict the impact of marketing research ideas that have never been published. The proposed four-step framework outperforms other methods for concept extraction such as author-provided keywords, frequency-based algorithms such as RAKE, and topic modeling techniques such as LDA. The authors also systematically evaluate the proposed research ideas through a Discovery Matrix, which reveals four distinct types of evolutionary trajectories for marketing scholarship. The authors further enrich their findings by using additional filtering criteria in their analyses, specifically, (i) different levels of citation impact (≥10, ≥ 50 citations), (ii) different time spans (5-, 10-, 20 years), and (iii) a portfolio of cross-disciplinary journals (from management, MIS, and accounting). Contributing to marketing knowledge, this research does not aim to merely develop a superior prediction model. Rather, it introduces a comprehensive process that encompasses the formulation of useful network data, the prediction of future conceptual links, and the extraction of meaningful insights.

title: How Well Do LLMs Predict the Effect of Discounts? Benchmarki...
speaker: Isabelle Engeler
authors: ['Isabelle Engeler', 'Cristian Besliu', 'Alexander Junod', 'Andrea Bernardino', 'Mariel Gandarillas Calderon']
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as promising new tools for generating customer insights. Recent research has shown their potential in simulating consumer brand perceptions, willingness-to-pay, or product attitudes. To assess their accuracy, prior research has typically benchmarked synthetic predictions against human survey responses. However, decades of research highlight that self-reports are prone to systematic biases (e.g., intention-action gap). Focusing on price discounts, a central marketing tactic, our research is the first to benchmark synthetic predictions (N = 48,400) against both real purchase behavior from two company field experiments (N = 1,342) and consumers’ self-reported purchase intentions from market research (N = 1,342). While the synthetic data accurately predicted actual purchase behavior in the no-discount condition, both synthetic and survey predictions substantially overestimated actual purchase behavior in the discount condition. Crucially, we identified three prompting strategies, contextual grounding, probability elicitation, and balanced wording—that proved effective in enhancing prediction accuracy. We test robustness across different data generation methods (e.g., zero-shot, few-shot, and digital twins), models and model parameters. Our findings shed light on the mechanisms that foster accuracy of synthetic data in estimating discount effects, offer practical guidance for managers seeking to use synthetic data to support decision-making, and will hopefully spur a discussion on appropriate benchmarks for evaluating the validity of synthetic data.

title: Strategic Design of Shopping LLMs Under Prompt-Induced Evalu...
speaker: Weize Yin
abstract: We study how to strategically control prompt sensitivity in shopping large language models (LLMs) when their product evaluations shape consumer demand and market outcomes. Through controlled experiments, we document a prompt-induced evaluation gap: meaning-preserving syntactic variations in consumer prompts systematically shift LLM product evaluations. Using an analytical model, we then find that eliminating the evaluation gap is not universally optimal. With a monopoly seller, a nonzero evaluation gap can benefit consumer surplus by increasing dispersion in the distribution of willingness to pay. With duopoly sellers, a nonzero evaluation gap can increase total seller profit by mitigating price competition. Finally, using an inference-time intervention that steers the LLM’s internal representations, we show that the evaluation gap is controllable. Overall, this paper shows that the prompt-induced evaluation gap can be strategically managed in shopping LLM design.

title: Personalizing Language Models for Targeted Content Generatio...
speaker: Mingzhang Yin
abstract: Firms increasingly rely on generative AI to engage consumers, yet most large language models produce generic content that overlooks heterogeneity in individual preferences. This talk introduces GPT², a framework that personalizes text generation by integrating language modeling with preference learning. GPT² is a latent-variable model that infers user preferences from textual content and large-scale non-textual interaction data such as upvotes and clicks. User representations learned from historical feedback are injected into a language model as soft prompts, enabling targeted and preference-aligned generation without human annotations. Applied to a large digital news platform and a Q&A platform, GPT² produces responses that better match users’ stylistic and content preferences and outperforms generic and personalized LLM benchmarks. The results highlight how generative targeting can complement traditional recommendation systems and help firms address cold-start and content scarcity challenges.

title: What Makes a Dating Profile Attractive? Interpretable Genera...
speaker: Seung Yoon Lee
abstract: Online platforms increasingly rely on AI-assisted content generation to drive user engagement. We study conditional text generation within the context of online dating, where the goal is to produce personalized profile descriptions that maximize "likes." Optimizing text in this setting is challenging because engagement signals are primarily driven by visual and structural features, and these modalities are deeply coupled. Furthermore, receiver preferences are highly heterogeneous; optimizing for a single aggregate reward often results in generic, "mode-collapsed" text. To address these challenges, we utilize prompt-based learning via textual gradient to evolve interpretable LLM prompts that generate text conditioned on a profile’s specific visual and structural attributes. Our framework incorporates a multimodal engagement scorer that jointly models visual, structural, and textual features, enabling the estimation of text’s incremental contribution. To account for unobserved receiver heterogeneity, we estimate a latent class choice model using data from a major dating platform to develop segment-specific engagement scorers. The resulting receiver-type-specific prompts reveal the textual content preferred by different segments and can generate personalized descriptions targeting either the full population or a sender-specified segment. We further assess the value of cross-modal interactions and latent receiver modalities to understand how visual and textual information interact across different segments. While we focus on text generation, this framework generalizes to other controllable modalities, such as image selection or structured attribute optimization, providing a robust approach for personalized, multimodal content generation.

title: Love, Actually? a Randomized Experiment on AI Companion use ...
speaker: Jiaming Jiang
abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) companions have quickly become a new category of consumer technology, attracting significant public attention and regulatory scrutiny. Advocates highlight their potential to offer emotional support and build social confidence, while critics warn of isolation, dependence, and risks to vulnerable groups. Despite the intensity of this debate, empirical evidence on their real-world effects remains limited. This paper presents causal evidence from a six-week randomized encouragement experiment conducted in collaboration with a major AI-companion company and involving adults with no prior AI-companion experience. Leveraging granular behavioral usage logs and weekly relationship status surveys, we examine three questions: whether virtual romantic interactions function as substitutes for, or complements to, real-life romantic relationships; how gender differences shape usage intensity and relational risk factors in AI-user interactions; and how users switch between virtual partners in ways that reveal underlying variety-seeking dynamics. By approaching these questions through an economic and behavioral lens, the study offers policy-relevant insights into the interpersonal implications of AI companionship and provides guidance for responsible platform design.

title: When Ads GO Native in Short-Form Video: The Dual Effects of ...
speaker: Runhua Huang
abstract: This study investigates the causal impact of native advertising on audience engagement in short-form videos, addressing the critical tension between monetization and user experience. Overcoming the misclassification challenges of prior observational research, we leverage a unique proprietary dataset of 379,023 videos from Douyin (TikTok China) containing internal, platform-verified commercial tags. This granular "ground truth" data enables the precise, large-scale distinction between customized brand promotions, embedded sales ads, and integrated hybrids, avoiding the measurement errors common in observational studies. To address endogeneity, we employ a novel cross-platform natural experiment using "twin videos" reposted on Bilibili without ads—leaving ad presence as the sole differentiating factor—augmented by Double Machine Learning (DML) to control for high-dimensional confounders. Our results reveal a sharp divergence: while hard-sell embedded ads significantly suppress engagement (approximately -54%), well-integrated customized promotions unexpectedly increase likes (approximately +15%) relative to organic content. We demonstrate that sponsorship resources often drive a content-quality uplift that effectively counteracts baseline advertising aversion—a mechanism we further validate via LLM-based semantic analysis of over 46,000 user comments. Furthermore, we identify meaningful heterogeneity: engagement benefits are pronounced in utilitarian genres but diminish in emotional categories, and we observe a concave, inverted-U relationship suggesting an optimal sponsorship intensity of 60–70%. These findings provide the first large-scale causal evidence that native ad effectiveness hinges on execution and content-ad congruence.

title: The Ripple Effects of Tariffs on Digital Advertising: Eviden...
speaker: Işın Acun
abstract: Trade policy interventions are typically designed to affect production costs, prices, and trade flows, yet their consequences may extend well beyond those. In particular, sudden increases in trade costs may alter firms’ discretionary investments, such as advertising, amplifying the economic effects of trade barriers. However, empirical evidence on how trade policy shocks affect firms’ digital advertising investments remains limited. We study the impact of the 2025 U.S. tariff changes on digital advertising markets, exploiting two policy events as natural experiments: the April 2, 2025 tariff announcement and the subsequent tariff implementation on August 7, 2025. Using weekly advertising spend data from a major digital advertising platform, combined with firm-level geographic and industry characteristics, we examine how tariff-induced cost shocks affect firms’ advertising expenditures. Our identification strategy leverages variation in firms’ exposure to U.S. tariffs. We apply difference-in-differences and triple-difference designs, comparing changes in advertising spend for U.S.-based advertisers relative to international advertisers before and after the policy events, with prior-year observations serving as placebo tests. Our sample consists of approximately 2,850 U.S. domains and 9,800 international domains after filtering. We further investigate heterogeneous effects by industry exposure using an LLM-based classification of firm tariff vulnerability across dimensions, including import intensity, China-sourcing. This enables analysis of whether firms with greater supply chain exposure to tariffed goods exhibit larger advertising reductions. Our findings provide novel evidence on how trade policy shocks propagate into digital advertising markets, highlighting an important but understudied adjustment with implications for platform revenues and advertising market dynamics.

title: Keep It Simple -or Not? The Role of Visual Complexity in New...
speaker: Sajeev Nair
abstract: Packaging is central to attracting consumer attention and influencing product choice, especially in crowded consumer packaged goods categories where visual cues often serve as the first point of interaction. Although prior research has examined visual complexity, less is known about how distinct dimensions of complexity captured directly from real-world packaging relate to new product performance. This study investigates how two specific dimensions – shape complexity and color complexity – affect sales of new products. Using computer vision techniques, the authors derive objective measures of shape and color complexity from packaging images of 332 U.S. product launches, which are then linked to retail sales data across more than 40,000 stores. The results indicate that only specific forms of complexity are associated with new product sales, highlighting the value of treating visual complexity as a multi-dimensional construct. While elements of complexity are beneficial on their own, their interaction harms sales. The study advances understanding of visual complexity as a strategic design lever, shows the value of machine learning-based measurement in field settings, and clarifies when different forms of complexity enhance or undermine new product success.

title: When Humans Lead and AI Supports:Task Allocation and Perform...
speaker: Adrien Audoin
abstract: Entrepreneurial firms often lack the resources to sustain creative social media engagement, yet social media visibility is vital for growth. Advances in generative AI offer new opportunities for these firms to produce professional-quality video and image content. However, integrating AI into creative, customer-facing work poses organizational challenges: success depends not only on using AI but on how it is embedded into the production process. We address this question through a randomized field experiment with an Italian entrepreneurial firm specializing in lighting products. The experiment manipulates the division of creative labor between humans and AI in producing images and videos for the firm’s Facebook and Instagram accounts, distinguishing between core tasks (strategic meaning and emotional connection) and peripheral tasks (editing and formatting). We analyze both performance (visibility and engagement on social media) and process (iterations and feedback in production). Preliminary findings show that combining human input for core components with AI assistance for peripheral ones enhances visibility by expanding audience reach among both followers and non-followers, but without increasing audience engagement. This configuration also improves efficiency in developing core content but requires more minor refinements of peripheral elements. The study advances understanding of how off-the-shelf AI tools assist resource-constrained entrepreneurs in visual media production.

title: Replying in Public: Firm-to-One Communication, Congruence, a...
speaker: Ceren Kolsarici
abstract: Firms communicate on social media by broadcasting posts to broad audiences (firm-to-many, FTM) or replying publicly to individual customers (firm-to-one, FTO). We develop and test a congruence account of engagement. Observers infer relational intent from communication style, and messages that feel congruent with their form are perceived as more authentic, spontaneous, and approachable, increasing engagement. We test this framework using 127,616 tweets from six Canadian financial institutions on X from July 2018 to September 2024 and a set of online experiments. Congruence is measured by combining LLM-coded ratings of authenticity, spontaneity, and approachability into a factor-based composite. Field analyses show that congruence is systematically higher in public replies than in broadcasts, and it robustly predicts engagement. Causal mediation results indicate that congruence is a key pathway through which communication form shapes engagement. Moderated mediation reveals content–form asymmetries. Informational content is better received in FTO replies, where it increases congruence and engagement, but it is discounted in FTM broadcasts. Emotional intensity shows the opposite pattern. Emotional cues tend to strengthen congruence and engagement more in FTM than in FTO, consistent with different observer inferences across forms. We control for response time and semantic similarity and use control-function terms to mitigate endogeneity in content and style. Across experiments, manipulating form and style causes shifts in perceived congruence and downstream engagement intentions, supporting the proposed mechanism. Together, the results provide actionable guidance on when firms should emphasize informational versus emotional content in public replies versus broadcast posts.

title: Institutional Consequences of Research Misconduct
speaker: Aukje Wijnen
abstract: Over the past decade, academic paper retractions have increased more than fivefold. Many of these retractions stem from research misconduct, including fabrication, falsification, plagiarism, and more recently, the production of fraudulent papers using AI tools. Existing research has primarily examined the consequences of research misconduct for individual authors, showing post-retraction declines in funding, research output, and citations. However, the broader institutional consequences of such misconduct remain underexplored. We address this gap by examining spillover effects of research misconduct on affiliated institutions. Across five studies, we analyze the institutional-level consequences of retractions for universities (Studies 1a–1c) and for firms involved in retracted university–industry collaborations (Studies 2a–2b). Study 1a uses a difference-in-differences design to examine whether research misconduct at a university reduces media mentions of unaffected papers from the same institution. Studies 1b–1c use experiments to assess how such misconduct shapes student perceptions of university quality and public perceptions of scientific legitimacy. Study 2a employs an event study to examine investor responses to firms implicated in research misconduct, and Study 2b uses an error-correction model to assess changes in consumer perceptions following firms’ involvement. Together, the findings broaden our understanding of research misconduct by revealing its institutional-level consequences for both universities and firms.

title: Beyond the Ivory Tower: How Transmission Media Increase the ...
speaker: Samuel Stäbler
abstract: This research examines how publishing managerial summaries of academic research in transmission media—such as managerial journals and blogs—can enhance the societal and managerial impact of scholarly work. Although practitioner-oriented transmission media have long been advocated as a bridge between academia and practice, systematic evidence of their effectiveness remains limited. Across three studies, we examine whether and why managerial summaries increase the impact of academic research and how to maximize such impact. Study 1 analyzes archival data from 15,900 academic articles and shows that the presence of managerial summaries in transmission journals significantly increases multiple impact metrics, including Altmetric attention, media citations, and policy mentions. These effects are particularly strong for articles focusing on consumer behavior, published in top-tier journals, and authored by researchers from North American institutions. Study 2 employs a large-scale online experiment with 1,389 business professionals and demonstrates that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)–generated blog summaries, compared with academic articles, significantly enhance the perceived managerial impact of academic research. This effect is especially pronounced among individuals who are less educated, older, and lower in belief in science. Study 3, an experiment with 177 respondents, further reveals that these effects are driven by greater ease of understanding and perceived relevance to practice. Together, the findings provide robust evidence that transmission media—and GenAI-assisted translation in particular—play a critical role in extending the reach, relevance, and real-world influence of academic research.

title: Learning by Evaluating: Evidence from Large-Scale Peer Feedb...
abstract: In modern service ecosystems, value co-creation increasingly depends on the critical thinking and evaluative judgment of participants. These cognitive capabilities are essential for integrating complex information, yet scaling their development remains a significant challenge across professional and educational sectors. We investigate structured peer feedback as a data-rich, user-generated service process that serves as a primary mechanism for developing these skills. Using a large longitudinal dataset from a digital assessment platform implemented across North American higher education institutions, we examine the reciprocal exchange of evaluative services. The platform structures interaction through repeated cycles of content submission, rubric-based evaluation, and recipient ratings, generating detailed behavioral and textual data. Our research identifies empirical evidence of critical thinking by analyzing both numeric performance metrics and granular text data. By applying longitudinal behavioral analysis, we examine how participation in evaluation activities relates to subsequent performance, extending beyond the conventional focus on receiving feedback. Our results reveal systematic performance changes over time and a strong positive association between the quality of feedback individuals provide and their subsequent performance. Ongoing work combines econometric models with machine learning–based text analysis to characterize feedback along dimensions such as tone, specificity, and alignment. We also explore how perceptions of fairness and reciprocity influence engagement in this co-created environment. By framing peer feedback as a technology-enabled service process, this study contributes to interdisciplinary research on digital platforms, service design, and user-generated evaluation. The results highlight the value of large-scale behavioral and textual data for understanding performance dynamics in AI-augmented service.

title: Human Capital Formation in Professional Sales: a Longitudina...
speaker: Howard Dover
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly automates information processing, the sales field faces renewed questions about the formation and measurement of uniquely human capabilities. This study examines whether business acumen and curiosity—key latent constructs in selling and boundary-spanning roles—can be systematically developed and empirically tracked over time. Participants conducted six to ten structured interviews with senior executives using a fixed protocol. Interview transcripts were analyzed as unstructured text using non‑parametric time‑series methods, enabling the construction of longitudinal measures of business acumen and curiosity at the individual level. Results show monotonic increases in both constructs, with most participants exhibiting detectable growth by the third or fourth interview and significant gains by the end of the sequence. The findings contribute a scalable approach to measuring human capital development from longitudinal unstructured data and suggest avenues for linking these constructs to sales interactions and performance outcomes.

title: When Algorithms Fail: Governance, Accountability, and Transp...
speaker: Yansong Hu
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes how firms interact with consumers, automate decisions, and communicate in digital markets. Yet failures in AI design and deployment continue to generate severe and often underreported harms—from biased recommendation systems to unsafe automation and deceptive content. This paper develops and tests a theory of responsible AI governance to explain the organizational mechanisms linking ethical harm and visibility across these settings. We conceptualize responsible AI governance as a multidimensional system of structural, relational, and procedural practices that translate ethical principles into operational routines. Using a large-scale dataset of AI-related failures spanning consumer, platform, and autonomous technologies, we test a model linking governance design to two ethical outcomes: the severity of harm and the level of public reporting. Results show that centralized accountability structures and transparent coordination processes significantly reduce harm severity and increase disclosure likelihood. These findings advance research on marketing ethics, algorithmic accountability, and organizational governance, demonstrating that the architecture of responsibility within AI-intensive firms influences not only the magnitude of harm but also its visibility to stakeholders. The study offers actionable insights for designing AI systems and governance structures that reduce ethical risk, enhance transparency, and sustain trust in data-driven markets.

title: Categorical Thinking and Firm Responses
speaker: Andreas Kraft
abstract: When consumers exhibit discontinuous responses to numerical thresholds, are they failing to process digits or following a deliberate decision rule? I examine this question within the used car market, where consumers systematically distinguish between vehicles above and below focal mileage values. Applying large language models to two million online forum posts, I measure consumer categorical thresholds for vehicle mileage. The extracted rules reveal systematic heterogeneity across make-threshold combinations that inattention to digits alone cannot predict, and many reference 5,000-mile multiples like 75,000 or 125,000, where discontinuities are significantly larger than at neighboring thresholds like 74,000 or 76,000. Merging these measures with millions of used vehicle transactions, I find that the frequency of stated rules predicts price discontinuities: make-mileage combinations mentioned more frequently in consumer discussions exhibit larger price drops at the cutoff. Turning to firm behavior, dealers largely calibrate to this heterogeneity, with listing price differentials capturing the majority of transaction price differentials. The remaining gap closes through longer time on lot and larger negotiated discounts for high-intensity thresholds. These findings suggest that threshold effects reflect deliberate consumer decision rules operating alongside perceptual bias, and that firms respond substantially, though not perfectly, to segment-level variation in consumer sensitivity.

title: Understanding and Steering Impulsive Purchases in Live Comme...
speaker: Keyi Jiang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in capturing rational decision-making. However, their capacity to understand irrational consumer behavior has received relatively limited systematic examination. Irrational choices are sparsely documented in training data, often appear as idiosyncratic deviations from aggregate patterns, and are driven by latent psychological and contextual factors that are difficult to encode. Yet, accurately modeling such behavior is critical for both firms that seek realistic “silicon samples” for large-scale experimentation and marketing optimization, and consumers, as LLM-based agents increasingly mediate purchasing decisions. This study investigates LLMs’ ability to predict, diagnose, and inform interventions for irrational consumer behavior in the context of TikTok (Douyin) live-stream commerce, where rapid, socially mediated interactions generate high-frequency impulsive purchases. We first compare baseline LLM models with traditional models optimized via hyperparameter tuning. Our results show that traditional models outperform baseline LLMs. However, an XGBoost-enhanced LLM, in which XGBoost predictions and their corresponding confidence intervals are incorporated into the prompt, significantly outperforms all standalone models. We further examine the mechanisms underlying this improvement. Attention map visualizations reveals that the performance gains arise not from overriding the LLM’s reasoning, but from recalibrating its allocation of attention: increasing focus on textual product cues while reducing reliance on influencer-level signals. Finally, we demonstrate an iterative LLM-based refinement procedure that proposes adjustments to product titles, reducing the likelihood of impulse-driven, high-return outcomes for high-risk products. Together, our findings clarify how LLMs can be systematically augmented to better capture irrational consumer behavior and inform actionable intervention design.

title: How Visual Designs Drive Success: Interpretable Generative A...
speaker: Lan Luo
abstract: Visual designs are often used in marketing (e.g., packaging, ads, media covers) to achieve a variety of business outcomes. Since designs are complex, unstructured data, it is difficult to determine what features drive their success in a way that is interpretable and managerially actionable. To address this challenge, I develop a novel methodological framework to automatically discover what interpretable features make visual designs in a given domain successful. I first leverage a deep generative text-to-image AI model that adopts the role of designer and enables visual designs to be described by low-dimensional design representations. Then, I apply a novel adaptation of cutting-edge "mechanistic interpretability" methods to scalably discover a taxonomy of interpretable and managerially relevant features predictive of success. Finally, I generate image redesigns by manipulating features of interest to help managers scalably pilot data-driven design changes. I apply this framework to discover how book cover redesigns predict sales on Amazon.com using a unique dataset I collected of over 160,000 books. I discover a diverse set of interpretable features related to illustration, typography, composition, and layout. In a holdout analysis with a rich set of control variables, including just 30 of these discovered features (out of 9,728) improves variation explained in sales by nearly as much as prices and by more than reviews. In a lab study, I find causal evidence that the proposed methodological framework can redesign covers to significantly improve consumer preferences, and that generative AI can help level the playing field in the publishing industry.

title: The Creator&Rsquo;S Paradox: Visual Framing as a Reputation ...
speaker: Guofeng Xiao
abstract: Influencers monetize authenticity, yet sponsorship disclosures often trigger “reputation burning,” eroding the very communal trust they rely on. We propose a “Visual Repletion” mechanism, positing that recovery requires visual strategies that precisely fill specific reputational deficits (Warmth vs. Competence) rather than universal aesthetic enhancements. Methodologically, we introduce an end-to-end “Abductive Discovery” pipeline for unstructured data. First, Measurement: We construct interpretable visual proxies from 16 million posts on Instagram using a hybrid architecture that combines Sparse β-VAE for unsupervised disentanglement and BLIP-2 for semantic grounding. Second, Discovery: We employ a probabilistic interaction engine to identify heterogeneous effects, using parametric bootstrapping to correct for measurement error in high-dimensional regressors strictly. Third, Validation: To establish causality, we overcome the identification challenge in visual experiments by deploying a Generative AI Landing Page RCT. Leveraging Stable Diffusion XL, ControlNet, and IP-Adapter, we exogenously manipulate visual framing while mathematically preserving influencer identity and scene composition. Our findings confirm that visual signaling is compensatory: “Warmth” strategies drive engagement recovery only for influencers with baseline warmth deficits. This research bridges deep learning and causal inference, offering a blueprint for rigorous “Generative Marketing Science”.

title: Agentic AI for Marketing Video Analytics: Application to Liv...
speaker: Jia Liu
abstract: Video content such as short-form social media clips and livestream commerce has become central to contemporary digital marketing, serving not just as visual media but as strategic vehicles for narratives, persuasion, and product demonstration. Standard Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) are limited in capturing these marketing-relevant elements because prompt-based approaches often miss persuasive logic and produce factually weak outputs. To address this gap, we develop a Reflexive Agentic Measurement Framework tailored to marketing video analytics. The framework involves nine AI agents in two phases. The first phase constructs agent behavior, involving iteratively discovering latent narratives and persuasive cues and then autonomously generating context-aware coding prompts. The second phase generates and verifies content analysis: decomposing marketing videos into discrete propositions tied to key marketing elements and validating each element against the raw footage to ensure factual reliability. Applying this framework to 5,000 livestream commerce videos, we show that it delivers richer and more accurate descriptions of marketing strategies—such as dynamic screen layouts, product effect demonstrations, and narrative framing—than standard prompt-based methods and human-crafted baselines. Our approach also achieves this at a low marginal cost per video minute ($0.005 per video minute), offering a scalable methodology for automated marketing video coding. By enabling systematic measurement of previously elusive strategic elements in marketing videos, this research advances measurement tools for digital marketing and supports data-driven investigations into the drivers of video marketing effectiveness.

title: Embedding the Basket: Integrating Graph Neural Networks into...
speaker: Qiang (Steven) Lu
abstract: Consumers build baskets of interdependent products, but traditional models struggle at scale, relying on sparse co-purchase data and strong assumptions that make cross-category effects difficult to estimate.  This paper proposes a two-stage hybrid framework that integrates Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with a conditional logit model to address these challenges. In the first stage, a GNN is used to construct low-dimensional embeddings of product relationships based on co-purchase behavior, using a DeepWalk-based random walk approach. In the second stage, these embeddings are built into a conditional logit model as cross-effect parameters, enabling scalable, data-driven estimation of interdependent category choices. Empirical results using a large retail transactional dataset with 23,812 unique products and 2,012 unique product categories demonstrate that the proposed model with graph embedding cross-effects significantly outperforms traditional discrete choice models in measuring basket composition. The model improves computation efficiency, explanatory power, and interpretability, offering practical solutions for category management and inventory decisions. Overall, this study contributes a novel method for uncovering complex product relationships and advancing basket-level consumer choice modeling, providing a foundation for future extensions using end-to-end deep learning architectures.

title: Consumer Responses to AI Involvement in Product Creation
speaker: Meng Zhu
abstract: Across multiple studies, we examine how consumers respond to AI involvement in product creation. Participants evaluated products described as involving varying degrees of AI use and could financially support the creator. Consistently, introducing AI reduced consumer support relative to human-only creation. This effect was categorical rather than continuous: support declined once AI was present, regardless of the degree of involvement. Exploratory tests suggest that this response is not explained by perceived effort, labor, or creativity contributions. The findings highlight a robust form of consumer aversion to AI involvement with implications for emerging AI-enabled offerings.

title: Eis-Enhanced Doubly Robust Evaluation for AI Marketing Syste...
speaker: Jian Ni
abstract: AI marketing systems, such as sequential recommendation engines, cross-market ML deployment, and graph-based social targeting, promise transformative personalization but resist reliable offline evaluation. Standard off-policy evaluation fails precisely where it matters most: importance weights explode over long RL horizons, covariate shift destabilizes transported ML models, and network interference requires intractable integration over latent social structure. We develop an AI-native evaluation framework integrating Efficient Importance Sampling (EIS) with doubly robust estimation. EIS constructs variance-minimizing proposals that stabilize sequential policy evaluation, enable reliable cross-market transportability assessment, and via block-structured extensions, tractably handle network spillovers. When policy divergence is extreme, optional geometric tempering provides additional robustness. The framework achieves much variance reduction with practical diagnostics guiding offline versus online evaluation decisions, which enables reliable assessment of thousands of AI policies from a single experiment and dramatically compressing the marketing AI development cycle.

title: Targeting Adaptive Consumers: How Exploration-Exploitation D...
speaker: Ting-Tse Chen
abstract: Heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) estimation is foundational to personalized marketing, yet standard approaches model consumers as static entities characterized by time-invariant covariates. We introduce a framework that incorporates behavioral dynamics from reinforcement learning into causal targeting. Our core proposition: a consumer's conditional average treatment effect (CATE) is moderated by their latent learning state, specifically, their position along the exploration-exploitation continuum. We operationalize this through theory-driven proxies for behavioral uncertainty, including entropy-based measures of choice variability, integrated within a Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML) estimator. Across extensive simulations spanning heterogeneous data-generating processes, we establish that stratifying on exploration state yields improvements in targeting precision relative to covariate-based baselines. A key methodological finding emerges: under non-stationary environments, parsimonious behavioral features dominate sequential deep learning architectures (Transformers) in CATE estimation. Oracle bounds reveal fundamental identifiability limits—path-dependent treatment response heterogeneity exists beyond what reduced-form behavioral summaries can recover. We validate the framework on a large-scale retail dataset, demonstrating actionable lift improvements.

title: From Aesthetics to Analytics: Measuring Product Design with ...
speaker: Wenshu Zhang
abstract: This study develops a framework for incorporating large language models (LLM)–derived representations of product aesthetics into empirical analyses of market outcomes in the automobile industry. We show how LLMs can be used to extract and structure high-dimensional aesthetic information from unstructured product descriptions and images, and integrate these representations with conventional product attributes in quantitative marketing models. Rather than treating aesthetics as an isolated driver of demand, the proposed approach positions aesthetic features as part of a broader product attribute space, allowing researchers to examine how design-related information complements standard observables and competitive structure. More broadly, this work illustrates how LLM-based measurement can extend existing empirical frameworks by enabling the systematic use of rich unstructured data without altering their underlying economic foundations.

title: Beyond Single LLMs: Using Model Ensembles to Improve Synthet...
speaker: Sedigheh Monavari
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential surrogates for human participants, offering inexpensive, rapid, and scalable data generation. Existing research has largely evaluated single LLMs in isolation, focusing on single-model performance and overlooking gains from combining models. This paper investigates the gains from multi-model synthesis. Utilizing a dataset of approximately 20 established marketing experiments, we compare human responses with synthetic data generated by leading LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok) under varied prompting strategies. Using Prediction-Powered Inference, we combine human samples (N = 300–500) with LLM-generated responses to assess whether hybrid designs can reduce reliance on human data. Principal Component Analysis reveals that while LLMs share over 50% of variance on a common "bias dimension," multi-factor representations significantly outperform single-factor models. Our empirical results demonstrate that multi-model ensembles improve correlations with human data from r ≈ .15–.20 for single LLMs to r ≈ .30–.35, representing a 75–100% relative improvement over single models. However, we find that absolute correlations remain modest, providing limited gains in narrowing confidence intervals. We conclude by proposing a simple and low-cost approach for combining multiple LLMs inputs, which improves alignment with human data and can be readily implemented in marketing research and practice. Keywords: large language models, synthetic data, marketing experiments, prediction-powered inference, digital twins

title: When Hallucination of LLMs Leads to Creative Idea
speaker: Minkyu Shin
abstract: Large language models often produce hallucinations—statements that are incorrect yet linguistically coherent. In this paper, we argue that such outputs can have systematic creative value. We model an LLM response as a stochastic suggestion generated by high-dimensional text associations, making the output typically near a user’s conceptual neighborhood and therefore plausibly true ex ante. A user observes the suggestion but not its correctness and chooses whether to incur a verification-and-repair cost. Verification can (i) reject the literal claim while (ii) uncovering an intermediate chain of valid associations that yields a usable idea. We characterize when a false-but-plausible suggestion increases expected innovation relative to no suggestion, and how the effect varies across users with different knowledge depth, breadth, and checking technologies.

title: Do LLMs Cannibalize Search?: Evidence from Italy's ChatGPT B...
speaker: Marc Enrico Pocsay
abstract: This study investigates whether large language models (LLMs), particularly ChatGPT, substitute for traditional web search engines by exploiting Italy’s temporary ban on ChatGPT in April 2023 as a quasi-natural experiment. Using a proprietary weekly Google AdSense panel comprising over 13,000 web domains across the United States, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom,we implement a difference-in-differences design with event-study diagnostics to estimate the causal impact of LLM availability on search activity. The results show that during the one-month ban, total search impressions in Italy increased by approximately 1.1%, while impressions declined by 1.3% following the restoration of ChatGPT access, indicating net substitution between LLMs and search engines. Disaggregating by query intent reveals that the substitution effect is concentrated in informational and commercial searches, which rose by 3.6% and 1.9% respectively during the ban. In contrast, navigational and transactional queries exhibit no statistically significant changes, suggesting that LLMs primarily displace exploratory and synthesis-heavy information-seeking behavior rather than action-oriented searches. Robustness checks using click data produce consistent directional effects, though with reduced statistical precision. Overall, the findings provide market-scale causal evidence that LLMs alter consumer reliance on traditional search engines in intent-specific ways. The study highlights that while generative AI competes with search engines for early-stage informational queries, high-value transactional search remains resilient, with important implications for digital platforms, advertisers, and policymakers navigating the evolving AI-driven information ecosystem.

title: LLM-Consensus Filtering as An Upstream Fix for Noisy Marketi...
speaker: Lavy Khoushinsky
abstract: Topic models do not fail because they cannot cluster; they fail because they are asked to cluster the wrong corpus. In marketing settings where meaning is implicit, sarcastic, or politically entangled, lexicon-based scraping becomes a gatekeeper that misses the very discourse researchers care about (Humphreys and Wang, 2017; Berger et al., 2022). We introduce a scalable workflow that treats large language models (LLMs) not as topic generators, but as high-precision semantic filters that upgrade the curation layer upstream of topic discovery. Using Reddit discourse around Nike’s 2018 Dream Crazy campaign (n≈76.9k) (Hydock et al., 2020), we implement a three-stage pipeline: (1) zero-shot “aboutness” adjudication by 6 LLMs with majority-vote consensus to reduce idiosyncratic errors (Chae and Davidson, 2023); (2) teacher–student distillation, training a logistic classifier on sentence embeddings to approximate the ensemble at scale (Miric et al., 2023); and (3) precision-first seeding (≥0.90 precision) followed by embedding-based semantic expansion to recover euphemistic, stance-based, and indirect references that omit surface markers. LLM consensus aligns strongly with human judgments (κ = 0.805). The distilled classifier reaches 0.90 accuracy on holdout data, enabling full-corpus filtering at low cost. Precision-thresholding yields a high-purity seed set (n = 500), and semantic expansion produces a coherent curated corpus of 5,712 posts that captures indirect campaign talk while reducing irrelevant Nike chatter relative to dictionary scraping. We show that LLMs add the most value to topic modeling not by replacing clustering, but by making corpus inclusion lexicon-free, auditable, and robust to vocabulary drift.

title: The Impact of Sustainability Claims in Advertisements on Bra...
speaker: Maren Becker
abstract: Sustainability-related claims have become increasingly prevalent in brand advertising, yet evidence on their effectiveness remains limited. In particular, it is unclear whether such claims improve brand performance, create positive spillovers for sustainability (e.g., increased sustainable purchases, reduced emissions), or how their impact depends on the broader public discourse on sustainability. This study quantifies the dynamic effects of sustainability claims in television advertising on brand-level and societal outcomes, while explicitly accounting for the intensity and tone of sustainability-related media coverage. The authors analyze a comprehensive dataset linking 20,000+ TV advertisements to brand outcomes (mindset metrics and sales for 380 FMCG brands) and societal outcomes (e.g., the share of sustainable products in household purchases across 20,000+ brands, green party voting) in Germany from 2013–2023. Sustainability cues are measured using machine learning models that process video, audio, and text from ad creatives. The broader sustainability discourse is measured using sustainability-related articles from several major German newspapers (via Nexis Uni), with debate intensity captured through article volume and debate tone through sentiment analysis. The authors develop a dynamic advertising response model with time-varying elasticities, allowing advertising effectiveness to vary as a function of sustainability cues and contemporaneous media coverage volume and sentiment. The model jointly captures direct brand effects and indirect societal spillovers while controlling for time trends and major environmental events.

title: When AI Bites Back: The Hidden Consequences of AI in Food De...
speaker: Yumeng Zhang
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly adopted by on-demand food delivery platforms to improve routing efficiency and delivery-time estimation accuracy. While these improvements can enhance consumer satisfaction, they also exacerbate time pressure on couriers, raising operational and ethical concerns. We develop a game-theoretic model to study the interaction between a platform and a freelance courier. The platform determines a buffer time added to the estimated time of arrival (ETA) augmented by AI, while the courier decides whether to accept the order and how fast to deliver. We characterize four behavioral regions for the courier (i.e., comfort, speed-up, penalty-tolerating, and rejection) based on ETA tightness and lateness penalties. Our results show that AI efficiency does not raise the courier’s payoff, nor does it guarantee a monotonic increase in the platform’s payoff. A “penalty trap” can arise when lateness penalties are low for couriers but high for the platform, generating tighter ETAs that cause more late deliveries and reduced platform payoff. By extending the analysis from a single-order to a multi-order setting, we show how these effects accumulate at the system level. These findings highlight the need to align AI-augmented targets with human capabilities and incentive choices to ensure fair and sustainable outcomes.

title: How to Get Rich on Spotify... Without Being a Famous Musicia...
speaker: Jakob Zgonc
abstract: On music streaming platforms, the prevalent pro-rata remuneration model pays artists by their share of total streams. This incentivizes illicit actors to inflate streams with automated "listeners", diluting payouts for legitimate artists. Tens of thousands of new uploads every day and low-quality AI-generated music ("AI slop") create a large long tail with content that is barely listened to by humans. This makes coordinated fraud easy to scale and hard to distinguish from organic low-demand listening. Platform countermeasures remain opaque, and the extent of coordinated fraud is unknown. We develop a scalable fraud-detection approach, which tackles two challenges: the lack of ground truth for supervised calibration, and limited effectiveness of spike-based anomaly detection when bot activity is dispersed across many artists and tracks. We shift the unit of analysis from individual tracks or artists to portfolios. For a scheme to be profitable, listener accounts must be reused across multiple target artists, creating a distinctive co-listening structure. We leverage this insight to identify suspicious artist communities and refine our network-based approach with listener counts and geographic concentration. We apply our method to 4.5 million active artists on Spotify and validate flagged communities through independent industry-expert assessments. Preliminary results reveal numerous active communities exhibiting patterns of coordinated artificial streaming. Evasion would require reducing listener reuse, which raises costs and lowers expected payouts. Thus, coordinated fraud leaves structural traces even when individual bot behavior is engineered to appear organic. Our method complements track-level approaches and is portable across platforms without internal ground truth.

title: AI Personalization in Data-Scarce Markets
speaker: Yixiang Xu
abstract: This paper investigates the effectiveness of AI trained on public web data for personalization in data-scarce markets. I develop a theoretical framework showing how two fundamental aspects of data scarcity and AI algorithms’ tendency to default to dominant patterns interact to determine personalization effectiveness. Data representation gaps arise when user segments are absent from training data; data precision gaps occur when existing user data provides noisy preference signal. I test this framework through a large-scale field experiment with 30,111 retail merchants in India. Results reveal that only merchants facing minimal data gaps show significant sales improvements (+0.23 standard deviations). As data gaps intensify, AI defaults to serving merchants broadly appealing content rather than delivering tailored content. Merchants facing representation gaps receive further poorly matched content due to algorithmic misalignment. I propose two targeted augmentation strategies to mitigate this problem: integrating local data and enabling user agency. Using data from the experiment, I show that the approaches are effective, highlighting the value of theory-based AI personalization in data-scarce environments.

title: Exploring Digital Voice Assistants: Factors Shaping Customer...
speaker: Mahlakane Mafoko
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping global fashion retail by transforming how consumers search for information, interact with brands, and complete online shopping tasks. As digital voice assistants (DVAs) become increasingly integrated into e‑commerce environments, understanding the factors that influence their adoption and the resulting customer experience is essential. This study investigates technological, experiential, and social‑relational drivers of DVA adoption in online fashion shopping. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), and Consumption Value Theory, the research develops an integrated framework that captures utilitarian, emotional, and social dimensions of consumer behaviour. Para‑social interaction, perceived intelligence, animacy, and anthropomorphism are incorporated to reflect the human‑AI relational dynamics shaping consumer engagement. The study also introduces accent as a moderating variable, addressing emerging evidence that linguistic cues influence user perceptions of credibility, intelligence, and social presence. Using data from an online survey completed by 444 respondents across South Africa, the study employed Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS‑SEM) to test the proposed research model. Results found that DVAs are driven by perceived usefulness, ease of use, customer experience, perceived intelligence, convenience value, and para‑social interactions. Consumption values, particularly functional and conditional value enhance customer experience. The findings advance AI-enabled retail literature by highlighting the importance of experiential and human‑like factors in technology adoption. Managerial insights emphasise the strategic design and deployment of DVAs to enhance customer experience and support digital transformation in fashion retail.

title: Voice Modality in Conversational Commerce with AI Chatbots
speaker: Ashwi...
abstract: Conversational commerce has evolved rapidly, with over eight billion voice-enabled devices in circulation globally. Yet, leading platforms like Amazon’s Alexa have struggled to achieve commercial viability, incurring significant losses due to the inherent limitations of voice-only interfaces in facilitating complex purchase decisions. As the industry shifts toward multimodal AI chatbots that integrate voice, text, and visual cues, retailers face a critical question: how do distinct input modalities influence consumer outcomes? This research investigates the trade-offs between voice and text inputs within hybrid e-commerce interfaces. While voice input offers speed and heightened social presence, we identify a countervailing force: ‘vocal cognitive costs.’ These costs arise from the cognitive load required to plan spoken queries without the ability to pause or edit, and the attention diverted to monitor real-time transcription accuracy. We propose that the impact of these vocal cognitive costs is not static but varies systematically across the customer journey. We argue that during the exploration and re-engagement phases, where curiosity and enjoyment drive interaction, the social benefits of voice outweigh its costs. Conversely, during the purchase decision phase, where consumers prioritize precision and control, vocal cognitive costs become prohibitive, making text the superior modality. This framework provides a theoretical basis for understanding multimodal interactions and offers actionable guidelines for designing AI-mediated customer experiences that align input modalities with specific journey stages.

title: When and How Should Firms use AI for Creative Tasks? The Rol...
speaker: Sara Caprioli
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used by firms to perform creative tasks across domains. For example, firms rely on AI to develop food recipes, design fashion items, and support architectural design. Despite these advances, consumers often remain skeptical of AI-generated creative work. This skepticism matters because AI-driven creativity only creates value if consumers perceive AI-generated outputs as valuable. This research examines when and why consumers evaluate AI-generated creative work more favorably and how firms can increase such evaluations. Drawing on the dual-pathway to creativity model, we distinguish between tasks driven by persistence—systematic, iterative exploration within a defined problem space (e.g., optimizing a kitchen layout by refining spatial arrangements, storage, and workflow)—and flexibility, which relies on associative, divergent thinking (e.g., developing an original kitchen concept or aesthetic that combines distant styles or themes). We propose that consumers evaluate the quality of AI-generated work more positively when the task relies on persistence rather than flexibility. Across nine studies (N = 2,000), using experimental and field data across diverse contexts, we find that AI-generated outputs are perceived as higher quality and more likely to be chosen when creativity stems from persistence-based processes. Importantly, highlighting the persistence-based nature of the creative process increases perceived quality and choice of AI-generated outputs. These findings offer actionable guidance on (1) which creative tasks are best suited for AI, (2) how firms should communicate AI’s role in creative processes, and (3) how to design interventions that enhance consumer acceptance of AI-generated creative work.

title: Human&Ndash;AI Co-Creation in User Design: How Feelings of A...
speaker: Eva Pflanzer
abstract: Consumers frequently pay a premium for products they have participated in designing. Such higher valuations stem from both outcome-related factors, such as preference fit, and process-related factors, particularly feelings of accomplishment. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to improve user-design outcomes but may also undermine process-related sources of value creation. Drawing on self-signaling theory, we examine consumer–AI cocreation in user design and investigate how outcome- and process-related factors jointly shape consumers’ willingness to pay. Across two online experiments, we show that high preference fit increases consumers’ willingness to pay for self-designed products indirectly by enhancing feelings of accomplishment. Importantly, this causal pathway remains robust across different levels of AI support (high vs. low) and across different AI interaction formats (text vs. sketch prompting). In addition, sketch-based prompting (vs. text prompting) increases users’ perceived contribution to the design outcome and further strengthens feelings of accomplishment. These findings contribute to the literature on user design and mass customization by demonstrating a causal link between preference fit and accomplishment in AI-supported co-creation. They also offer managerial implications by showing that effective AI-supported user design requires both preference-congruent outcomes and interaction formats that make consumers’ creative contributions salient.

title: Sharing Choice Responsibility with AI: How Chatbot Identity ...
speaker: Yijia Sun
abstract: Despite the widespread adoption of AI-powered chatbots across industries, consumers often find chatbots as incapable of understanding and responding to personalized requests, resulting in reluctance to interact with chatbots and resistance towards chatbot-generated advice. To improve the effectiveness of chatbots, this study examines the role of chatbot identity in shaping consumer responses towards recommendations provided by chatbots. Across seven studies, we demonstrate that specialist (vs. generalist) chatbots are more effective in enhancing consumers’ intention to follow chatbot-generated recommendations. This effect occurs because specialist chatbots are more capable of sharing consumers’ choice responsibility during decision-making. Furthermore, the advantage of specialist chatbots is more prominent when choice involves a high (vs. low) level of uncertainty. Importantly, while specialist chatbots increase consumers’ recommendation adherence intention, they are more susceptible to blame for service failures. Our findings contribute to the emerging research on human-AI interaction by examining chatbot identity as a critical determinant of chatbot effectiveness and identifying choice responsibility as a valuable lens to understand chatbot effects.

title: Genai Product Recommendations for Sustainable Consumer Decis...
speaker: Alexander Meister
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) becomes deeply integrated into marketing practices. Research has so far largely focused on algorithmic recommendation systems, while consumers increasingly leverage conversational generative AI tools such as ChatGPT to seek advice in purchase decision-making. Hence, scholars emphasize the transformative potential of generative AI to reshape consumer behavior through personalized recommendations and technology interactions; however, further in-depth research is needed. Therefore, this study adopts a qualitative, inductive approach based on interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) while employing a quasi-experimental research design involving ChatGPT interaction scenarios. Doing so, we explore how consumers experience generative AI interactions and how they make sense of the given recommendations for sustainable products across different recommendation styles. IPA, as the chosen methodological approach, enables an in-depth understanding of participants’ subjective perceptions and sense-making of their interactions with the generative AI tool (ChatGPT) in product-related advisory situations, reconstructing how participants interpret and assign meaning to their experiences. Sustainable consumer decision-making is chosen as the research context, providing a personally and socially relevant setting. Specifically, we draw on parasocial relationship theory to investigate how a parasocial relationship with the AI chatbot is experienced during interaction and how the perceived recommendations shape the development of sustainable purchase intentions. Based on our analysis, we uncover key mechanisms and develop a framework illustrating consumers’ sense-making of AI-mediated interaction and recommendations in sustainable decision-making.

title: The Price of Ethical Coherence in Charitable Giving
speaker: Roman Antoschin
abstract: Charities face the challenge of designing elements of fundraising communications— including images and texts—that attract donations and maintain ethical coherence, meaning they are perceived as ethically acceptable. While financial success can be objectively measured, ethical coherence is a matter of perspective, varying between stakeholders, and is more difficult to assess. Past research suggests that these goals often conflict; however, the price of ethical coherence—that is, the opportunity cost of maintaining ethical coherence in terms of foregone donations—has yet to be quantified. The authors (1) propose a framework to measure the price of ethical coherence by combining a field experiment with survey data, (2) demonstrate its application across communication elements, and (3) show how the framework helps derive personalized campaigns. Given that traditional data collection can be costly and timeconsuming, the authors (4) examine whether large language models can serve as artificial experts to predict ethical perceptions and donation responses, offering a scalable shortcut for exploratory testing. To demonstrate the practicality of the proposed framework, the authors partnered with an international charity. The framework reveals that the price of ethical coherence varies across communication elements and depends on donors’ proximity to the charity, offering valuable insights for marketing strategies.

title: Why Not Come in and Talk? Quantifying the Impact of Nonanswe...
speaker: Yinfei Jiang
abstract: In high-involvement purchases, sales–customer interactions play a central role in shaping whether consumers progress from initial interest to offline conversion. After customers leave contact information, the first substantive interaction typically occurs through outbound sales calls, whose primary objective is to move customers from remote inquiry to an in-person dealership visit. During these calls, customers often request concrete, decision-relevant information. Yet salespeople sometimes respond without fully resolving the request within the call; we refer to such responses as nonanswers. Using proprietary outbound call transcripts from a leading automotive manufacturer, we document a counterintuitive pattern: calls that contain nonanswers are followed by higher dealership-visit rates than otherwise comparable calls. To study this relationship at scale, we combine large language models with causal inference designs to measure nonanswer usage, conversational topics, and within-call changes in visit intention, and link these process measures to both intention-based and realized behavioral outcomes. Across multiple identification strategies and robustness analyses, nonanswers are associated with a 2.3% higher probability of a subsequent dealership visit. We provide direct process evidence for a novel engagement mechanism. By leaving key information temporarily unresolved while remaining action-oriented, nonanswers stimulate customers’ interest and curiosity, leading them to ask more follow-up questions toward the end of the call. This heightened questioning behavior strongly predicts subsequent dealership visits and mediates the effect of nonanswers on offline conversion. The findings show that strategically incomplete responses can shape offline conversion not by reducing uncertainty, but by sustaining engagement and extending the decision process beyond the call.
